News.title: Married doctor who Lucy Letby was ‘infatuated’ with could be identified if Lucy Letby has retrial, says Tory MP
News.content:
LUCY Letby campaigner David Davis MP says the anonymity order given to a doctor she was infatuated with is likely to be reviewed in the wake of his death.

The MP said it could take place at any future retrial.



The Sun on Sunday revealed how the medic, who was granted anonymity and referred to in court as Doctor A, died last month.

Mr Davies said: “I don’t think this changes much, I assume that the anonymity orders will be reviewed in the event of a retrial.”



At trial, prosecutors alleged Lucy would create “crisis situations” to gain his sympathy.

Her supporters later turned on him because he said in court that she might have “manipulated” him.



The married registrar – known as Doctor A – previously gave evidence against Letby during her trial for the murder of seven babies and the attempted murder of seven others.

It is understood the medic – who was in his 50s – had been ill before passing away last month.

Prosecutors alleged Letby was infatuated with the physician and would create “crisis situations” by attacking infants to ensure he would be bleeped to attend.

Although the pair exchanged 1,300 messages and enjoyed day trips to London, Letby denied a romance and insisted they were simply “trusted friends”.



The 2024 Thirlwall Inquiry later found the doctor had been “misled” and “maybe manipulated” into giving Letby information about the babies she had attacked.

Letby continues to claim her innocence while serving a whole-life sentence at Bronzefield Prison.

News.title: Brit teen, 16, dead and two siblings badly injured after ‘terrible accident’ on family holiday as tributes pour in
News.content:
'FOREVER LOVED' Brit teen, 16, dead and two siblings badly injured after ‘terrible accident’ on family holiday as tributes pour in

A TEENAGE girl has died in a “terrible accident” and two siblings were badly injured while on a family holiday, as tributes flood in.

Abbie Lainton, 16, from Swindon, Wiltshire, died while on vacation in the Dominican Republic on July 30.

A GoFundMe page, which was set up to help her family has already received more than £5,000 in donations.



The fundraiser was set up by Becky Jamieson, who described Abbie as someone who was loved by everyone who knew her.



Becky said: “On July 30, 2026, Abbie Lainton tragically lost her life in a terrible accident while on holiday in the Dominican Republic.

“Becky and Gary have lost their beautiful 16-year-old daughter, and Carley and Bradley were also badly injured in the accident.

“Abbie had her whole life ahead of her. She should have been enjoying the summer with her friends and looking forward to receiving her GCSE results.



“She was so loved by her family, friends and everyone who knew her.

“This page has been set up to support the family through this unimaginable time.

“For Abbie, forever 16, forever loved and never forgotten.”

Abbie’s former school Tanwood School for Performing Arts, paid tribute to her in a statement.



A spokesperson said: “Abbie joined Tanwood as a dinky dot and was part of an exceptional group of dancers who formed strong friendships which spilled over to the audience when they performed together.

“She always performed with a huge smile, and those beautiful feet.

“We are all in complete shock at this heartbreaking news and send so much love and support to her family and friends at this unimaginable time.

“You will always be in our hearts.”

Abbie joined Swindon Lightning Cheerleading club at a later date where she excelled and took part in competitions around the world.



The club invited people to come together and remember Abbie as well as celebrate her life and share memories.

A spokesperson for the club said: “There are simply no words that feel enough.

“Abbie was a much-loved member of our Swindon Lightning family.

“Her kindness, infectious smile, unwavering encouragement and love for cheerleading touched the lives of so many athletes, coaches and families over the years.

“She brought so much light to our gym, and her loss has left us all heartbroken.”

“Our thoughts, love and deepest condolences are with Abbie’s family and loved ones during this unimaginable time.”

News.title: Islamist terrorists who plotted to blow up 10 planes must not be eligible for early release from prison
News.content:
Too dangerous

IT could have been the worst mass murder in criminal history.

A gang of Islamist terrorists plotted to blow ten passenger jets out of the sky with liquid explosives smuggled through Heathrow disguised in hand luggage as drinks, shampoo and toothpaste.



Had the plot succeeded, up to 10,000 innocent people could have been killed — three times the death toll of the 9/11 attacks on New York’s Twin Towers.

Britain was spared that unimaginable slaughter thanks to the bravery, skill and ingenuity of MI5 and the police, who smashed the conspiracy just days before the planned attacks.



But three of the men convicted of conspiracy to murder — Waheed Zaman, Ibrahim Savant and Arafat Waheed Khan — could soon be eligible for parole after serving 20 years of their life terms.

These were not misguided young men caught up in some minor offence.

They were convicted of planning mass murder on an appalling scale.

All three recorded “martyrdom” videos, intended to be released by al-Qaeda after the attacks.

The British public has had enough of violent criminals being released early while victims and their families are left to live with the consequences.

The Parole Board must not allow pressure to ease prison overcrowding to cloud their cold-headed judgment when considering these cases.



Some prisoners are just too dangerous to release.

These terrorists should be among them.

Off to prison

BRITAIN’S overcrowded prisons are at breaking point — yet 10,000 foreign lags are taking up scarce places.

Most of them would have been booted out long ago if their home countries had agreed to take them back.

Instead, the Government has been forced to free thousands of offenders early to stop the system collapsing.



So Nigel Farage’s idea to ship foreign convicts to serve their sentences 5,500 miles away in the grim jails of El Salvador is worth exploring.

It would end the sickening spectacle of violent crooks being freed halfway through their sentence.

And make foreign visitors think twice about bringing criminal activities to Britain.

Back to work

FRESH back from holiday, Andy Burnham will embark on a cost of living tour tomorrow — and recycle an idea first unveiled by Sir Keir Starmer three years ago.

He will re-announce plans to end “subscription traps” which deliberately make it tricky for people to stop recurring charges after ordering online.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Perhaps when he’s delivered his latest “easy win”, the PM might find time to turn his mind to more pressing issues.

Like the economy, illegal migration, hospital waiting lists and rebuilding our hollowed-out Armed Forces.

News.title: Andy Burnham kicks off cost-of-living tour with reheated Labour pledge to crack down on subscription traps
News.content:
ANDY Burnham will kick off his cost-of- living tour tomorrow with a reheated pledge first announced by Labour in 2023.

The PM is promising to end so-called subscription traps that lure customers into costly and hard-to-cancel online plans for the likes of streaming services.



Back from his holiday, Mr Burnham will accuse Westminster of “telling people that everyday hassles like this are just part of life” for too long.

But the crackdown on subscription traps was first unveiled by Sir Keir Starmer three years ago and started in April before his resignation.



It will force companies to give customers clearer information when subscriptions are automatically renewed at a higher cost, and impose a 14-day cooling-off period allowing them to cancel after a trial.

Like Sir Keir — who was seen playing football yesterday in an Arsenal strip — Mr Burnham claims this will save an average £14 a month for every unwanted subscription, ending an estimated total of £1.6billion a year being wasted.



The only difference in the cut-and-paste policy appears to be the PM bringing forward the date from spring next year to January.

Mr Burnham is also announcing plans to end rip-off discounts whereby sellers deliberately raise their prices before slashing them to give the impression of a bargain.

He will launch a consultation to see whether such practices should be banned by law.

Tory Shadow Chancellor Sir Mel Stride said: “Burnham has already run out of ideas.



“Labour’s tax hikes have sent costs soaring for hardworking families and destroyed jobs.

“Consultations and reheated measures won’t make up for that.”

News.title: Terrorists who planned to kill thousands in liquid bomb jet plot could be freed in WEEKS as they launch parole bids
News.content:
THREE Al-Qaeda terrorists who were part of the infamous plot to blow up airliners with liquid explosives could be released back on the streets within weeks.

Their 2006 al-Qaeda-inspired plan to hide liquid explosives in drinks bottles changed air travel around the world.



It also sparked airport chaos, cost airlines millions and ultimately forced the aviation industry to invest in sophisticated new scanners.

All three, who are British citizens of Pakistani descent, are now ­eligible to ask the Parole Board to decide whether the danger they once represented can safely be managed outside prison.



They were sentenced to life with a minimum of 20 years after a jury heard they recorded chilling “martyrdom videos” in preparation for suicide attacks.

Ibrahim Savant, of Stoke Newington, North London, Arafat Waheed Khan and Waheed Zaman, both of Walthamstow, East London, were recruited by Abdulla Ahmed Ali.



Zaman has a Parole Board hearing listed for September 7.

Khan’s case will be considered on September 21, while Savant is due before the board on November 12.

If the Parole Board considers them rehabilitated they could be freed by Christmas.

Reform UK’s home affairs spokesperson Zia Yusuf said last night: “The public will be rightly appalled that these appalling individuals could soon be back on our streets.



“Our justice system is fundamentally broken when people convicted of conspiracy to commit mass murder on such a terrifying scale are even considered for release. They should be locked up for life.”

Tory Shadow Justice Secretary Nick Timothy added: “It’s unconscionable that Islamist terrorists — who planned to blow up planes, killing hundreds of innocent civilians — should be let out of prison.

“If they are, the public will rightly be outraged.”



Police moved against the plotters on August 10, 2006, amid fears that an attack could be imminent.

The UK terror threat level was raised to “critical” and normal hand luggage was initially banned from flights leaving British airports.

Thousands of passengers were caught in huge queues in the peak summer holiday season.



British Airways cancelled 1,280 flights in eight days and later estimated that the disruption had cost it £40million.

The conspirators planned to manufacture bombs using liquid explosives which could be concealed inside bottles of drinks including Oasis and Lucozade.

The main charges were to contain hydrogen peroxide and other chemicals capable of producing the highly unstable explosive TATP.

Small detonators fashioned using components from disposable cameras could then have been used to ­trigger explosions in mid-air.

Within months, restrictions were introduced limiting liquids in hand luggage to containers of no more than 100ml, which had to be presented for security screening inside transparent one-litre plastic bags.



Bottles of water were routinely surrendered at airport security.

Shampoo, toothpaste, deodorant, perfume, suncream and cosmetics were decanted into tiny containers.

The annoying and time- consuming process became as familiar to holidaymakers as passports and boarding cards.



Manufacturers and retailers responded with travel-sized ­toiletries, while passengers also bought empty 100ml bottles and transparent security bags.

The global market for such items is now valued at £5.7billion.

Airports have since spent millions installing CT security scanners capable of detecting liquid explosives technology, which is finally allowing some of the restrictions to be relaxed.

Yet the scale of the atrocity which prompted them could have been almost unimaginable.

The plot centred on plans to destroy multiple passenger aircraft travelling simultaneously from Britain to the US and Canada.



Flights from Heathrow to San Francisco, Toronto, Montreal, Chicago, Washington DC and New York were among those considered.

Investigators discovered discussions involving an operation which could potentially have used up to 18 suicide bombers.

Six suspects recorded martyrdom videos denouncing the West and explaining their willingness to die.

The recordings were intended to be distributed by al-Qaeda supporters after the attacks.

At the centre of the conspiracy was Abdulla Ahmed Ali.



Ali and fellow plotters Assad Sarwar and Tanvir Hussain were eventually convicted of conspiring specifically to murder passengers by detonating liquid bombs aboard transatlantic aircraft.

Ali was sentenced to life with a minimum term of 40 years.

Sarwar received a minimum of 36 years and Hussain 32 years.

Another conspirator, Umar Islam, was convicted of conspiracy to murder and sentenced to life with a minimum term of 22 years.



But bringing Savant, Khan and Zaman to justice proved consider-ably more complicated.

They were cleared of conspiring specifically to blow up aircraft after prosecutors failed to prove they knew the intended targets of the suicide operation were airliners.



But the Crown argued that the evidence nevertheless showed each had committed himself to taking part in a murderous suicide attack.

Then-Director of Public Prosecutions Sir Keir Starmer authorised the exceptional step of seeking another trial after deciding there remained a realistic prospect of conviction.

In 2010 a third jury convicted all three of conspiracy to murder.

Jailing the trio for life, Mr Justice Holroyde told them: “Each of you agreed to join with others in this conspiracy, with each of you intending that you would kill members of the general public and yourselves by acting as a suicide bomber.”

The three are now eligible to ask the Parole Board to decide if the danger they once represented can safely be managed outside prison.



But Ghaffar Hussain, a former counter-terror officer on the Government’s Prevent programme, told The Sun: “For terrorists who intended on killing hundreds of innocent people, life sentences should mean lifelong imprisonment.

“Threat assessment with such individuals is notoriously difficult and released terrorists have reoffended before. We need to be very careful.”

The Parole Board said: “Reviews are undertaken thoroughly and with extreme care. Protecting the public is our number one priority.”

News.title: Andy Burnham’s ten-year journey to No10 is over but now the real battles begin – he has to deliver on promises
News.content:
ANDY BURNHAM’S path to power has been an epic political odyssey.

While other Prime Ministers enjoyed swifter triumphs, his ten-year journey to Downing Street has been plagued by setbacks, detours and outright failure.



Heavily defeated in two ­Labour leadership contests, he stubbornly refused to give up.

Instead, he retreated 200 miles to Manchester, to build a power base and plot his route back to Westminster.



He returned as King of the North to seize the crown in an almost bloodless coup just three weeks ago.

And now? He’s spent the last week on holiday.

After a decade of scheming, Burnham apparently needs a breather before tackling the little matter of running the country.

He’ll need the rest.

Because, like Odysseus, our new PM will soon discover that getting home is only half the battle.

Homer’s hero had barely made it back to Ithaca before he was forced to take on a hall full of grasping suitors wooing his wife.



Burnham’s homecoming will be no less bruising.

His own monsters are already waiting: a £3trillion mountain of debt, threadbare Armed Forces, a battalion of disgruntled Starmer loyalists and, lurking in the shadows, Labour’s hard left.

Fasten your seatbelts. When Parliament returns next month it’ll be pure political box office.



Already the problems are piling up for Andysseus.

His biggest challenge is clear: to deliver on his promise to get things done and put “hope in every heart”.

Feelgood vibes and instant giveaways, like the £2 cap on bus fares and 86p-a-week cut in energy bills, have given Labour a Burnham bounce and sent expectations sky high.

But soon an impatient public will demand real change — and some already suspect he’ll end up like the rest of them: big on promises and short on delivery.

Labour’s decision to free thousands of offenders from prison early — including the killers of PC Andrew Harper — is Burnham’s first big test.



He raised hopes of an intervention when he “paused” the process.

But anger went off the scale when he claimed he was powerless to halt their release, with 850,000 people signing a protest petition.

Now he’s wisely decided to explore other options.



Like Pandora’s box, the scheme has released future misery and mayhem, which may soon come back to haunt the PM.

His proud boast of assembling the first Cabinet with more women than men will ring hollow if 9,000 domestic abusers walk free in the next three years.

Burnham must resolve this brewing crisis before his next major test in just three weeks — taking on the Mino-Tory.

Kemi Badenoch is gearing up for her first Commons joust with the new PM by watching old videos of his performance at the despatch box.

Burnham’s at his best when delivering passionate arguments.



But as a minister he lacked the razor-sharp wit and quickfire repartee of top parliamentary gladiators and is easily rattled when put on the spot.

His top team will no doubt put him through his paces when he returns from his sunbed to prepare him for something he has so far avoided: full public scrutiny.

The Conservative leader is bound to challenge him on the real-life Trojan horse: the small boats used by illegal migrants and criminals to enter Britain.

Burnham has promised to be “relentless” in tackling the crisis.



Yet 2,000 have made the perilous crossing since he became PM and he cannot allow things to drift as Keir Starmer did.

But his real Achilles’ heel is the estimated £96billion in new spending pledges — to build more council houses, fix social care and beef up our Armed Forces.

Where is the money coming from?

Britain is £3trillion in debt. That’s £43,000 for every man, woman and child.



But now there’s talk in Number 10 North and South about tampering with fiscal rules to allow more borrowing.

Taxpayers already fork out £12million in interest charges every HOUR, twice what we spend on defence.

The market gods will unleash their fury if Burnham dares to borrow more.

His only real options are to break a manifesto pledge not to increase taxes, already at an 80-year high, or to take the axe to the bloated £334billion welfare bill.

Burnham must use his clout to drive through the necessary cuts before his power ebbs away.



He has undoubtedly brought a new air of optimism to government.

But after years of economic mayhem and political upheaval, Britain still feels like a ship searching for its Ithaca.

The past four Prime Ministers have promised that home is just beyond the horizon, only for another storm to blow them off course.

Will Burnham’s voyage be as treacherous as The Odyssey, or will he steer us to calmer waters?

We’ll soon discover whether he’s a hit or a myth.



THE Prime Minister’s flagship plan to move power out of Westminster is being run by a civil ­servant . . . from London.

Sam Lister, the new director general of No 10 North, spends four days a week in the ­Manchester office, clocking up an £800 weekly bill for hotel and rail fares as he commutes from the capital.

And there was me thinking Burnham wanted to improve job opportunities for northerners.

KILLJOY council chiefs want to end the centuries-old tradition of ordering a pint while standing at the bar.



They plan to call time on “vertical drinking” by imposing compulsory table service on busy pubs.

But how do the clipboard-wielding party poopers plan to enforce the rule?

Can we expect spot-checks from inspectors using protractors to check the angle at which we are seated?

“Pardon me, sir, but you are leaning at 31 degrees, which is nearly upright.

“I’m going to ask you to sit back in your chair or leave.”



What happens if we slouch after feeling worse for wear after two pints?

Or if we have a few too many and find ourselves horizontal?

Well, here’s a message for those councils thinking of following the crackdown proposed by the City of Westminster:

British pubs have survived the plague, the Blitz, a smoking ban and the pandemic.

They’ve even survived the advent of karaoke and won’t be beaten by a bunch of meddling jobsworths.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

We’ll remain on our feet at the bar.

And we won’t stand for this nonsense.

News.title: Nigel Farage in talks with El Salvador to deport ALL foreign criminals to its hellhole prisons if he becomes PM
News.content:
NIGEL Farage has opened talks with El Salvador on deporting ALL foreign criminals to its hellhole prisons should he become PM.

The Sun can reveal that a Reform delegation will head to the Central American country within months for feasibility discussions with its government.



Mr Farage will announce a drastic expansion of his plans to send Britain’s most depraved murderers and rapists to its jails.

He will now seek to deport around 10,000 foreign lags currently in the UK to third countries to free up desperately-needed spaces.



Following initial conversations with the El Salvador government about renting prison spots, party chairman Lee Anderson will lead a team of officials for a visit later this year.

Donald Trump struck a similar agreement with El Salvador to deport migrants from the United States, which sparked controversy given the harsh prison conditions.

It comes as Andy Burnham faces pressure on Labour’s early release scheme that will see thousands of inmates freed after serving just a third of their sentence.

While he has since exempted sex offenders from the scheme, two of PC Andrew Harper’s killers will get out despite more than 800,000 signing a petition to keep them locked up.



Mr Farage will today also vow to build pop-up “Nightingale prisons” to create 12,000 more prison places.

And he will vow to stop dangerous lags benefitting from the early release scheme and also reintroduce short sentences for shoplifters.

Home Affairs spokesman Zia Yusuf said: “We will deport all 10,000 foreign nationals from our prisons, sending them to serve their sentences in countries like El Salvador.

“We will use the space created to ensure that serious criminals stay where they belong: behind bars.”

A Ministry of Justice spokesman said: “We have been clear that we wanted to go further and block more offenders from getting out sooner into their sentence but could not do so without risking prisons reaching capacity and collapsing.



“If that happened, police could not make arrests, courts could not remand offenders and there would be unchecked criminality on our streets.”

News.title: F-16 fighter jets scrambled over Trump’s golf course to intercept two planes flying close to where president was staying
News.content:
F-16 FIGHTER jets have been scrambled to intercept aircraft flying near Donald Trump’s golf course while the president was staying there.

Following the breach, the North American Aerospace Defense Command (NORAD) confirmed that it had escorted two aircraft out of the area.



Trump travelled to the golf club in Bedminster, New Jersey, on Friday to spend the weekend.

Officials described the intercepted planes as civilian general aviation aircraft.



An investigation is now ongoing to determine the exact reason behind the incursion.

A social media post said: “NORAD F-16s intercepted multiple general aviation aircraft today that violated temporary flight restrictions over Bedminster, NJ.



“All aircraft were safely escorted out of the area by NORAD aircraft.”



Restricting airspace is common practice during special events, including presidential movements.

Pilots were reminded to ‘Check NOTAMs (Notices To Airmen) before EVERY flight!

The Digital Visual Information Distribution System, which is operated by the Department of War, also shared a pointed reminder with pilots.

It said: “Should NORAD aircraft intercept a general aviation aircraft, the pilot should immediately come up on frequency 121.5 or 243.0 and turn around to reverse course until receiving additional instructions on one of those frequencies.”

This is not the first airspace violation near Trump that has prompted NORAD fighter jets to intervene during his second term.



In March, F-16 fighter jets deployed flares at Palm Beach International Airport hours before the President was due to take off.

Later in July, NORAD said more than 10 general aviation aircraft entered restricted airspace over Bedminster and East Rutherford, New Jersey, in a single day.

In three of the cases, F-16s were required to intercept the aircraft, and in two of them they released flares intended to get the pilots’ attention.

Trump spent Sunday at his Bedminster golf course once again as LIV Golf played its final round.

The President was on hand for the LIV Golf New York event towards the end of the breakaway tour’s season.



The day before, Trump was spotted driving around the course in a golf cart as he was followed by security and his daughter, Ivanka.

News.title: Andy Burnham promises crackdown on costly subscription traps and 'rip-off discounts'
News.content:
Andy Burnham promises crackdown on costly subscription traps and 'rip-off discounts'

The Prime Minister will bring forward 'easy to exit' rules, making it less painful for consumers to cancel subscriptions and avoid automatic renewal at a higher cost

View 2 Images Andy Burnham will bring forward 'easy to exit' rules (Image: Annabel Lee-Ellis/PA Wire)

Andy Burnham has promised everyday fixes on the cost of living including an end to costly subscription traps and rip-off discounts.

‌



The Prime Minister will bring forward “easy to exit” rules, making it less painful for consumers to cancel subscriptions and avoid automatic renewals at a higher cost. The crackdown was previously unveiled under ex-PM Keir Starmer and is set to include mandatory reminders before renewals of 12-month contracts.

‌



The rules had been due to come into force in Spring 2027, but Mr Burnham will now bring forward by several months to January in time for when customers often start new subscriptions. Downing Street has said it will save consumers an estimated £400 million - or £14 each month per unwanted subscription.

‌



Andy Burnham kicks off summer tour of UK to hear from voters on cost of living READ MORE :

Voters say mental health support over benefit cuts is best way to get young back into work READ MORE :

View 2 Images Andy Burnham has said his government wants to put more money in people's pockets (Image: Getty Images)

No10 also said “pretend prices and deceptive deals will be a thing of the past” under new proposals. They said the Prime Minister plans to ban retailers from making misleading claims to customers about discounts after complaints prices are being artificially hiked to give a false sense of value.

Mr Burnham said: “I know people are sick and tired of rip-off discounts and subscription traps. Westminster has got used to telling people that everyday hassles like this are just part of life.

‌



“I don’t think that’s right, especially when the cost of living continues to weigh heavily on so many people’s lives. I’m determined to pull every single lever we can to provide people with some room to breathe on the cost of living.”

He added: “We’re putting an end to phoney bargains. If something is advertised as half price, it should actually be half price. We’re also making it as easy to leave a subscription as it is to join.

“These are just two of the everyday fixes we’re going to be rolling out – today is just the start. We want to put more money in people’s pockets and give people hope that politics really can work for them and their everyday lives.”

Article continues below

Chief executive of Citizens Advice, Dame Clare Moriarty, said: “For too long consumers have been tricked into paying for products or services they don’t use - or didn’t even want to begin with - costing millions of pounds each year. So we really welcome the government’s move to speed up action on subscription traps and look at banning other tactics firms use to catch consumers out.”

She added: “At Citizens Advice, we’ve sounded the alarm on this for years, because we know subscription traps and sneaky online practices that hit consumers’ pockets hard are a widespread problem. We previously found that over 13 million people (26% of UK adults) accidentally took out a subscription in a year.”

Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds added: “There’s nothing worse than realising you’ve been fleeced by a dodgy deal, or seen money leaving your account because of a subscription you didn’t want to renew or couldn’t easily cancel. This Government is on the side of families working hard to make ends meet, while making sure the rules are clear for businesses and easy to follow.”

News.title: Huge fire erupts on A31 as flames spread from vehicle to dry heathland
News.content:
Huge fire erupts on A31 as flames spread from vehicle to dry heathland

Members of the public made more than 160 calls to emergency services as flames spread rapidly from the roadway on the eastbound A31 onto nearby heathland

View 2 Images Smoke from a wild fire near the A31 at Ringwood this afternoon (Image: Alamy Live News.)

A massive fire has broken out after a vehicle fire spread to dry vegetation on the A31 in Hampshire.

‌



More than 20 fire engines are trying to extinguish the blaze after a vehicle fire spread to nearby heathland, the fire service has said.

‌



Horrified members of the public made more than 160 emergency calls reporting the vehicle on fire on the eastbound A31 as plumes of smoke rose high into the air this afternoon.

‌



Twenty six fire engines, four water carriers, six off-road vehicles and several command vehicles had been dispatched to the scene after the first reports came in at around 5.24pm, the fire service said.

The fire has broken out at a site near Ringwood, authorities said, with flames spreading rapidly from the roadway to nearby heathland.

Content cannot be displayed without consent

‌



The fire service said: “The fire spread from the vehicle to the central reservation before progressing into nearby heathland.

“Crews from across Hampshire, supported by colleagues from Dorset and Wiltshire Fire and Rescue Service, are currently attending the incident.”

The A31 is closed between Picket Post and junction two of the M27.

‌



Motorists have been urged to avoid the area and use alternative routes whenever possible.

The fire service added: “Please follow diversion signs, allow extra time for your journey and avoid the area to allow emergency crews to work safely.”

View 2 Images Smoke could be seen for miles around

‌



Meanwhile, Nottinghamshire Fire and Rescue Service declared a major incident on Sunday as two large fires in woodland put a strain on resources.

Several wildfires have broken out in the UK over recent weeks, including large blazes at Dunwich Heath in Suffolk, Headon Warren on the Isle of Wight, Llanwonno in the Rhondda Valleys, South Wales, and the Cairngorms National Park in Scotland.

Hot weather continued to build on Sunday, with the south and south-eastern parts of England expected to have the highest temperatures.

‌



According to the Fire Severity Index, any wildfires are likely to be exceptionally severe on Sunday in almost all of the east and south-east of England.

“Exceptional” severity is its highest ranking.

The Met Office data includes rainfall, temperature and humidity, and agencies use the index to assess the severity of fire if it starts.

‌



It does not cover the chances of wildfires occurring.

Heatwave conditions will likely return next week, with a high of 36C expected in parts of East Anglia and south-east England by Thursday, according to the Met Office.

So far the extreme weather of summer 2026 has included two record-breaking heatwaves in May and June that led to more than 2,800 excess deaths.

Article continues below

Two more heatwaves in July, the driest July in England and Wales since records began in 1836, have fuelled drought and wildfires.

News.title: 'Fifth UK heatwave of the year brings deadly danger - action on open-water deaths cannot wait'
News.content:
'Fifth UK heatwave of the year brings deadly danger - action on open-water deaths cannot wait'

'The grim statistics tell us that, before this week is out, a teenager will leave home for a swim and never return. We desperately hope that prediction is wrong. How many more families need to pay the price before meaningful change comes?'

View Image Voice of the Mirror has its say...

Another UK heatwave means more tragic deaths - action cannot wait

The fifth heatwave of the year is bearing down on Britain, with temperatures forecast to hit a punishing 36C. As the mercury rises, so will the temptation to cool off in rivers, lakes and reservoirs. And with it comes a deadly danger.

‌



The grim statistics tell us that, before this week is out, a teenager will leave home for a swim and never return. We desperately hope that prediction is wrong. That every youngster who heads out into the heat comes safely home.

‌



Simon Haycock knows the agony when they do not. His son Sam was just 16 when he drowned at Ulley Reservoir in 2021. His family’s lives changed in an instant. That is why The Mirror’s Save Lives for Sam campaign, which demands stronger action to prevent needless open-water deaths, is so urgent.

‌



Successive Prime Ministers have backed us. But with another heatwave on the way, action cannot wait. Open water can kill without warning. How many more families need to pay the price before meaningful change comes?

Listen to families living with SEND failures before reshaping system

No parent should have to choose between sending their child into misery or breaking the law. Yet that is the desperate reality facing families whose children have special educational needs and disabilities (SEND).

Article continues below

They describe a system that has left parents on their knees, children shut out and, most harrowing of all, some youngsters contemplating suicide. Their warning over plans to move more SEND support into mainstream schools must be heard.

Mainstream education can work brilliantly for many children, but specialist provision is a lifeline for others. Taking it away without the staff, funding and support to replace it would be cruel. More than 150 families are asking Andy Burnham to meet them. He should. Before ministers reshape SEND, they must listen to the families living with its failures every day.

Extraordinary Pride of Britain nominees deserve to be celebrated

Pride of Britain has always been a reminder that amid the noise and gloom, extraordinary people are quietly doing extraordinary things. This year’s nominees have moved even hardened judges to tears. Their courage, kindness and selflessness deserve to be celebrated. They show Hollywood's star Michael Sheen is right: there is more good around us.

News.title: 'Nigel Farage has made clown of himself with Clacton by-election - it's funnier than any show on the pier'
News.content:
No show on Clacton pier will ever be as funny as Nigel Farage making a complete clown of himself with the pointless £250,000 by-election only he wanted.

Beating a bin at the end of the week may speed the wheels coming off a spluttering Reform UK bandwagon by exposing the greed and misjudgement of Mr Hissy Fit rather than saving the skin of this political fraud. What has changed is the wealthfare bungster unwittingly reinforced how he no longer sets the agenda and, given advisers incorrectly believed the futile contest would scupper a parliamentary inquiry into his personal £5million bung and Reform’s dodgy loot, Farage lost the plot.

Sleaze and criminal inquiries into the dictator’s secret booster to join the global financial elite, Posh George and his aristo mam’s favours and cash, crypto donations, Reform deputy Richard Tice’s bank accounts plus much else continue.

View 5 Images Farage might defeat a bin in the Clacton by-election - but things are not going well for Reform UK (Image: NEIL HALL/EPA/Shutterstock)

‌



And details of the Farage chum and Brexit co-conspirator, Arron Banks, hiring private investigators to spy on a Sunday Times journalist, Gabriel Pogrund, suggest this mob is not so much rattled as terrified of scrutiny. The transformation of British politics this summer since Andy Burnham succeeded Keir Starmer is astonishing, with Labour back from the dead and often neck-and-neck or ahead of Reform in polls.

Of course, it may not last, the Burnham bounce will flatten unless he delivers on improved living standards, in particular. But a Reform recovery looks less and less likely, Farage is history as a Downing Street shoo-in.

View 5 Images Arron Banks is alleged to have hired private investigators to spy on a Sunday Times journalist (Image: PAUL GILLIS / Reach PLC)

Bashing migrants is all he’s got and chasing even more extreme Restore risks alienating voters concerned about levels and boats but revolted by racist bigotry. And we may have a proper, second by-election should Farage be suspended for 10 days or more over that pocketed £5m before contemplating, and I’ll put it no higher than this, possible criminal charges against Reform.

‌



Tory bigwig David Davis, an independent-minded Tory I admire, never fully recovered calling a by-election on himself in 2008, similarly boycotted by rival mainstream parties, despite hailing his empty triumph a “stunning victory” over 25 mainly oddball candidates including the Church of the Militant Elvis Party and Miss Great Britain Party. Davis picked up 72% of votes and Farage finishing with a similar share against three Monster Raving Loonies, Everyone is God Party and entertaining Count Binface in a record 34-weak field would be equally pyrrhic.

Declaring his own stunning victory, pitching himself as St George slaying an establishment dragon, will be to sustain Nigel’s spirits when he knows the wheels are coming off Reform. The une scapable fact is Farage lost ground, respect and command of events.

He’s a joke figure rather than dictating the national conversation. It’s why opponents will be laughing loudest on Friday.

View 5 Images There's no sign of a Tory renaissance under Kemi Badenoch (Image: Jordan Pettitt/PA Wire)

‌



'Reform tribute act won't save Tories'

Of all the ditches to die in, championing a former neo-Nazi jailbird illustrated why there is no Kemi-naissance for the Tories under leader Badenoch. To defend a Conservative council candidate in Somerset, the convicted criminal Joshua Bonehill-Paine, right, behind bars as recently as 2018 for the ugliest anti-Semitism, including racially harassing the Jewish former Labour MP now peer, Luciana Berger, was Kemi-kaze politics.

Finally relenting as he stepped down and trying to save face by appointing so-called Crewkerne Man as an anti-extremism adviser only reaffirmed Badenough’s tin ear. I’m all for redemption and second chances, and those sucked down vile rabbit holes subsequently popping up remorseful can usefully help stop others becoming monsters too.

But it wasn’t only too soon or inappropriate for her retired neo-Nazi to stand for election. When Badenough’s simultaneously booting out moderate Tories to create a Reform tribute act, any Kemi-naissance wouldn’t benefit Britain.

View 5 Images Renewables powered over 50% of Britain's electricity this weekend (Image: NEIL HALL/EPA/Shutterstock)

‌



Small boat crossings down

Small boat crossings were down 43% compared with January to mid-July last year and the fewest since 2021 as the Labour Government begins to get on top of another issue bequeathed by the Conservatives. Not that you’d know that from frothing Reformers, Tories responsible for the problem including Robert “Honest Bob” Jenrick and Suella Braverman who jumped ship to Reform, or Hard Right propaganda TV channels, newspapers and social media liars.

Because good news is bad news for reactionaries who sell disasters instead of answers and deliberately ignore the fall from 21,690 people last year to 12,469. Yes, the crossings aren’t stopped completely, and probably never will be when desperate folk are prepared to risk their lives for a fresh start.

But keeping voters ignorant, a majority wrongly believing the total’s still going up, is the deceitful tactics of Right-whingers who should never be trusted.

Net-zero revolution is happening

Solar powered 36.4% and wind 14.3% – that’s more than half of Britain’s electricity – at 11am on Sunday. The greener, cleaner, renewable net-zero revolution is happening, with hydro supplying another 0.5% and nuclear 13.7%.

‌



Biomass contributed 7.0% with dirty gas down to a low of 6% but use of that expensive, price-fluctuating carbon-polluting fuel soars at peak times and hit 29.8% at 8pm Saturday. British Electricity Tracker updates also reveal a vulnerable dependency on imports by cables from Europe, particularly French nuclear, to keep a fifth of lights on.

Yet, Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh can boast that Britain is powering ahead, as she wrestles with balancing bills and saving the planet too. Going green will be cheaper in the long run, and leave the flat-earthers boiling their brains, as Europe has scorched with summer.

News.title: Suspected Irish gang boss Daniel Kinahan charged with directing organised crime group
News.content:
Suspected Irish gang boss Daniel Kinahan charged with directing organised crime group

Daniel Kinahan was flown from Dubai back to Ireland aboard a £39 million jet to face charges of directing a criminal organisation and taken to court with a guard of armed cops and Irish Defence Forces

View Image Daniel Kinahan

Daniel Kinahan, 49, has been remanded in custody after appearing before the Special Criminal Court in Dublin charged with directing an organised crime group.

It comes after the arrest in April in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) of the Dublin boxing promoter, who is an alleged leader of the Kinahan organised crime group.

Mr Kinahan, in his late 40s, was flown on a £39 million government jet belonging to the Irish Air Corps from Dubai to Ireland today where he was arrested after touching down at Dublin's Baldonnel Airport at around 6.30pm.

Kinahan was then whisked under armed guard from both law enforcement and the Irish Defence Forces to a special Sunday hearing at the Special Criminal Court to face charges of directing an organised crime group.

Shortly after the plane landed, a convoy of vehicles with blacked-out windows left the aerodrome at high speed. Two separate convoys then arrived at Dublin’s Special Criminal Court, as crowds watched.

The Irish Prison Service reportedly bought a bulletproof and bombproof van for transporting high-risk prisoners ahead of the operation. Several BMWs drove through an open gate and into the underground car park at the court, with the gate swiftly closing behind them.

Mr Kinahan, 49, was not represented by a lawyer during the brief hearing before three judges at the Special Criminal Court in Dublin. He was charged with directing the activities of a criminal organisation between October 18 2015 and April 6 2017.

He appeared in the dock wearing a black hoodie and put on a pair of dark-rimmed glasses after taking his seat. Detective Sergeant Colin Davidson told the court that he had arrested Mr Kinahan at Casement Aerodrome in Baldonnel at 6.49pm that day.

Article continues below

Mr Kinahan was remanded to next appear on October 5.

News.title: Nearly £1m of crystal meth and cannabis seized at Dublin Airport
News.content:
Nearly £1m of crystal meth and cannabis seized at Dublin Airport

The massive bust, with an estimated value of more than £814,000, saw officers and a sniffer dog named Charlie uncover 29kg of cannabis and 6kg of crystal methamphetamine in a passenger's luggage

View Image The huge haul of crystal meth and cannabis seized at Dublin Airport from a passenger's luggage on Sunday (Image: Revenue/PA Wire)

A woman has been arrested after cops seized a massive haul of crystal meth and cannabis inside luggage at Dublin Airport.

The massive drug bust saw two large suitcases filled with 35kg of crystal meth and cannabis seized by officers with an estimated value of more than £814,000.

A woman has been detained after the drugs were discovered, vacuum-packed in the baggage of a passenger who had got off a flight from Canada.

With the help of a sniffer dog called Charlie, revenue officers at Dublin airport found an estimated 29kg of herbal cannabis and 6kg of crystal methamphetamine in the luggage.

Pictures of the bust show bags of the illicit drugs spilling out of two large suitcases. The cannabis has an estimated value of half a million pounds and the crystal meth is valued at more than £315,000.

Article continues below

The woman, in her 50s, has been arrested and is being held at Dublin Garda Station under the Criminal Justice (Drug Trafficking) Act 1996.

Revenue officers have said their investigations are ongoing.

If businesses, or members of the public, have any information regarding smuggling in Ireland, they can contact Revenue on confidential phone number 1800 295 295.

News.title: How Kinahan's hearing unfolded inside the courtroom in Dublin
News.content:
Suspected crime boss Daniel Kinahan appeared in court in Dublin on Sunday after being extradited from Dubai following his arrest there in April.

Kinahan has been charged with directing the activities of a criminal organisation between October 2015 and April 2017.

The 49-year-old was remanded in custody after appearing at the non-jury Special Criminal Court in Dublin, telling the court: " I think we all know I won't be getting bail."

The Kinahan cartel has been responsible for trafficking tonnes of drugs and firearms around the world for more than 20 years, according to the UK's National Crime Agency.

The BBC's Ireland correspondent, Chris Page, was inside the court during the hearing.

More on this story.

News.title: How weight-loss medication is changing relationships with alcohol
News.content:
There is a growing body of research into the link between weight-loss drugs and alcohol consumption.

The drugs, with brands including Wegovy, Mounjaro and Ozempic, contain semaglutide or tirzepatide, which mimic a natural hormone called GLP-1. This suppresses appetite and keeps people feeling fuller for longer, helping them to lose weight.

Early research suggests that because these drugs affect the reward response in the brain, they can reduce cravings for substances including alcohol and nicotine, says Dr Christian Hendershot of the University of South Carolina.

He published a small-scale study, external in 2025 in which participants with alcohol use disorder craved alcohol less while taking Ozempic. Alcohol use disorder, sometimes referred to as alcoholism, is described by the NHS as drinking in a way that is harmful.

A study, external from the University of Colorado Anschutz published last week also suggested that GLP-1 medications in pill form led to fewer days of heavy drinking in people with mild to moderate alcohol use disorder.

People taking the drugs told BBC News that alcohol had affected them in different ways: some said their cravings for it had gone, drinking had made them feel nauseous or uncomfortably full, or they had got drunk more quickly. Others said they had not noticed any effect on their relationship with alcohol.

Before she started taking Wegovy, Lisa says she drank between six and eight bottles of wine a week with friends. But she had sometimes worried about whether this was too much and whether it could damage her health.

NHS guidance, external is that people should not drink more than 14 units a week on a regular basis, which is about six medium glasses of wine or six pints. Drinking too much in the long term can lead to liver damage, high blood pressure and increased risk of cancer.

Lisa says that since starting on the medication she has more than halved her consumption. At a recent day festival, she drank three glasses of wine over the course of nine hours. Previously, she would have had two bottles plus a couple of vodka mixers, she says.

Alcohol has always been a big part of her social life and when she stopped drinking for a few weeks in the late 2010s, she realised friends had stopped inviting her to social events. It led her to start drinking again.

This time round, Lisa says that she still looks forward to drinking wine, but after having a couple of glasses she simply cannot stomach any more.

"I still feel involved in things because I'm still drinking but drinking a lot less," Lisa says.

For years, Warren Thomas, 45, from Colchester, had enjoyed an occasional beer with his family after work, as well as one or two heavy drinking sessions with his friends each month.

But when he spoke to his friends on weight-loss medication about his plans to start taking Mounjaro, they warned him that it could affect how much he drank.

Warren says he noticed the effect within 24 hours of his first dose in mid-June. "I just don't want to drink," he says. "I've just got no appetite for it."

When he went out for his friend's birthday last month, he felt "light-headed and a little bit giddy" after two beers, he says.

"My tolerance level to drinking is now zero," he says.

There is no formal advice in the British National Formulary, a guide to dispensing medicine used by doctors and pharmacists, about whether people on weight-loss drugs should stop drinking alcohol, says Prof Russell Hearn, a GP and professor of medicine at King's College London.

But he gives careful advice to his patients. "Alcohol has a lot of calories in it and if your goal is to lose weight, drinking less will definitely help you with that alongside changing your diet while you're on a GLP-1," he says.

For people like Lisa and Warren, drinking less alcohol has been a happy bonus. But recent graduate Faye Goodwin, 20, feels that it has hampered her social life.

When Faye drinks she says she gets nauseous very quickly and sometimes throws up or gets bad acid reflux.

Faye, who got in touch with BBC Your Voice, has been taking Mounjaro since she was 18 and does not really know what it is like to drink alcohol without the impact of weight-loss medication. But she says she once took a month off the jabs and was able to drink without experiencing any nausea.

News.title: Banksy works cost public almost £150,000
News.content:
Three artworks by street artist Banksy have cost taxpayers almost Â£150,000 in cleaning operations and security so far, with the bill expected to rise.

The largest single cost relates to a mural painted on the Royal Courts of Justice in September 2025, where removal efforts and security have so far cost more than Â£85,000.

The Ministry of Justice (MoJ) says it has spent Â£50,000 trying to remove paint from the wall of the Grade II-listed building in Carey Street. A further Â£35,300 was spent on overtime and security costs.

The spending was disclosed to the BBC through Freedom of Information requests and is likely to reignite debate over whether Banksy's work is vandalism or valuable public art.

Banksy, who emerged from Bristol's graffiti scene in the 1990s and became one of the world's most famous street artists, is known for murals and installations that often appear overnight and attract large crowds.

The latest costs relate to a mural depicting a judge in a wig battering a protester with his gavel, which appeared on the Royal Courts of Justice in London on 8 September 2025.

Banksy claimed the image as his own work, by posting it on his website and Instagram account.

News.title: Hundreds arrested over French wildfires, but who is to blame?
News.content:
After wildfires caused more damage in France this year than at any time since World War Two, many are left asking a single question: why?

A major driver is that climate is changing as a result of the well-documented way humanity is burning fossil fuels. Temperatures are only rising.

But with records showing that nine out of 10 French wildfires are started by humans, the government in Paris is trying to attribute blame - although it is itself accused of being underprepared for the infernos that have now scorched more than 300,000 acres this summer.

The interior ministry has announced 420 arrests of people alleged to have either started the fires deliberately or by accident. Among them are 166 minors.

In one case, a 23-year-old man has been accused of deliberately starting 10 fires in the space of five days in the south-eastern Var area last month. He faces 15 years in prison and a â¬150,000 (Â£128,000) fine, if convicted.

Many others have been tried and immediately sentenced, such as a man who received a three-year jail sentence for starting three recent fires in the Raon-L'Ãtape forest in the Vosges region.

"Only a few square metres of vegetation went up in smoke," noted L'Est RÃ©publicain, the newspaper that reported the story.

Other prosecutions have been perceived as heavy-handed and unjust. A homeless man and someone with severe autism have reportedly been handed jail terms for throwing cigarette butts.

"I was amazed at the number of arrests, it feels excessive," admits Muriel Gestas, a lawyer who has represented several people accused of arson, including two firefighters. She doubts many will lead to a conviction.

The newspaper Le Monde is also unconvinced. It questions to what extent police have examined these cases, given the short time frame.

The authorities' silence on the details - the specific charges, notably whether they involve intent and how the numbers compare with past seasons - rules out any meaningful comparison with previous years, it argues.

But Bordeaux prosecutor Renaud Gaudeul told Le Monde that a tough approach was justified by current circumstances.

"The conditions for a charge of endangering lives are met for those who throw a cigarette butt or light a barbecue in wooded areas. It only takes a tiny spark for it to start," the newspaper quoted him as saying.

News.title: Harry Potter fans force diversion of UK-Ireland power link to avoid 'Dobby's grave'
News.content:
He said a colleague told him the nature of the calls, and that "apparently we're going to go straight through Dobby's grave".

"I said 'Dobby, who's Dobby? I don't know Dobby?'

"I said 'he's a fictitious character in a fictitious book, the whole thing is fictitious what are you talking about?'

"[The colleague] said 'no it's very, very serious'."

Ludlam said he then discussed with planners "exactly how to reroute the cable so we wouldn't go anywhere close to Dobby's grave".

He added: "A lot of people were very happy about that, and the project is now going [ahead] and Dobby's happy."

The Bronze Age remains the cable went close to were mentioned in Pembrokeshire council planning documents, external about the power link.

It said archaeological trenches dug near the route of the underground cable "contained the rim of an inverted pottery vessel whose fabric suggests a Bronze Age collared urn circa 1700-1500BC, typically associated with human burial".

The cable diversion is not the first time Dobby's grave has been saved.

In 2022 the National Trust agreed it could remain in place following a consultation, but urged visitors not to leave souvenirs.

Fans were asked not to leave socks on the mock grave, made of pebbles with messages written on them, because the beach was environmentally sensitive.

News.title: Man arrested after boat capsizes near Statue of Liberty killing woman and infant
News.content:
The operator of a boat that overturned near the Statue of Liberty, killing a woman and a baby, has been arrested and charged with reckless endangerment, New York police said.

Officials said a large search and rescue operation was launched after the incident near New York Harbour on Saturday night. Twelve people who were initially rescued from the water are all reported to be in stable condition.

New York police divers later found a 27-year-old woman and a five-month-old girl, who were transported to a nearby hospital where they later died.

The names of passengers and the specific cause of the incident have not been released by officials.

Around 22:25 local time (03:25 BST), police received a 911 call reporting an overturned boat in the waters near Liberty Island, which houses the iconic statue.

A nearby tour operator Sea the City saw the capsized boat and helped pull 11 people from the water, the company's founder Adam Schwartz said according to the BBC's US partner CBS News.

The rescue involved two Coast Guard boats, four fire department boats, two police boats and a police helicopter, the USCG said.

The investigation into the incident is ongoing, officials said.

The boat's operator, a 46-year-old Manhattan resident, faces 13 counts of reckless endangerment, officials said.

Coast Guard investigators are also determining whether the boat was illegally chartered.

An illegal charter is any passenger-for-hire vessel operation that does not have required credentials, safety equipment, and certificate of inspection.

"We are extremely grateful for the heroic, swift actions of our partner agencies and Good Samaritan vessel who assisted in rescuing survivors from the water," said Capt Doreen McCarthy of the USCG.

News.title: More areas of UK likely to move into drought as fifth heatwave builds
News.content:
As the hot and dry weather continues for much of the UK, drought status could be declared in additional parts of England this week.

The Environment Agency (EA) has suggested that "several areas" of England could enter drought status as "public water supplies remain under increasing pressure with continued dry weather and high demand".

For the seventh consecutive week, less than 10mm of rain fell across the country, with east and south-east England seeing less than 1mm of rain, according to data from the agency's latest drought summary.

More than half of England and the whole of Wales are already under drought conditions.

Reservoir levels have continued to fall, with almost all across England below normal and five classed as 'exceptionally low', according to the EA.

Wisley in Surrey has gone more than 50 days without a drop of rain. Southern England is approaching two months without any notable rainfall.

Customers of South West Water were the latest to see a hosepipe ban introduced on Saturday.

There are now more than 20 million people in the UK living in an area where prolonged dry weather combined with heatwaves and high demand for water has led to restrictions on usage.

Update: A previous version of this story said that the UK had recorded 35 days of temperatures exceeding 30C, breaking the previous record. As of 9 August, the UK has equalled the 1995 record, with 34 days of temperatures exceeding 30C.

News.title: Australia is the planet's extinction hotspot, but one animal offers a glimmer of hope
News.content:
"Eyes peeled," comes the order from the front passenger seat.

Obediently, we scan the ends and tops of logs, looking between low scrub and patches of vivid wildflowers for a flash of stripes or a dart of movement.

Eluding us is the numbat, a rare Australian marsupial which could be the love-child of a chipmunk and an anteater.

Numbats were once populous across the bottom half of the continent, but Dryandra Woodland â in the south-western corner of Australia â is one of the few places they remain.

As we slowly roll along bush tracks, researchers explain how this annual trip helps plot the species' survival.

Classified as endangered until this month, numbats have been bouncing back. This team's efforts have seen them scratched off the international red list of threatened species - a rare glimmer of hope in a country facing an extinction emergency.

This part of Australia is the front line of that crisis: a last stand for many species driven to the brink by feral pests, disease, urban development, habitat destruction and climate change.

Winging over our car at one point is the endangered Carnaby's cockatoo. On an island just off the coast is one of the last surviving pockets of the world's rarest marsupial, the Gilbert's potoroo. Diving in the sapphire waters around it is the increasingly scarce Australian sea lion.

News.title: Andy Burnham to embark on cost of living tour through the UK
News.content:
The prime minister is set to announce "a series of measures to make life easier" for those struggling with the cost of living in the coming days, Downing Street says.

No 10 says Andy Burnham's plans are to "give people some room to breathe". He will also focus on ways of "improving high streets" as he embarks on a tour of the UK.

But the government is facing continued pressure over its early release scheme for prisoners in England and Wales â with criticism of the fact that two of PC Andrew Harper's killers will be eligible from next year.

Burnham is also likely to face pressure for more action on the cost of living â although significant interventions are unlikely before October's Budget.

Even then, Chancellor John Healey has made it clear he will oversee "strong fiscal discipline" â which will limit how much the government has to spend.

The prime minister has been on holiday this week, but Downing Street said he would be in "listening mode" in the coming days as he tours the UK's nations and regions and works on a "10-year plan to bring back hope".

A spokesman for the prime minister said: "He thinks Westminster has got used to telling people that everyday hassles â like hidden pricing and consumers being ripped off â must be accepted as part of life.

"He doesn't think that's right. That's why he's going to start rolling out a series of pro-consumer cost of living measures to give people some room to breathe."

The spokesman added: "He's also going to be kicking off his summer tour around the country, getting out of Westminster and meeting people where they are.

"The prime minister is going to be in listening mode to help inform his 10-year plan to bring back hope and make Britain better off."

There are, though, likely to be continued questions about the forthcoming early release scheme, due to start in October.

One of Burnham's first acts in Downing Street was to order a review which limited the range of people who would be eligible.

But those convicted of manslaughter will still qualify for the scheme â including two of the killers of PC Andrew Harper.

The prime minister has faced calls from PC Harper's family, former senior police officers and opposition politicians for them to be denied early release.

But he has said he cannot go any further without risking prison capacity. Downing Street said on Saturday night that position remained unchanged, despite reports the prime minister could revisit the case.

News.title: Family 'devastated' as hit-and-run driver who killed boy, 13, to have early prison release
News.content:
The family of a 13-year-old boy killed in a hit-and-run say they are "devastated" after being told the driver who caused his death has had his sentence reduced.

Kaylan Hippsley died three days after being struck by a car driven by Harley Whiteman on Brecon Road in Hirwaun, Rhondda Cynon Taf, on 29 February 2024.

Whiteman was originally sentenced to six years and nine months in prison and banned from driving for eight years and four months but, after Kaylan's family appealed, High Court judges increased the sentence to nine years.

Now, the family has been told Whiteman can be released under licence as early as this autumn as part of the UK government's Sentencing Act early release scheme.

News.title: Holiday 'completely overshadowed' by loss of airport luggage
News.content:
Travellers have described struggling to enjoy their holidays, days after hundreds of people flying out of Birmingham Airport were left without their luggage.

While it seems the issues that first emerged on Friday are yet to be remedied completely, the airport said the "vast majority" of baggage was now travelling as planned with passengers, and it was working to reunite others with their luggage.

Louise Fenton said she and her family had had no communication from the airline, holiday company or the airport after their luggage failed to arrive in Gran Canaria on Friday.

She is travelling with three teenagers, and said her daughter, who is autistic, had "struggled enormously" with replacement clothes, and had "barely slept because she is unable to tolerate the alternatives".

"We are staying in a tourist area where the shops are predominantly beach shops, with very limited clothing options, particularly for someone with sensory sensitivities," the mum explained.

"We still have no luggage and, no meaningful information about where it is."

She added the situation had "completely overshadowed" the holiday.

"We have worked hard and saved for this holiday, and we simply don't deserve to have the entire experience taken over by something that isn't our fault."

Speaking to the BBC on Friday and Saturday, travellers variously described the situation as "absolute chaos" and "carnage".

Other flights affected include ones to Turkey, Cyprus, Glasgow and Rome, covering a number of airlines.

News.title: Rare turtle to be sent back home in 5,000-mile 'incredibly emotional' trip
News.content:
It has taken almost two years to plan, including building a special temperature-controlled crate for him, and co-ordinating complex paperwork across two countries.

Rhossi normally lives in the sea, but has to travel out of the water â first by helicopter from Anglesey to London, then by cargo flight to Houston, Texas, USA.

It means the journey needs to be completed as quickly as possible, and staff have to be constantly on hand to make sure he does not dry out or dehydrate.

Davidson said: "We have to make sure that the shell is really well lubricated, so we spread Vaseline all over to stop it drying out and flaking off.

"The same for the skin â it's really delicate â and especially the eyes, which both have to be lubricated before he goes into the crate and again just before takeoff, or he will start to peel like someone getting sunburned.

"But I have had to go to the checkout in a chemist's with about eight tubes of KY Jelly and three tubs of Vaseline and explain what's happening when I get strange looks."

News.title: Kellie Bright to leave EastEnders after 13 years
News.content:
EastEnders star Kellie Bright is to leave the soap after playing one of its key characters, Linda Carter, for 13 years.

She arrived in Albert Square with on-screen husband Mick, portrayed by Danny Dyer, when they became the new owners of the Queen Vic pub.

Carter's matriarch character has been central to major storylines including plots about murder, sexual assault and alcoholism.

Bright said she made the "tough decision" to leave more than a year ago but "happily" agreed to stay on to be part of an "exciting storyline".

The BBC has promised "unmissable drama" before her on-screen exit, which is said to be a "while away" yet.

Executive producer Ben Wadey described the actor as being "the beating heart of EastEnders" and said she had become "a classic EastEnders icon".

Viewers have seen the much-loved character at the heart of many emotional storylines including in 2014 when she was raped by her brother-in-law Dean Wicks.

More than 7 million people watched the episode which prompted dozens of complaints. The sexual assault led to long-running story arc about family conflict and trauma.

News.title: Hot weather reveals hidden history across the South
News.content:
As the south of England continues to enjoy an unusually warm and dry summer, parch marks on lawns across the region have revealed the hidden histories of their location.

Among the sites which have seen the outlines of historic installations exposed by the hot weather are Portchester Castle and Blenheim Palace.

At Blenheim, the footprint of an 18th Century garden - which had once stretched across the width of the entire palace - has revealed itself on a lawn.

Andy Mills, the Unesco World Heritage Site's head gardener, told the BBC it was "absolutely magical" to see the outlines of the historic parterre - 260 years after it was demolished.

Mills explained that the original parterre - which is a French word meaning "on the ground" - had been constructed in 1705, and would have "cost an absolute fortune to install".

"It was a very large extravagant thing to do, but it was a way of showing your wealth and importance and that sort of thing," he said.

News.title: Attempted murder arrest after three hit by car
News.content:
A man has been arrested on suspicion of attempted murder and dangerous driving after three pedestrians were hit by a car following reports of a disturbance.

The incident happened on Stokes Croft in Bristol at about 06:30 BST, according to Avon and Somerset Police.

A spokesperson for the force said one of the pedestrians was taken to hospital, but their injuries were not considered to be life-changing or life-threatening. The two others were not seriously injured.

A man police believe to be the car's driver was treated for facial injuries after his arrest.

Thomas Street, Hepburn Road, Stokes Croft and City Road are all closed while police make enquiries, with more officers than usual in the area as investigations continue.

The Best Off Licence in Stokes Croft was also damaged in the incident.

Bristol Supt Matt Ebbs said: "We would like to assure the public we do not believe there to be any wider threat.

"Anybody with concerns is welcome to speak to officers on the ground, but we would also appeal to anybody with CCTV, dashcam or mobile phone footage which may assist our enquiries to contact us."

News.title: Stray cats showing up at raves, gigs and pubs now have own merchandise
News.content:
Celebs pulling in punters with a club appearance is nothing new. But did they ever have so much fur?

At venues in Coventry at least, the glitterati wear whiskers these days.

It began when two stray cats made city venues their home, becoming social media stars thanks to the incongruous sights of tail and turntable, pint and paw.

While one shows up at gigs and rave nights, the other is a bit more pub than dub. But each now has his own range of merch... and visitors flock for a glimpse of these meeow-vers and shakers.

Murphy was first spotted living beneath a bush before wandering into the car park of The Old Windmill pub in the city centre, "rake thin" and in need of care.

Now a permanent resident, he has become a firm favourite with customers.

"We've had people who've never been in the pub before, but have seen him on social media," said the venue's Peter Dunkley. "They come in and the first question is 'where's Murphy'?"

Across town, Fargo is a well-known figure at Fargo Village, the creative hub after which he is named.

Regularly spotted around the site's shops and bars, he too has become an attraction in his own right, mixing among ravers and drinkers.

Fargo Village staff have set up an Instagram account in an effort to track down his owner, and it has attracted a loyal following of fans eager to keep up with his daily adventures.

Hall of Famer Don Nelson, the second-winningest coach in NBA history, has died at the age of 86. His family announced the passing of the five-time champion as a player on Sunday, though they did not disclose the manner of death.

"On Sunday morning our beloved husband, dad, grandfather and great-grandfather Don Nelson peacefully went to be with the Lord, surrounded by his loving family," the Nelson family statement read. "Throughout his last week, friends and family encircled him with love, sharing the blessing of his friendship and revisiting treasured memories."

Nelson retired in 2010 as the all-time leader with 1,335 regular-season coaching victories, a record later surpassed by San Antonio Spurs coach Gregg Popovich (1,390). His distinctive fast-paced style, utilizing smaller athletic players, became famously known as "Nellie Ball."

open image in gallery Nelson retired in 2010 as the all-time leader with 1,335 regular-season coaching victories ( Jim Rogash/Getty Images )

The three-time Coach of the Year didn't win any NBA titles during his 31-year overall tenure with the Milwaukee Bucks (1976-87), Golden State Warriors (1988-95, 2006-10), New York Knicks (1995-96) and Dallas Mavericks (1997-2005). But he put together 13 seasons of 50 or more wins, twice reaching 60 (once with the Bucks, once with the Mavericks).

"[Nelson] was a true basketball visionary who saw the game differently and was never afraid to challenge conventional thinking," the Warriors said in a statement. "His approach helped shape the game and paved the way for generations of players and coaches who followed.

"More than anything, Don Nelson will be remembered for his authenticity, larger-than-life personality, and incredible passion for basketball, and his influence on the Warriors franchise will endure for years to come."

He was inducted into the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame as a coach in 2012.

As a player, Nelson won five NBA titles during 11 seasons with the Boston Celtics.

He initially reached the NBA with the Chicago Zephyrs (1962-63) after being the No. 3 overall pick. He then spent two seasons with the Los Angeles Lakers before joining behind a loaded Boston starting five and was one of seven Boston players to average double digits in scoring in 1967-68. He averaged a career best 15.4 points and 7.3 rebounds in 1969-70.

In 134 career playoff games, Nelson averaged 11.1 points and 4.8 rebounds. The Celtics retired his No. 19 jersey in 1978.

"Don Nelson revolutionized NBA basketball through his fearlessness, ingenuity and deep conviction," NBA commissioner Adam Silver said in a statement. "He spent nearly 50 years in the NBA - winning five championships as a player with the Boston Celtics before building one of the most successful and pioneering coaching careers in league history. He brought an unmistakable personality to everything he did, and his impact on our sport will continue to be felt for generations.

"I send my deepest condolences to Don's family and many friends throughout our league."

In college, Nelson averaged 21.1 points and 10.9 rebounds in 72 games over three seasons at Iowa.

Nelson won the 2025 Chuck Daly Lifetime Achievement Award to honor his overall contributions to basketball.

A newly released Food and Drug Administration report details the full scope of a massive produce recall connected to a nationwide cyclospora outbreak, naming major restaurant chains and retail brands that pulled nearly 240,000 cases of lettuce.

Saturday’s update identifies potential cyclospora contamination as the cause for the July 2026 recall initiated by supplier Taylor Farms.

In total, 236,192 cases of iceberg and romaine lettuce — some mixed with carrots and red cabbage — were removed from distribution across Mexico and 27 U.S. states.

Walmart’s house brand Marketside received the largest share of the recalled produce, accounting for 109,476 cases of salad and shredded lettuce.

Fast-food chains were also heavily affected. Subway removed 8,075 cases, Yum! Brands — the parent company of Taco Bell, KFC and Pizza Hut — recalled 5,900 cases, and Jack in the Box removed 5,130 cases. While Yum! Brands operates multiple companies, only Taco Bell has been tied to the recall so far.

open image in gallery A newly published FDA report reveals the scale of a major produce recall tied to a national cyclospora outbreak, listing the top grocery brands and fast-food chains that removed almost 240,000 cases of lettuce from distribution ( AP )

Other commercial accounts listed in the federal report include major food distributors Sysco, Markon, Peak Lettuce Salad and US Foods subsidiary Cross Valley Farms.

The disclosure comes after nonprofit consumer advocacy group Consumer Federation of America criticized Taylor Farms on July 21 for using obscure shorthand abbreviations on recall notices, such as “MKTSD” for Marketside and “CV” for Cross Valley Farms.

The recalled produce was sourced from central Mexico and distributed across a wide geographic footprint, including Florida, Illinois, Pennsylvania, Texas and Virginia.

The report offers the clearest picture yet of a health crisis that escalated over the summer.

As reported by The Independent, federal health officials have tracked more than 22,700 cyclospora cases nationwide, leading to more than 500 hospitalizations and two deaths.

The microscopic parasite, which is transmitted through exposure to human fecal matter, causes severe gastrointestinal illness, explosive diarrhea and dehydration.

open image in gallery Federal health officials have linked the parasite outbreak to more than 22,000 illnesses and 500 hospitalizations nationwide, with Michigan hit hardest ( Wiki Commons )

Michigan has been as the epicenter of the crisis, accounting for more than 12,000 reported cases.

However, state health officials recently advised residents that they could resume eating bagged salads, noting that new case reports and emergency room visits were slowing down and that contaminated produce from the early summer harvest wa no longer in circulation.

In an interview with CBS Face the Nation on Sunday, National Institutes of Health Director Jay Bhattacharya defended the Trump administration’s response to the outbreak, hailing FDA officials who did a “great job” trying to identify the source.

The outbreak has also taken a toll on the restaurant industry. Taco Bell reported a sales decline of roughly 2 percent during its recent fiscal quarter.

“The brand has seen a meaningful near-term sales impact,” Yum! Brands CEO Chris Turner told analysts on a recent earnings call, according to CNBC.
