World.title: 'Volatile' wildfire in B.C. unsafe for ground crews to tackle directly, officials say
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

THE LATEST:

B.C. declared a state of emergency amid growing wildfire threat.

Nearly 22,000 people have been forced from their homes across B.C., more than 10,000 people on evacuation alert.

The Bald Range wildfire near Summerland grew from 103 to 136 square kilometres on Sunday.

The Kelowna International Airport cancelled 14 flights on Sunday and an additional four were delayed.

Ottawa has approved a B.C. request for federal assistance to help provide accommodations for evacuees.

Parts of Highway 97, Highway 1, Westside Road remain closed.

The B.C. Wildfire Service is now expecting more lightning-caused fire starts across the Interior and the Okanagan.

The French Bar Creek and Bonanza Creek wildfires may combine in coming days.

Wildfire threatens Summerland

About 12,000 people from Summerland and thousands more from the surrounding area remain evacuated from their homes on Sunday due to the Bald Range fire, while evacuation alerts stretch south to the edge of Penticton and north through Peachland to Highway 97C.

In a Sunday update just after 9:30 a.m. PT, the B.C. Wildfire Service said the wildfire is displaying extreme Rank 5 and 6 behaviour — the latter being the highest rank a wildfire can reach.

Crews observed rapid rates of spread and embers carried one kilometre ahead of the main fire, starting spot fires.

"Fire behaviour at this intensity is extremely volatile and aggressive, which makes direct attack unsafe for ground crews," the service said on Sunday.

The Regional District of Okanagan-Similkameen expanded an evacuation order for the fire to properties in the Brent Lake and Shingle Creek area south of Summerland on Sunday morning.

Most evacuees have headed to Penticton for support, where they are being urged to stay with family or friends if they can due to limited accommodations.

An evacuee sits next to Greg Krauter's goats that he evacuated with from his property in Summerland due to the Bald Range fire, at the evacuation centre in Penticton, B.C., on Sunday Aug. 9, 2026. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

Interior Health is extending hours at the Penticton and West Kelowna urgent and primary care centres on Sunday for people who need access to non-emergency care.

Premier David Eby said homes have been lost in the fire, though officials have yet to say how many.

The RCMP said it is also investigating a possible fatality in the Meadow Valley area northwest of the city.

The fire, first spotted Friday evening, grew so rapidly it forced wildfire crews to use helicopters to rescue dozens of people cut off by the flames, officials said Saturday. As of Saturday night it had burned 103 square kilometres.

The B.C. Wildfire Service (BCWS) says its top priorities are building control lines, protecting structures and ongoing search and rescue operations.

CEO of the Central Okanagan Food Bank, Trevor Moss, says volunteers in West Kelowna have been feeding wildfire evacuees with full meals and easy-to-grab boxes filled with instant foods. (Brady Stachan/CBC)

Extreme fire behaviour

The provincial government declared a state of emergency on Saturday, amid what Eby called "a remarkable escalation in fire activity."

BCWS director of wildfire operations Cliff Chapman said prolonged hot and dry weather has left southern B.C. facing "explosive" fire conditions "we have never seen before."

Thunderstorms forecast for parts of the interior could also bring dry lightning on Sunday, the BCWS said.

A helicopter is pictured near the Bald Range wildfire in Summerland on Saturday. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

There are over 100 wildfires burning across B.C., including the 485 square kilometre Ainslie Creek wildfire east of Boston Bar, which continues to expand.

The BCWS says to the north it has grown within nine kilometres of Highway 8, triggering a new evacuation order from the Nooaitch Indian Band, while to the east it is now within 12 kilometres of Highway 5.

The Bradley Creek wildfire, which is believed to have destroyed at least 230 properties on Okanagan Indian Band land, was classified as "being held" on Saturday, meaning it is not expected to grow under current conditions.

However, thousands of people remain evacuated from their homes due to that fire and the 12.4 square kilometre Quilpituk Creek fire, both burning at the north end of Okanagan Lake.

The massive Pear Lake wildfire, which has forced the evacuation of Clinton and 70 Mile House and destroyed structures on about 120 properties, grew slightly on Saturday to 1,429 square kilometres.

Highway closures

The Bald Range fire has closed Highway 97 from the south end of Peachland to Kickaninee Provincial Park.

Further up Okanagan Lake, the Quilpituk Creek fire has closed Westside Road for 50 kilometres between Lake Okanagan Resort and Highway 97 North.

Highway 97 is also closed for 60 kilometres in the Clinton area between Loon Lake Road and 76 Mile Frontage Road due to the Big Bar Complex wildfires.

Highway 1 remains closed for about 40 kilometres between Yale and Boston Bar due to the Brunswick Lake complex.

World.title: RCMP investigating homicide of 12-year-old Edmonton boy after remains found in northern Alberta
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

RCMP say they are investigating the homicide of a 12-year-old Edmonton boy after remains were found in a rural area of northern Alberta.

In a news release on Sunday, police said Athabasca RCMP officers responded to a report of human remains found on Thursday, Aug. 6, just before 3:30 a.m.

Police said an autopsy was completed on Friday at the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner in Edmonton, and the boy’s manner of death was deemed a homicide.

RCMP Cpl. Gina Slaney told CBC News in an interview that the boy had not been reported missing to police prior to Thursday, and his family has been notified of his death.

Police said investigators are seeking the public’s assistance with the case.

“If you were around Highway 813 near Calling Lake or Range Road 213A (referred to as the ‘C-Road’), on Aug. 6, 2026, between 12 a.m. and 4:30 a.m., and have dash cam video, please contact Athabasca RCMP,” the news release said.

Calling Lake is located more than 200 kilometres north of Edmonton.

The RCMP Major Crimes Unit is investigating the incident.

World.title: 'No more caving': Poilievre's letter to Carney urges him not to concede to U.S. tariff demands
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre is calling on Prime Minister Mark Carney to show some "backbone" as trade negotiations ramp up with the United States.

In a letter to Carney that was shared with reporters, Poilievre and his Canada-U.S. relations critic, Shuvaloy Majumdar, said Ottawa has given in to several of Trump's demands in the last year.

The pair cited scrapping the digital service tax, removing Canada's counter-tariffs and cutting the United States into a deal to share net toll revenue from the recently opened Gordie Howe International Bridge connecting Windsor, Ont., and Detroit, Mich.

Poilievre and Majumdar argued against Carney's previous claim that no deal is better than a bad deal by pointing to job losses in manufacturing-heavy Canadian cities that rely on cross-border supply chains.

"For the past year and a half, you have backed down to one American demand after another while getting nothing in return, with concession after concession," Poilievre tells Carney in the letter.

WATCH | Canada weighs ending U.S. booze bans for tariff relief. Not so fast, say provinces: Canada weighs ending U.S. booze bans for tariff relief. Not so fast, say provinces | Duration 4:11 Canada could be willing to end provincial bans on U.S. liquor and make concessions on dairy products in exchange for relief from U.S. tariffs, sources tell CBC News, but provinces are already pushing back.

"Worse, you have lost ground with American tariffs on Canadian steel and aluminum doubling and broadening and tariffs on lumber tripling."

Poilievre said Canadians deserve a "good deal" that includes zero tariffs on softwood lumber, an end to sectoral tariffs on steel and aluminum, a tariff-free auto pact and full exemption to Buy America rules on infrastructure projects at all levels of government.

"No more pursuing policies of a managed decline at home. No more caving."

A new round of 50 per cent U.S. tariffs on a range of Canadian goods is set to take effect on Aug. 19. Trade talks between the nations have intensified ahead of that deadline.

The Conservatives reiterated their call to strengthen Canada's negotiating position with the creation of a strategic reserve of critical minerals, which would be open to countries that provide tariff-free access to their own markets.

Canada and Mexico both indicated last month that they want to see the Canada-United States-Mexico Agreement (CUSMA) extended for another 16-year term. The United States instead opted to let the agreement move to rolling annual reviews.

Dairy farmers urge PM against making concessions

The U.S. has cited the supply management system that protects Canadian dairy as a key trade irritant, and Trump has repeatedly complained about the level of U.S. dairy farmers' access to Canada's market.

Carney said Thursday his government is loyal to the supply management system as the group Dairy Farmers of Canada urged the government not to offer concessions regarding its industry in trade talks.

The dairy group has also said Canada has already made several concessions, only to be met each time with fresh demands.

WATCH | U.S. senator says there's 'momentum' toward trade deal after LeBlanc meeting: U.S. senator says there's 'momentum' toward trade deal after LeBlanc meeting | Duration 10:57 North Dakota Republican Sen. Kevin Cramer says 'this is the moment' to get a Canada-U.S. trade deal. Plus, Power & Politics guest host Katie Simpson asks Cramer what wildfire smoke 'punishment' Canada can expect from U.S. President Donald Trump.

According to industry sources who spoke to CBC News, the Canadian government is preparing to meet some U.S. demands — including ending bans on American alcohol sales — in exchange for tariff relief.

In addition to ending the booze bans, the Canadian side is considering lifting retaliatory tariffs on U.S. autos and making some changes on dairy, the sources said. They didn't say what changes were on the table in regards to the dairy sector.

In exchange, Canada is pushing for the U.S. to drop the new 50 per cent tariffs, as well as relief from the sectoral tariffs on industries such as steel and aluminum, and a joint announcement that talks on the Canada-United States-Mexico Agreement (CUSMA) will resume in the fall.

World.title: N.L. has a hard bread shortage — but why do we eat it in the first place?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Grocery stores across Newfoundland and Labrador have been struggling to keep hard bread in stock since a fire at the Purity factory in March put a crimp in the company’s baking operations.

Purity is the province’s primary provider of hard bread, also called hard tack, ship’s biscuit, and sea biscuit — a dry, unleavened bread made of flour, water and salt.

But why is the jaw-breaking baked good so popular here?

Dehydrated bread has been a mainstay of the traveller’s diet since ancient times. Because it’s long lasting and easy to carry, military leaders issued it to soldiers on campaign when they couldn’t count on being able to access enough local provisions to feed an army.

Roman legionaries received bucellatum , a twice-baked bread, among their field rations. King Richard the Lionheart loaded his ships with “ biskit ” when he left for the Crusades in 1190.

The non-perishable fare was also a useful provision for sailors, who could spend weeks or months at sea and often needed enough supplies to see them not only to their destination but home again afterward.

Basque seasonal fishermen brought hard bread to the coasts of Newfoundland and Labrador in the 1500s.

Between the sail out, the fishing season, and the journey home, they could be away for six months at a stretch, and they packed enough for nine months in case their ships became locked in ice and they were stranded for the winter.

When the British visited the region, they stocked up on hard bread, too.

In 1620, Richard Whitbourne, an English mariner who briefly served as governor of Renews, published a record of all the supplies he had brought with him on a trip to the colony of Newfoundland from Great Britain.

At the top of the list is “eleven thousand [weight] of Bisket bread,” the equivalent of nearly 5,600 kilograms, and enough to feed 40 people for 12 months.

After European settlement, fishing families baked their own “soft” bread at home, but they continued to rely on hard bread when they were out at sea, berry picking or hunting.

Proper hard bread couldn’t be home baked. It was made from a special winter wheat flour and slowly dried in a kiln or an evaporation loft to remove all its moisture, giving it its longevity.

Like most other food that couldn’t be caught locally or grown in a kitchen garden, hard bread had to be imported. By the 1770s, Newfoundland was dependent on the American colonies not only for hard bread but for flour and livestock, as well as rum, sugar and molasses shipped up from the West Indies.

In 1775, as tensions escalated between the British Crown and its American colonists after the Boston Tea Party, the House of Commons passed an act to restrict trade out of Massachusetts .

The American reaction was unexpected: the colonies closed ranks and retaliated. New York, Philadelphia and most other major ports cut off all trade to Newfoundland.

It was a strategic move intended to strike at the heart of the European food fishery. Without American supplies to keep them going, Newfoundland settlers wouldn’t be able to fish and the British would lose a key food source.

The ban couldn’t have come at a worse time. It was spring, and Newfoundlanders had exhausted their provisions over the winter.

There was panic. People hoarded wheat, and the price of goods skyrocketed.

Near the end of the American Civil War, artist Winslow Homer designed a set of collector’s cards showing an unvarnished view of life in the Union army. Here, a soldier spits out his first bite of hard tack. (Metropolitan Museum of Art)

By 1776, America was at war with Great Britain, and Newfoundland was starving.

European suppliers eventually scaled up production to meet Newfoundland’s needs, though the trade ban led to long-term inflation in the price of food. The town of Hamburg, Germany, cornered the market on hard bread, so much so that Newfoundlanders nicknamed it Hamburg bread.

Hard bread wasn’t manufactured locally until the Scottish Rennie brothers opened a flour mill and bakery in St. John’s in the 1830s — Rennie’s Mill, which gave its name to the river and the road. Their baking equipment was imported from Hamburg.

The demand for hard bread didn’t slacken. If anything, it increased.

In his travels across Newfoundland in the 1850s, Anglican bishop Edward Feild described “tea and biscuit” as “the ordinary hospitality extended to visitors.” He and his companions were so desperate for “soft” bread they provided flour to local women to bake it for them.

By the 1880s, 180,000 residents were eating 40 million hard biscuits a year , over 200 per person.

A large portion of those biscuits would have gone into the traditional dish fish and brewis. Pronounced “brews,” brewis is made by soaking hard bread in water overnight then boiling it to soften it before serving it with salt cod.

In 1885, Nova Scotia journalist George Patterson wrote that brewis “occupies almost the same place at a Newfoundlander’s breakfast-table that baked beans are supposed to do on that of a Bostonian.”

Sprinkled with molasses or scrunchions (small chunks of salted fat-back pork), fish and brewis was a hearty, high-calorie meal fishers could eat before a day at sea. Among the merchant class, it was a Sunday breakfast treat .

Joey Smallwood’s Book of Newfoundland called brewis as much the national dish of Newfoundland as roast beef is of England, spaghetti is of Italy, or rice is of China.

Purity has confirmed their bakery resumed production in July , so local shelves should soon be reloaded.

That’s good news for today’s hard bread die-hards.

World.title: As more EVs hit the road, will we have the mechanics to keep them running?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Welcome to our weekly newsletter where we highlight environmental trends and solutions that are moving us to a more sustainable world.

Hey, it's Bridget. I recently went to Vancouver Community College to visit their auto shop and learn about how they’re teaching apprentices about electric vehicles. I was curious about efforts to train the next generation of automotive technicians, so I decided to dig a little deeper.

This week:

As more EVs hit the road, will we have the mechanics to keep them running?

The Big Picture: A landmark battery

This town tested a drone show as an animal-friendly alternative to fireworks

As more EVs hit the road, will we have the mechanics to keep them running?

Vancouver Community College instructor Mike Coard stands with some of the electric vehicles used to train apprentices in the school's Automotive Service Tech Department. (Bridget Stringer-Holden/CBC)

EV sales are ramping up — not just cars but also trucks and buses. Canada wants EVs to make up 75 per cent of new vehicle sales by 2035 to help meet its goal of net-zero emissions by 2050 .

Electric school buses have gained traction in some parts of the country , but a new report suggests a challenge to keeping them running in the future — and it's one that could affect other EVs, too.

The report from the environmental think-tank Pollution Probe finds "key gaps" in training and certification of technicians to maintain and repair electric school buses.

Marc Saleh, Pollution Probe's director of transportation, said EVs require skills related to high-voltage safety, battery diagnostics, power electronics and charging infrastructure management that still aren't being taught in standard automotive service programs.

He and others in the auto service industry say this challenge applies not just to school buses but to all electric vehicles. There remain barriers to both training new automotive technicians and upgrading the skills of already certified Red Seal technicians.

Challenges for EV training

Saleh says technician training for EVs is primarily handled by manufacturers. But this will eventually need to change to properly support adoption, as there may soon be so many EVs that the dealerships can't service them all.

Emily Chung (no relation to the editor of this newsletter), president of the Automotive Industries Association of Canada, said what's involved in servicing an EV depends heavily on the make and model because EV technology, including high-voltage battery systems, is developing rapidly and varies more among manufacturers than the relatively standardized technology used in internal combustion engine vehicles.

Pictured are two of the training aids that VCC instructor Mike Coard uses to teach students about batteries. On the left is a Tesla battery, and on the right is a hybrid battery pack from a Toyota Prius. (Bridget Stringer-Holden/CBC)

"There's no standardization, even amongst the car manufacturers, and everybody started doing their own thing and have their own flavour," she said.

This is why she says proprietary technology is also an issue, because shops and classrooms don't always have access to all of the information needed to understand each vehicle.

Many manufacturers refuse to provide that access, or they charge extremely high fees that repair shops can't afford.

There is also no universal certification for EV training courses or any requirement for ongoing training after technicians receive a Red Seal certification — Canada's national standard for skilled trades such as automotive.

Some solutions

Despite these barriers, both independent auto shops and community colleges are trying to fill the gap.

Andrew Ackers owns a NAPA AutoPro shop in Hamilton.

He has been training technicians who are already familiar with traditional, internal combustion engine vehicles through an EV training program called Next Drive started by NAPA, an automotive co-operative that distributes replacement auto parts.

The program has five levels — there will be six starting in September — and goes from basic electrical theory all the way to diagnosing problems inside battery packs.

Ackers says it’s about a $20,000 investment per technician but is worth the price — and each level can be done in a week, meaning they don’t have to leave their jobs for long to complete the training.

"A strong technician that is comfortable with electrical work could be up to speed within a week's worth of training to be able to handle about 90 per cent of the high-voltage repairs that are necessary on vehicles," he said.

Ackers said he's dedicated about 15 per cent of his business to electric vehicles.

Vancouver Community College trains students on a variety of EVs and hybrids. In the shop is a Ford Fusion, Tesla Model 3, Nissan Leaf, Volkswagen ID.4, Rivian pickup truck and a Toyota Mirai. (Bridget Stringer-Holden/CBC)

Colleges are also stepping up to expand their clean energy programs and prepare technicians for the growing demand of EV repairs.

Vancouver Community College already has some training in place but is expanding the school’s offerings in September. To accommodate that, it is building a new Centre for Clean Energy that is scheduled to be completed in 2027. It will include space to train refrigeration technicians and electricians who will need to work on charging infrastructure.

Centennial College in Ontario is also expanding its offerings to help upskill existing Red Seal certified technicians and train new apprentices.

Pollution Probe's report recommends integrating electric vehicle content into trade curricula, and Michael Lomnicki, a professor in the School of Transportation and a Red Seal mechanic, said that's exactly what they’re working on at Centennial College.

"There's careers to be had, absolutely," he said. "I definitely think that it's important to invest in, so that all of our students can create value for themselves and lead this industry as technology evolves."

Chung of the Automotive Industries Association of Canada says this is a crucial component of the EV transition.

"Repairing and maintaining these cars is the most sustainable solution, right?" she said. "And so it goes hand in hand with the whole thought of being eco-friendly and moving towards clean energy."

– Bridget Stringer-Holden

Check out our podcast and radio show. In our latest episode : Flood-prone communities are doing everything to keep water out. But as climate-fuelled storms become more severe, some architects say we need to work with water, not fight it. We learn how amphibious engineering kept Bangladeshi kids in school and allowed a Louisiana community to stay afloat.

LISTEN | What if your home could float when a flood hits?: What On Earth 23:10 What if your home could float when a flood hits?

Check the CBC News Climate Dashboard for live updates on record-breaking weather and current conditions across the country. Set your location to find out how today's temperatures compare to historical trends.

(CBC)

Reader feedback

Last week, Emily Chung wrote about Canadian technology to cool subway stations , with the goal of recovering the heat in the future.

David Fujiwara wrote: "That’s great that energy efficient chilled water will be used in the East Broadway subway station, but nowhere do you tell us where that chilled water is coming from. If you are chilling the water with electric refrigeration is it so energy efficient? And if [the system] doesn’t yet have a district heat system to connect to, where is excess heat going in the interim?"

Yes, the system uses electric refrigeration. As mentioned in the article, because it is passive cooling without fans, it is expected to be 25 to 35 per cent more efficient and more compact than a traditional air conditioning system. During the pilot, the excess heat will be measured and vented above ground. But both the MTA and Cascara Energy are interested in making use of it in the future, to heat water (such as swimming pools) and buildings.

Write us at whatonearth@cbc.ca (and send photos there, too!)

The Big Picture: A landmark battery

(John Laytner/Civic Grid)

Stationary batteries are becoming a bigger part of our electricity system, helping support the use of clean but intermittent energy such as wind and solar . Batteries can store power when it's plentiful, feed extra power onto the grid when supplies are short and provide backup power during outages. But where should those batteries go?

Distributed energy storage firm Civic Grid argues they should be close to where people live and use the power. The photo above shows an example of its vision — a pilot project launched Wednesday in Cannington, Ont. The 60 kW battery is lit up beside the building on the right "transforming an invisible piece of electrical infrastructure into a public landmark," the company says. Its goal is to explore how energy storage can "move beyond industrial sites and become part of the communities it serves."

The battery is charged from the grid at night when power is plentiful. During the day, it can supply up to six hours of power to two buildings used by the Nourish and Develop Foundation, which provides local food and social services (on the right and at the back of the photo). It also supplies lighting to a privately owned public square on the property, including a sheltered seating area (back left).

— Emily Chung

Hot and bothered: Provocative ideas from around the web

The presence of cougars in a region can reduce the risk of car crashes, a new study finds. Here's how .

A U.S. company has effectively brought a geothermal well back from the dead to become one of the most productive pumped geothermal wells in the country.

Do small, individual green habits like recycling and taking transit distract people from taking bigger, more meaningful action? Or do they prime people to support or participate in larger climate initiatives? A new study may have solved this debate .

Big industrial offshore wind farms can impact wildlife such as birds that can fly into them. But researchers are finding they also provide habitat to creatures, from oyster larvae to porpoises. Atmos brings you up close to some of these wind farm dwellers .

This town tested a drone show as an animal-friendly alternative to fireworks

Images of fireworks, seen in a screenshot from a YouTube video, were among those created by 100 drones as an alternative to fireworks in the Town of Three Rivers, P.E.I., on Aug. 1. (H3xan01c/YouTube)

The Town of Three Rivers in P.E.I. replaced fireworks with a drone light show for its summer festival this year.

The town's Montague Arts and Culture Festival on Aug. 1 featured acclaimed P.E.I. singer-songwriter Lennie Gallant, along with what the town believes to be Prince Edward Island’s first-ever drone light show instead of a traditional fireworks display.

Jonathon Gardner, events and facilities co-ordinator for the Town of Three Rivers, said the idea began with an email from P.E.I. CARES — the Companion Animal Rescue Education Society — outlining some of the downsides of fireworks.

"There were quite a few reasons why fireworks aren't great for the environment and animals and people," Gardner told Mainstreet P.E.I. host Nicola MacLeod.

"Originally, we thought it was going to be far too expensive as well.... After looking into it, it was mildly affordable and [we] thought it would be a really neat change."

The show used 100 illuminated drones to create animated images and patterns in the night sky, synchronized to music.

WATCH | A YouTube video that captured the drone show:

Gardner said there is also growing awareness of how fireworks can affect people who are sensitive to noise, including those who have post-traumatic stress disorder.

"With our first responders or military, the amount of PTSD, absolutely, that could trigger [it]," he said.

Karla Shalley, founder and president of P.E.I. CARES, said the organization sent the same email to every municipality on P.E.I., hoping to encourage communities to rethink fireworks.

"We know what a thunderstorm causes with animals. Imagine that tenfold with fireworks," she said.

The P.E.I. Humane Society has also welcomed the move.

Ashley Travis, the organization's development and communications co-ordinator, said it regularly sees the fallout from fireworks displays.

"Nearly every year when there's a community fireworks display, we will receive a call from someone who either wasn't aware that there was going to be fireworks that evening or who perhaps brought their animal to a fireworks display," she said.

"There have been incidents where animals have fled, and ... we've seen animals get seriously injured when fleeing from loud noises like fireworks."

People often forget that what feels festive to humans can be frightening for animals, Travis said.

"Your animal does not know what's going on. They don't understand what a firework is. They just hear a very loud noise, an explosion. They can see very bright lights sometimes and it can be very, very scary for them," she said.

"We always say that the best-case scenario is to leave your pet at home during a fireworks display to make sure that they're going to be safe."

Both Travis and Shalley hope other communities will now consider alternatives to fireworks.

Ahead of the show, Gardner said the reaction from the community was encouraging.

"There’s been a lot of positive feedback. Lots of people are saying, 'I want to come and check it out, and I want to see it,'" he said.

— Thinh Nguyen

World.title: When mom was diagnosed with dementia, we had a blueprint for her care written by her
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

This First Person column is the experience of Crystal MacCormac, who lives in Charlottetown. For more information about CBC's First Person stories, please see the FAQ.

My mother walks into my apartment in P.E.I. for the first time after 11 years of living in Ontario. She smiles brightly as she hugs me and looks around.

Her eyes fall upon a photo on my wall: a picture of her at two years old, sitting in front of a birthday cake.

“Oh wow. Look, that's me!” she says, walking closer for a better look.

Fast forward a couple of days to her second visit. Mom looks around, another bright smile on her lips.

“Oh wow. Look, that’s me!”

It happens again a week later.

My spidey senses started to tingle and fear began to seep in.

“Well, that’s not a good sign,” I thought.

I paid closer attention after that — watching, listening to everything mom did and said. It was 2020, so I spent more time with her, thanks to the rules imposed by the pandemic. Mom became one of the 10 people in my social bubble during lockdown, and with so few distractions, I was able to put most of my focus into my mom and her declining mental capacity.

My younger sister, who’d lived with mom for a long time, noticed changes, too.

By 2024, mom’s memory continued to decline, as did other things.

She was 65 when she was diagnosed so if it were just the pain in her hip, the digestion issues or the decline in her eyesight, we may not have raised the alarm. But it all happened at once, forcing us to take notice.

Ultimately, mom was diagnosed with vascular dementia. The diagnosis took almost a year as her swift decline continued.

That’s when our lives took a detour onto an unexpected and bumpy road.

This photo of MacCormac’s mom, Barb, as a child served as one of the first indicators that her mom’s memory might be failing. (Submitted by Crystal MacCormac)

But luckily, we knew what to do because mom had already shown us. When her own mother — my grandmother — suffered an unrelated physical and cognitive decline, my mother and the rest of our family stepped up to care for Nanny for the following five years.

My mom moved into her parents home to help. She had an inside look at the struggles that came up during that time.

A couple years after losing Nanny, mom sat me and my two siblings down to talk to us. She told us what she wanted, who she wanted advocating for her, under what circumstances we were to transition her into a nursing home, who was to arrange her funeral and at what point to end care or sign a "do not resuscitate" order.

I’m grateful we didn’t have to make these decisions on the fly while juggling mom’s care and our own emotions. There is so much to learn and so much information coming in, but knowing our roles made the process so much easier.

But it left me wondering: how would we have survived if we hadn’t made plans in advance? I don’t know how I would have learned all the medical jargon while also trying to connect with the right people and agencies. Weaving through all the twists and turns would have taken my attention away from mom and her care.

Social services gave us terrific guidance. We also relied on P.E.I.’s home care program, which helped us obtain medical supplies and respite care, and connected us with medical professionals in the community to help mom at home when she was less mobile.

The Alzheimer’s Society was another lifeline. The counselling I got through them was geared toward my own mental health as a caregiver.

Because even with our blueprint, parenting my parent is so hard. The dynamic switch came with fear and so much sadness I sometimes felt like I was drowning.

The hardest is when what mom wants now doesn’t match what mom before the disease wanted.

When I told her she had to move into a nursing home, her reaction was heartbreaking.

Nanny lived at home until her death and I would have done the same for mom. But I knew I was doing what mom had wanted. She made it clear years earlier that under no circumstances were we to go against her wishes, but it took everything in me to follow through.

I’m grateful I had the support that allowed me to be vulnerable, to cry, to say the hard things out loud and to find the strength to do the next hard thing.

Now, I can cherish my time with mom because I’m confident in the decisions we made together as a family. We don’t have to guess what she would have wanted or argue amongst ourselves.

But it’s still hard. Mom is no longer mom. She is still here in body, but not cognizant of what is best for her. She has no control over her own life anymore except through the decisions she made earlier.

I love my mother, and all I want is for her to be happy and to know she is safe. Thanks to the blueprint, I am able to advocate for her with determination, with gusto and without guilt — knowing that I’m doing what I promised her I would do.

Are you an Islander with a compelling personal story that can bring understanding or help others? We want to hear from you. Here's more info on how to pitch to CBC P.E.I.

World.title: First Nations chiefs in B.C. call on Carney, Smith to halt advancing West Coast pipeline
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A group that represents numerous First Nations across British Columbia is calling on Ottawa and Alberta's government to halt efforts to advance the West Coast pipeline, saying expanding the oil industry will accelerate climate change and disasters.

"The destructive and disastrous consequences of expanding fossil fuel production extend far beyond any single territory," the Union of British Columbia Indian Chiefs said in a letter addressed to Prime Minister Mark Carney and Alberta Premier Danielle Smith.

"From catastrophic wildfires to destructive floods and rising seas, the impacts of climate change are already being felt across this country. Every new fossil fuel project deepens that crisis."

The letter came Sunday, a day after the B.C. government issued a state of emergency as more than 100 wildfires burned across the province, with one forcing nearly 25,000 people across two communities east of Vancouver to flee. Nearly half of the wildfires were burning out of control.

The Indigenous group said it is also publishing the letter on International Day of the World's Indigenous Peoples on Sunday to reaffirm that it's against the pipeline because government has not consulted and co-operated in good faith with the First Nations.

WATCH | Canada, Alberta advance West Coast pipeline project: Canada and Alberta advance west coast pipeline project | Duration 2:12 Prime Minister Mark Carney and Alberta Premier Danielle Smith discuss details of the proposed 1 million-barrel-a-day pipeline to B.C.

It said government has already developed the project's corridor, named prospective development partners and is publicly promoting its economic case.

"Consultation cannot be meaningful if First Nations are invited only to discuss how a predetermined project will proceed."

Karah Folk, spokesperson for Alberta's Ministry of Indigenous Relations, said in an email to CBC News that the project provides "long-term benefits" for Indigenous communities, who will be consulted as it progresses.

"Our government remains committed to ongoing dialogue with First Nations and all partners as this work continues," Folk said.

Carney and Smith's offices did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Sunday.

The roughly 1,250-kilometre West Coast pipeline would carry upwards of one million barrels of crude oil per day from Bruderheim, Alta., to a port near Delta, B.C., for shipment to international markets.

The Alberta government is listed as the pipeline project's proponent. The pipeline would be owned by Trans Mountain, the Alberta Petroleum Marketing Commission and Pembina Pipeline Corp.

WATCH | A closer look at the pipeline route: The crowded, muddy reality of Alberta’s new pipeline route | Duration 5:40 Alberta’s new southern pipeline would mostly mirror the existing Trans Mountain corridor until Hope, B.C., where it would split and send oil to a marine terminal at Roberts Bank, but as CBC’s Georgie Smyth explains, this ‘easier’ plan won’t be straightforward.

Ottawa took a step last week toward giving the proposed project a national interest designation under the Building Canada Act, which would allow government to fast-track the pipeline and skirt some environmental laws.

The government said it is accepting public feedback until mid-September on the designation.

Ottawa and Alberta have agreed the pipeline would be conditional on a carbon storage project called Pathways, and vice versa. Pathways, which is owned by various companies, would prevent emissions from increased oil production from entering the atmosphere, and is tied to the pipeline going ahead. It involves a pipeline network that would carry carbon emissions from several sites in northern Alberta to an underground storage hub near Cold Lake, Alta.

A think-tank called the Canadian Climate Institute said in July, however, that emissions from the increased production that a new West Coast pipeline would enable far eclipse what Pathways would prevent from entering the atmosphere.

The West Coast pipeline is among several projects that have been approved or proposed under Carney's Major Projects Office, which is headquartered in Calgary.

Ottawa has said the projects are meant to be of national interest and strengthen Canada's autonomy, provide economic benefits, advance Indigenous interests and meet Canada's climate change goals in a rapidly shifting global landscape.

The Building Canada Act outlines the projects' regulatory pathway.

The Conservatives helped the government pass the Building Canada Act more than a year ago, and the government has so far moved three projects toward the national interest designation under the act.

Those projects are the Grays Bay road and port project in Nunavut, the Mackenzie Valley Highway in the Northwest Territories and the Nuclear Waste Management Organization's deep geological repository in northern Ontario.

World.title: What lives in the rivers near you? Why scientists want you to know
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

In a suburban creek steps from busy roads, biologists sent a mild, electrical current into the water and waited to see what surfaced.

The stunned fish they scooped up included spiky mottled sculpins, blacknose dace with striking red racing stripes and chunky creek chub — residents of the largely hidden freshwater world in and around Ontario's towns and cities.

Scientists are using techniques such as electrofishing and environmental DNA sampling to uncover that biodiversity. They are finding far more species than traditional methods have detected, even as many are disappearing or being replaced by invasive species.

Scientists say protecting creatures from dace and mayfly nymphs to mussels starts with knowing what is there.

But identifying and measuring freshwater life is challenging.

Physid pond snail. (Anthony Ricciardi/McGill University)

Uncovering little creatures — and bigger ones

A recent study published by University of Guelph biologist Mehrdad Hajibabaei and his team searched for environmental DNA (eDNA) in water from 18 Ontario rivers.

Organisms shed DNA through skin, scales and feces. Using those traces, researchers identified hundreds of aquatic invertebrates that had not been found through traditional methods.

Only 22 species identified through traditional methods were not detected by the DNA survey. Many species were found at just one site, showing how much river life can be missed.

Northern virile crayfish (Faxionius virilis). (Submitted by Anthony Ricciardi)

Nautilus ramshorn snail (Armiger crista). (Submitted by Anthony Ricciardi)

Last year, CBC News accompanied a team using another technique — electrofishing — to count fish in Tannery Creek in Aurora, Ont., near busy streets and subdivisions.

Wearing hip waders, gloves and battery-powered backpacks, Ontario Streams staff dipped pole-mounted rings into the creek, delivering mild electrical shocks that briefly stunned nearby fish. They netted, counted and measured the fish before returning them to the water.

To electrofish, scientists dip a ring into the water that delivers a mild shock from a powered backpack, stunning nearby fish. In this photo, Ontario Streams staff were teaching the technique to other biologists at Tannery Creek in Aurora, Ont., the spring of 2025. (Craig Chivers/CBC)

Kat Lucas, then the group's outreach co-ordinator and spokesperson, said passersby often ask what crews are doing when they see them electrofishing in urban parks around Toronto.

"They'll be surprised to hear that there are fishes that live in these rivers right through our big cities," said Lucas, who is now an outreach specialist with Credit Valley Conservation.

Urban creeks are even home to critically endangered species such as redside dace and an Ontario population of Atlantic salmon that went locally extinct a century ago and is now being reintroduced.

Kat Lucas, former outreach co-ordinator and spokesperson for Ontario Streams, peers at a mottled sculpin collected during the group's electrofishing workshop. Lucas is now an outreach specialist with Credit Valley Conservation. (Craig Chivers/CBC)

A 'silent mass extinction'

Scientists who compiled data from freshwater surveys around the world reported last year that one-quarter of freshwater animals on Earth are threatened with extinction .

Although half the world's population lives within three kilometres of freshwater , the researchers noted that "declines are continuing, generally out of sight and out of mind."

McGill University Prof. Anthony Ricciardi does research on the Richelieu River in Quebec. (Submitted by Anthony Ricciardi)

Anthony Ricciardi, a McGill University biology professor who studies freshwater biodiversity, said North America has already lost many species.

"At least 120 extinctions of freshwater animals in North America were recorded over the past 125 years," he said. "Hundreds of mussels, gastropods, fishes, crayfishes and amphibians are at risk of future extinction."

Ricciardi calls it a "silent" mass extinction because even conservation biologists "do not seem to be aware or paying much attention to it," he said.

That's partly because freshwater biodiversity has traditionally been difficult to measure, as Hajibabaei's findings show.

Water penny beetle larva. (Submitted by Anthony Ricciardi)

'What's going on underwater is dramatic'

People who work, play or live beside the water may know little about its inhabitants. That can put species at risk, Ricciardi suggested.

"How would people who don't know what's living underwater feel any empathy or any sense of loss?"

As a boy, he waded waist-deep to collect native crayfish and mussels in the St. Lawrence River near Lachine, Que. Many of those species are disappearing, pushed aside by invasive spinycheek crayfish and zebra and quagga mussels.

"Even if the river looks more or less the same," he said, "what's going on underwater is dramatic and rapid."

Eastern lampmussel (Lampsilis radiata) with some invasive zebra mussels attached. (Submitted by Anthony Ricciardi)

Freshwater species are going extinct five times faster than animals on land, Ricciardi said. Pollution, invasive species and dams have all taken a toll.

Why we need mussels — and other aquatic creatures

Each species disappearing from rivers and lakes has a job, Ricciardi said, "and as we lose species, some of those jobs don't get done."

Native mussels burrow into lake and river beds, helping replenish oxygen needed by other creatures. Insect larvae, including dragonflies, mayflies and caddisflies — groups experiencing " significant" species declines — are essential food for fish.

Mayfly nymph (Stenonema). (Submitted by Anthony Ricciardi)

Hajbabaei said many freshwater species are also important indicators of water quality.

"They are much more sensitive than any other chemical test or physical test," he said.

Knowing what lives where, and what is disappearing, is "critical" to their conservation, Hajbabaei said.

"You can't manage something that you cannot measure."

Freshwater sponge (Eunapius fragilis). (Submitted by Anthony Ricciardi)

He said greater public awareness of freshwater neighbours is key. When people know which species live nearby, "they can actually come up with creative ways to protect biodiversity."

Ricciardi said many declining freshwater creatures could still be saved by reducing polluted runoff, removing dams from rivers and fighting invasive species.

Migratory fish are returning to rivers where dams have been removed, he said, and no new invasive species have been recorded in the Great Lakes since ballast-water regulations were introduced in 2008.

"There are success stories," he added, "when we intervene to reverse a problem."

WATCH | Watch these endangered mussels return home to Canadian waters: Watch these endangered mussels return home to Canadian waters | Duration 1:57 Nearly 800 kidneyshell mussels were released in the Medway Creek in London, Ont. on Wednesday. This is the first time a freshwater mussel species has been reintroduced to a lost habitat in Canada. Find out how these little creatures protect biodiversity.

This is part of a series of articles highlighting the work of scientists looking at disappearing groups of species you may not have thought much about. It's a chance to get to know them and how they impact our lives, and find out what can be done to keep them around.

World.title: US seeks $1B aid package for Colombia’s new government
World.content:
Th US State Department said it will ask Congress for $1 billion for “deepening our shared and economic partnership” with the government of Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella.

The funding boost, which resembles that of the first year of Plan Colombia in 2000, seeks to “support the De la Espriella Administration’s efforts to defeat the vicious narcoterrorist and criminal organizations that threaten US, Colombian, and hemispheric security and economic prosperity.”

In preliminary talks, De la Espriella had already agreed to join the “Shield of the Americas,” a regional initiative of far-right governments to jointly fight crime.

According to a fact sheet, the funds that would require congressional approval would be used to:

Strengthen Colombia’s security forces

Disrupt illegal armed groups and organized crime’s ability to launder money

Significantly expand coca eradication and cocaine interdiction operations

Halt migration

Increase State presence in conflict regions

Combat child recruitment and exploitation by illegal armed groups

The administration of President Donald Trump also seeks to “increase trade and deepen economic ties between our countries.”

In order to do this, nominated US ambassador Nate Morris told the Senate that De la Espriella would withdraw from a memorandum of understanding with the government of China that sought to improve ties with the Asian giant.

Trump’s aid package would help Colombian communities “recover from potential El Niño-related flooding, drought,” which is expected to cause emergencies between December and March.

The US would also support a Bilateral Prosperity Dialogue to “stabilize” Colombia’s economy, “strengthening its energy generation and distribution sectors, exploring critical mineral investments, and creating new opportunities for US investors.”

The aid package would additionally “strengthen Colombian small and medium enterprises in agribusiness, manufacturing, and tech services by connecting them to US buyers and linking them to U.S.-aligned supply chains.”

The two governments would additionally seek to modernize Colombia’s digital, port and energy infrastructure while “positioning Colombia as a trusted nearshoring partner for supply chain diversification.”

World.title: De la Espriella sworn in as Colombia’s new president
World.content:
President Abelardo de la Espriella was sworn in in Colombia’s third largest city, Cali, under extreme security precautions.

De la Espriella was sworn in by the president of Congress, Senator Honorio Henriquez of the far-right Democratic Center party in the theater of the private University of Santiago de Cali.

The first part of the ceremony was attended by the Spanish King Felipe VI, multiple heads of state from Latin America and more than 60 ambassadors.

After being sworn in, De la Espriella went to the nearby Pichincha Battalion to assume the supreme command of the armed forces and hold his first speech as president.

The president vowed the security forces that he would be “an essential part of the miracle country” and vowed that at the end of his four-year mandate “authority will be felt in every corner of the country.”

De la Espriella also promised that “nobody will be persecuted for his opinions” and warned members of the “regime” of former President Gustavo Petro he would cooperate with “other States,” suggesting they could be extradited.

Both ceremonies were boycotted by Petro’s leftist political party, the Historic Pact, which organized political rallies elsewhere in Cali, and in the cities of Bogota and Barranquilla.

In Barranquilla, Senator Ivan Cepeda stressed the left does not recognize the incoming government because of De la Espriella’s US citizenship and his alleged debts with the US Department of Justice.

“De la Espriella, who once acted as an intermediary for drug traffickers and paramilitaries—from whose ill-gotten gains he has profited—has now become a figure who will be pressured by the United States, by his own government, and by its federal agencies to allow all kinds of foreign intervention in Colombia,” said Cepeda.

The leftist senator lost the elections to De la Espriella with a razor-thin margin of less than one percent. His supporters continue to seek a court order to nullify the election.

World.title: Colombia investigating governors, mayors over $941M corruption racket
World.content:
Prosecutors arrested 13 suspects and asked Colombia’s Supreme Court to investigate seven (former) governors over their alleged involvement in the embezzlement of COP3 trillion ($941 million).

The arrests and the investigation requests are related to the public-private partnership Sierra Nevada Mixed Fund, which was created by Martin Zuleta (U Party) and his family when he was mayor of La Paz, Cesar, in early 2021.

While supposedly serving the interests of La Paz, the Sierra Nevada Mixed Fund allegedly used forged documents to illegally appropriate funds from the General Royalties System with the help of governors from at least five provinces.

“So far, we’ve tracked 3 trillion pesos, of which it has been established that some were misappropriated through irregular contracts,” anti-corruption prosecutor Madeleyne Perez said at a press conference.

Among those whose cases were forwarded to the Supreme Court were the governors of Magdalena, Vichada, Amazonas Guaviare an Vaupes.

Former Governors Rafael Martinez of Magdalena and Alvaro Leon of Vichada will also be investigated by the Supreme Court.

Among those who were arrested is the mayor of Maria la Baja, a contractor and multiple (former) directors of the mixed fund.

The non-profit has been investigated since 2024 when authorities found irregularities in the construction of a high school in the Huila province, funds for school transport in Casanare and funds meant for indigenous reserves in La Guajira.

A report by the now-defunct radio station W from that year showed that Sierra Nevada had been hired by authorities from throughout Colombia for a wide variety of projects, avoiding any open bidding procedure.

W found more than 100 contracts between mainly local and regional government authorities and the non-profit.

According to Caracol, Zuleta was taken to hospital after his home was raided by prosecution officials and would be available to cooperate with the prosecutors investigating his alleged involvement in corruption.

World.title: Colombia’s left presents evidence suggesting De la Espriella won through fraud
World.content:
Colombia’s President Gustavo Petro and data analysts presented evidence suggesting that President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella won the election through the mass manipulation of tally sheets.

During a two-hour presentation, Petro claimed that almost all tally sheets that had been shared with his political party, the Historic Pact “lacked the Hash security lock,” which is inserted into official PDF documents to guarantee they can’t be changed.

The absence of a hash file implies that the so-called E14 tally sheets may have been altered, which appears to have happened, according to data analysts who accompanied the president.

Legal expert William Villanueva said that original tally sheets were scanned and subsequently reprocessed, removing the metadata that would allow them to determine whether the E14’s were uploaded or introduced digitally.

“We found documents marked ‘confidential’… and others that said ‘not digitized’ on a blank page, which—and this is important—were later republished with different information,” said one of the computer scientists.

The investigation, which was carried out by 75,000 “digital witnesses,” found that 95 municipalities had more voters than inhabitants. In all of these municipalities, the E-14’s gave De la Espriella landslide victories with more than 70% of the votes.

The president-elect’s opponent, leftist Senator Ivan Cepeda, achieved not a single victory in hundreds of towns where the electoral census was larger than 85% of the population.

In 1,350 polling centers in capital cities, the researchers found that block patterns in which De la Espriella won the first half of the voting booths and Cepeda won the second half.

According to a consulted statistician, this result would only be probably in some 80 polling stations, said Carlos Oñoro, one of the digital witnesses.

“This order is mathematically impossible for human voters,” Petro stated, arguing that automated software replaced actual citizen ballots.

The findings of the digital witnesses will be added to a lawsuit that seeks to nullify the election of De la Espriella and force the Council of State to order a recount of the votes.

Following the presentation, Cepeda said in a post on social media network X that “the competent authority must impartially examine our demands of nullity.”

World.title: De la Espriella says he won’t allow Colombia’s left to “destabilize democracy”
World.content:
Colombia’s far-right President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella said that he won’t allow his country’s left to “destabilize democracy” through civil disobedience against his US citizenship.

In his weekly address to the nation, De la Espriella stressed that after Friday he will be president and “with the force of the constitution and the law” ensure that his power will be upheld.

The civil disobedience announced by leftist opposition leader Ivan Cepeda “is nothing more than a euphemism for an attempt to destabilize democracy,” said De la Espriella.

“I will not allow it,” said the president-elect.

I am the president of all Colombians, and I will ensure, through the power of the Constitution and the law, that what the Colombian people decided—which was to elect me—is upheld. My call to the entire nation is that we stop normalizing what is wrong, illegal, and corrupt. Let’s call things by their proper names and confront them for what they are. This so-called “civil disobedience” is nothing more than a euphemism for an attempt to destabilize democracy, and I will not allow it. Abelardo de la Espriella

According to De la Espriella, the left “combined all forms of struggle,” a term used by the now-defunct guerrilla group FARC to justify the violence used by the insurgents, “and lost.”

Cepeda called on his followers to peaceful civil disobedience in response to the president-elect’s refusal to renounce his US citizenship.

The incoming opposition leader and his political party, the Historic Pact, support legal efforts to challenge De la Espriella’s election on claims that fraud concerns have not been tackled.

More radical elements within the Historic Pact, including outgoing President Gustavo Petro, have sustained that the far-right won the elections through deceit and fraud, but have failed to present evidence that would confirm a criminal conspiracy.

World.title: As De la Espriella takes office, his US-backed security policy for Colombia is raising questions
World.content:
Colombia’s far-right President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella assumes office on Friday, after elections with a razor-thin margin. He brings with him promises to wield “iron fist” policies against non-state armed groups (NSAGs) and organized criminal organizations in the country.

He has also promised to dismantle ongoing peace talks initiated by outgoing leftist President Gustavo Petro, including groups that are currently disarming. De la Espriella made scores of hardline promises on the campaign trail, many of which he will likely not be able to achieve with a minority coalition in the legislature, such as withdrawing Colombia from the United Nations.

On security issues, however, Colombia’s constitution grants the president broad unilateral powers. De la Espriella has promised to “end” armed groups within a month, an extremely unlikely goal. Despite the broad powers of the presidential office, De la Espriella faces historical and logistical limitations.

Despite claims from right-wing parties that Petro has gone easy on armed groups, Colombia’s military has been fully deployed against NSAGs in the country for the last two years.

As conflict expert Thomas Garrison reported for news website Pirate Wire Services in June, Colombia has ongoing and large military operations against FARC dissident group Estado Mayor Central (EMC), the National Liberation Army (ELN), and EMC splinter-group EMBF.

Colombia’s security forces are “already operating on all cylinders,” and “stretched to their limit,” according to the International Crisis Group. It isn’t clear how deployments can be increased without increasing the numbers of security forces themselves — hardly a goal that can be achieved in his first month in office.

Nonetheless, there are strategic changes that de La Espriella can impose to chart a more aggressive course. As part of those plans, the president-elect has promised to implement a “Plan Patriota remixed”, an allusion to highly aggressive US-backed military operations against armed groups under then-President Alvaro Uribe in 2003.

Uribe’s allies to this day hail Plan Patriota as a great success that forced the FARC to the negotiating table in 2016.

Critics, however, point to rampant human and civil rights violations, including working with paramilitary forces to kill thousands of civilians and frame them as guerrilla fighters to increase casualty counts.

The US, however, is pushing Latin America towards increased military spending and Bukele-style crackdowns on organized crime, and de la Espriella plans to comply.

What was Plan Patriota and how will Abelardo’s version be ‘remixed’?

Plan Patriota involved aerial bombardments, large-scale military deployments in FARC-controlled areas, and aggressive intelligence gathering against FARC guerrillas at the height of Colombia’s civil war.

Although paramilitary groups were not officially part of Plan Patriota, they cooperated closely with regular military forces during the operation, functioning as spies, informants, and death squads — ostensibly killing alleged guerrillas, but just as often murdering leftists in general, as well as non-politically involved civilians.

The operation, which continued until 2010, weakened the FARC considerably, but at a great price: gross human rights violations including massacres, torture, and using sexual violence against civilians as a weapon of war.

Paramilitary structures were also greatly empowered across the country, sowing the seeds of groups that still exist today, such as the Ejercito Gaitanista Colombiano (EGC) — often referred to in Western media as ‘the Clan del Golfo.’

The full extent of the atrocities committed by both sides of the war would not become clear until Colombia launched its Truth Commission in 2017. (De la Espriella wants to disband the Truth Commission as well as the Colombian Peace Court, which prosecutes the worst offenders of the civil war.)

Any new version of Plan Patriota would look very different. Colombia is not the same country it was in the early 2000’s. Modern armed groups are not interested in clashing with state forces on the battlefield. Most are not interested in overthrowing the state at all, and certainly not via military victory.

Technology has also advanced considerably. Drone warfare is a dangerous new weapon in the arsenal of NSAGs who wage asymmetrical attacks on state forces as well as one another. Digital surveillance and satellite optics also mean that unlike the FARC, which often relied upon jungle canopies to hide large training and logistics camps, modern NSAGs instead blend into civil society in the communities where they operate.

They do not wear uniforms to distinguish themselves and avoid direct confrontations with the military, which means there are no large targets to bomb, nor columns of marching fighters for the state to confront.

Modern NSAGs are far more flexible, transnational, and relatively decentralized in their operations compared to FARC at the height of the civil war.

De la Espriella’s security program is more likely to look like Daniel Noboa’s policies in Ecuador than the 2002 Plan Patriota. It will likely include US cooperation on target-finding, naval cooperation on drug trafficking, and joint US-Colombia operations within the country.

Most of those dynamics already exist. Despite a rocky relationship with Washington, D.C, Petro continued to cooperate with the US on intelligence-sharing and anti-narcotics operations.

Critics of de la Espriella, however, fear that logistics won’t be the only similarity to Ecuadorian-US operations, which have resulted in the murder of civilians by security forces, torture, arbitrary detentions, and bombings of civilian infrastructure.

One factor that may keep de la Espriella somewhat in check is a lack of a clear mandate. He won elections by less than 1%, and has already clashed with more established right-wing political parties, who will not be forming part of his coalition in the legislature.

De la Espriella signals he will follow Washington’s lead

On a recent trip to the U.S, de la Espriella’s vice-president, José Manuel Restrepo, met with US Deputy Assistant Secretary of War for the Americas, Joseph M. Humire, who spoke of investment by US companies in hydrocarbon and energy sectors as well as cooperation on security and migration issues.

“Colombia is historically one of the U.S. strongest security and defense partners,” he wrote on X on July 21. “Under the leadership of incoming President Abelardo De La Espriella, we plan to take this partnership to new levels with Plan Patriot 2.0.”

Before Humire joined the War Department, he worked as an anti-migration lobbyist propagating conspiracy theories that cartels have “weaponized” migrants as part of “asymmetrical warfare” against the U.S.

He falsely testified before the House Foreign Affairs Committee in February that Venezuelan gang Tren de Aragua had “opened” the Darien Gap to migrants during the Biden administration as part of a Venezuelan plan to destabilize the US.

De la Espriella has already signalled that he looks forward to closer cooperation with the administration of US President Donald Trump and largely follow the US lead on regional issues. Trump has made migration a key facet of his domestic and foreign policy.

The ultra-right Colombian president-elect has also promised to “secure” the country’s borders. Migrants “who are here illegally, or committing crimes will be deported to their countries of origin without delay,” he said in a press conference on July 13.

He has agreed, however, to keep commercial and migratory pathways open on the Venezuelan border. Petro re-initiated diplomatic and commercial ties with Venezuela in 2022.

De la Espriella has not criticized Chavista governments as heavily as many other right-wing politicians in the country, and provided legal representation for Maduro loyalist Alex Saab, who has been extradited for a second time to the US to face money laundering and corruption charges.

Aggressive military strategies have failed in the past

The nature of conflict has changed drastically in Colombia since the civil war, and presidents have tried aggressive military tactics against criminal organizations and NSAGs before.

Former President Ivan Duque failed to slow the rapid growth of either during his time in office from 2018 to 2022.

The Colombian state failed to fulfill its promises to invest in legitimate economies and develop regions long ignored by Bogotá. Regions that had previously been governed by the FARC became power vacuums that were quickly filled by other criminal organizations and NSAGs.

Duque left office the least popular president in the country’s history since records have been kept, in part because of his security policy. Bombings on rebel camps that killed minors created significant public controversy. When Petro turned to similar strategies, the military inadvertently killed children in bombings in children as well.

Armed groups have continued to grow under Petro despite his employment of increasingly aggressive military strategies. De la Espriella has not offered details about his plans, and it is unclear what he could do that Duque and Petro did not, or why the results would be any different for his administration when similar tactics have failed before.

Trump, however, has gained a new ally in the region. The US president has often shown that projection of US power is an end in and of itself, and de la Espriella is likely to allow Trump to do exactly that.

World.title: Colombia Reports and 21st-century fascism
World.content:
The coming four years will probably be the toughest yet and I will need your support to keep Colombia’s longest-living news source alive.

The Espriella administration will be the third far-right government I have reported on since I started Colombia Reports in 2008.

I expect the incoming government to be the worst because it seeks to undo socio-economic policies that pulled 4 million people out of poverty and end peace processes that kept us safe.

Independent journalists (and the New York Times) have criticized Abelardo de la Espriella for his ties to the now-defunct paramilitary organization AUC and drug traffickers, and his alleged corruption of the judicial system, specifically in Colombia.

Many of these journalists have been harassed by De la Espriella’s law firm through at least 109 frivolous lawsuits, and the publication of their private information.

I can only guess what’s ahead for us after De la Espriella appointed reported frauds as his spokespersons and put a conspiracy theorist in charge of my visa.

I will need your support as what’s coming is probably going to be expensive. The last time I reported on a far-right government, I was forced to spend months in my native country, the Netherlands.

If you are not yet a paid subscriber, please become one. If you don’t want to commit to a monthly contribution, please make a one-time donation.

I promise I will continue reporting on Colombia and will update you on the political situation in Colombia through my podcasts with Richard McColl of Colombia Calling.

World.title: De la Espriella desists from holding swearing-in ceremony at military base
World.content:
President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella has apparently given up trying to be sworn in before the military and asked Congress to allow the ceremony to take place in Cali, Colombia’s third largest city.

In an address to the nation, De la Espriella said Sunday that volcanic activity made travel to Popayan, the capital of Cauca, made a “secure, well-organized” inauguration ceremony all but impossible.

“For this reason, I respectfully ask the honorable House of Representatives, which has not yet debated my inauguration in a plenary session, to convene the August 7th session in the city of Cali,” said the president-elect.

“As soon as I am sworn in as president of the republic, my government’s first security council will be held in the Marco Fidel Suarez airbase in the city of Cali,” added De la Espriella, suggesting he has given up his aspiration to be sworn in inside a military base.

In an interview, Santiago de Cali University president Carlos Andres Perez, told Blu Radio on Tuesday that Valle del Cauca Governor Dilian Francisca Toro told him the university theater would be used for the inauguration.

Following the main ceremony, De la Espriella will travel to the Pichincha Military Canton, the base of the 3rd Division, to assume his role as supreme commander of the armed forces.

The apparent decision to desist from a military inauguration comes after major tensions with the outgoing government of President Gustavo Petro, who ordered the military not to cooperate with his elected successor.

An inauguration at a military base was also opposed by the Democratic Center, the largest political party in De la Espriella’s far-right congressional coalition.

The opponents claimed that Colombia’s constitution submits the armed forces to civilian authority. A swearing-in ceremony before them would have been confusing and inappropriate.

According to De la Espriella, his intention meant to stress his support for the Colombia’s “heroes.”

World.title: Chile’s Municipalities, Senapred Meet Ahead of Storm Forecast
World.content:
SANTIAGO, Chile â As Chile prepares for an approaching winter storm system, the Association of Municipalities of Chile (Amuch) held a high-level coordination meeting with the National Disaster Prevention and Response Service (Senapred) to strengthen municipal emergency response measures.

The discussions focused on improving collaboration among municipalities, national agencies, and private service providers to better protect residents during severe weather events.

Power Companies Face Pressure Over Response Times

A central topic in the meeting was the performance of electric utilities during past emergencies. JosÃ© Manuel Palacios, mayor of La Reina, expressed concern over delayed responses from power companies in recent years.

âWe are exploring ways, together with Senapred and other institutions, to develop more efficient actions and hold the companies accountable to meet the response times our residents need,â Palacios said.

Rural Water Supply Risks Tied to Electricity

For rural municipalities, electrical outages pose a dual threat, as potable water systems often rely on electric power. Paula GÃ¡rate, mayor of Melipilla, emphasized the heightened vulnerability of rural areas during storms.

âLosing electricity also means losing access to potable water. Many rural water systems depend on electricity, and that remains our greatest concern,â GÃ¡rate noted.

Coordinated Municipal Efforts to Mitigate Risks

Senapred Director Alicia CebriÃ¡n highlighted the essential role of municipal governments in both preparation and response phases.

âMunicipalities play a crucial role in coordination, information gathering, and implementing mitigation works to reduce the impact of winter threats on residents,â CebriÃ¡n stated.

She underscored that emergency prevention and mitigation is a shared responsibility across public agencies and institutions. âPublic authorities who are directly involved in disaster management bear this responsibility, and we are committed to fulfilling it,â she added.

Winter System Expected to Test Emergency Readiness

The coordination meeting comes as Chileâs central regions brace for a frontal system expected to bring heavy rain and strong winds. Authorities emphasized that ongoing preparation and inter-agency cooperation will be key to minimizing disruption and protecting vulnerable communities.

World.title: Brian Wilson, Legendary Beach Boys Co-Founder, Dies at 82
World.content:
LOS ANGELES â Brian Wilson, the legendary musician, songwriter and co-founder of The Beach Boys, has died at the age of 82, his family announced.

“We are heartbroken to announce that our beloved father Brian Wilson has passed away,” the family said in a statement. “We are at a loss for words right now. Please respect our privacy at this time as our family is grieving. We realize that we are sharing our grief with the world.”

Born in 1942 in Hawthorne, California, Wilson formed The Beach Boys in 1961 with his younger brothers Carl and Dennis, cousin Mike Love, and friend Al Jardine. The band became one of the most influential and commercially successful acts in music history, selling over 100 million records worldwide.

Wilson was the creative force behind the groupâs distinctive harmonies and groundbreaking studio sound. His 1966 album Pet Sounds is regarded as a masterpiece that reshaped the boundaries of pop music production.

Among The Beach Boys’ many hits, Wilson co-wrote and produced I Get Around, Help Me, Rhonda, and Good Vibrations. Rolling Stone ranked The Beach Boys 12th on its list of the “100 Greatest Artists of All Time.”

Tributes poured in following news of his death. Nancy Sinatra shared a photo with Wilson on Instagram, writing, âHis cherished music will live forever as he travels through the Universe and beyond. God bless you, sweet Brian.â

Sean Ono Lennon called Wilson the “American Mozart” and a “one of a kind genius from another world,” adding: âAnyone who really knows me knows how heartbroken I am about Brian Wilson passing. Not many people influenced me as much as he did. I feel very lucky that I was able to meet him and spend some time with him. He was always very kind and generous.”

Throughout his life, Wilson faced significant personal struggles. Diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia in 1984, his condition was linked by doctors to earlier psychedelic drug use. In early 2024, his family revealed he had developed dementia.

Wilson’s wife, Melinda, with whom he shared 24 years of marriage and five adopted children, died earlier in 2024. He also had two daughters, Carnie and Wendy, from his first marriage.

Despite his health battles, Wilsonâs legacy remains unparalleled. His influence on songwriting, vocal harmony, and studio innovation continues to inspire generations of musicians.

World.title: Chile and Norway Deepen Antarctic Cooperation with New Agreement
World.content:
Chile and Norway signed a memorandum of understanding on Antarctic cooperation Monday, reinforcing their shared commitment to peace, science, and environmental protection in the region.

The agreement, signed by Chilean Foreign Minister Alberto van Klaveren and Norwegian Minister of International Development Ã smund GrÃ¸ver, aims to strengthen bilateral coordination under the Antarctic Treaty System. It outlines enhanced collaboration on scientific research, climate monitoring, and the preservation of marine ecosystems through frameworks such as the Antarctic Treaty Consultative Meetings and the Commission for the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources (CCAMLR).

The accord includes provisions for regular dialogue between scientific and governmental institutions in both countries and seeks to optimize joint efforts in Antarctic and sub-Antarctic research. Both nations also pledged support for the Polar Codeâs implementation, aiming to improve safety and environmental standards for ships operating in polar waters.

Operational and logistical cooperation between Chileâs and Norwayâs national Antarctic programs will also be explored, particularly in alignment with CCAMLRâs conservation objectives.

This renewed alliance builds on the long-standing historical ties between the two nations and reaffirms their role as active stewards of one of the worldâs most fragile and strategically vital environments.
