World.title: Japan Tops Global Waste Index 2025; U.S., Israel, and Chile Rank as Worst Polluters
World.content:
Japan has emerged as the world leader in waste management, while Israel, Chile, and the United States rank among the worst-performing countries, according to the Global Waste Index 2025 released by Slovak-based waste technology company Sensoneo.

The report, which ranks all 38 OECD member states based on their waste generation and disposal practices, highlights significant disparities in global waste management. Sensoneoâs index evaluates countries on per capita waste generation, recycling, incineration, and landfill use.

Israel and Chile ranked last and second-to-last, respectively, primarily due to their heavy reliance on environmentally damaging landfilling practices. Israel sends 524 of the 650 kilograms of waste it generates per person each year directly to landfills. Chile recycles just 1% of its waste and sends more than 95% to landfill.

The United States, which increased its per capita waste generation from 811 to 951 kilograms since 2022, remains the highest generator of municipal solid waste globally. The U.S. disposes of nearly half of that â 447 kilograms â in landfills annually. Neighboring Canada also performed poorly, landfilling 67% of its annual 694 kg per capita waste.

At the other end of the spectrum, Japan ranked No. 1, followed by South Korea and Estonia, all of which combine relatively low waste generation with efficient disposal methods. Japan sends only 3 kilograms per capita to landfill, relying heavily on incineration (245 kg) and maintaining a controlled recycling rate.

European countries dominated the top 10 rankings, with Austria, Germany, Finland, Belgium, Sweden, Norway, and Switzerland all demonstrating strong waste management systems. Austria topped the recycling chart with 334 kilograms of municipal waste recycled per person annually â accounting for 42% of its total waste.

Meanwhile, Spain fell four places to 27th despite minor improvements. The country reduced its landfill and incineration rates slightly while increasing recycling by 10 kilograms per capita. However, its overall waste generation rose by 10 kg compared to the 2022 index.

The index revealed that in 12 of the 38 countries, over half of all waste is still landfilled â including in developed nations like Australia, New Zealand, and Canada. By contrast, Switzerland was the only country to report zero landfill disposal, while Belgium, Finland, Estonia, and Japan landfilled less than 3 kg per person.

Other key findings include:

New Zealand , Finland , and Iceland posted the largest reductions in waste generation per capita.

, , and posted the largest reductions in waste generation per capita. From an environmental standpoint, incineration is considered preferable to landfilling, but excessive reliance on either suggests a need for stronger waste reduction and recycling strategies.

About the Index and Sensoneo

First launched in 2019, the Global Waste Index is published every three years by Sensoneo, a company specializing in digital transformation for waste management systems. The 2025 edition is based on the latest available national data.

Sensoneo operates in 87 countries and provides waste monitoring solutions to cities, industries, and governments. It is the only company to have successfully implemented deposit return systems (DRS) IT infrastructure in nine countries, achieving recycling rates above 90%.

In Madrid, Sensoneo is deploying 11,100 smart sensors, marking the worldâs largest smart waste monitoring installation to date.

World.title: South Korean Model and Actor Kim Jong Suk Dies at 29, Family Urges Respect Amid Speculation
World.content:
South Korean model and television personality Kim Jong Suk has died at the age of 29, his family confirmed on June 6. The news has shocked fans and colleagues across the countryâs entertainment industry, where Kim rose to prominence following his appearance on tvNâs 2022 reality dating show Skip Dating.

Kim, who began his career in modeling before transitioning to television, had been steadily gaining popularity in recent years. His sudden death has prompted an outpouring of grief and speculation online.

While the exact cause of death remains unconfirmed, some media reports have linked Kimâs passing to an incident in Hanam involving a violent altercation between a young man and his girlfriend. According to the reports, law enforcement responded to the scene, after which the man allegedly died by suicide after jumping from a high-rise building.

Amid widespread online discussion and conjecture, Kimâs family issued a public plea for restraint, asking the public and media to refrain from spreading misinformation or making disrespectful assumptions.

Kimâs older sister posted on social media, expressing the family’s devastation and emotional exhaustion. âWe ask for privacy and understanding during this difficult time,â she wrote, emphasizing the familyâs wish to grieve in peace.

Details regarding funeral arrangements have not been made public.

World.title: Keiko Fujimori starts her term in Peru with 60% approval, Datum poll finds
World.content:
Keiko Fujimori starts her term in Peru with 60% approval, Datum poll finds

9th Sunday, August 2026 - 20:58 UTC Full article

The poll is the first national measurement since Fujimori took office on July 28, after winning the June 7 runoff by one of the narrowest margins in Peruvian electoral history

Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori has begun her five-year term with a 60% approval rating, against 24% disapproval and 16% who gave no opinion, according to a Datum Internacional survey published on Sunday by the newspaper El Comercio.

The poll is the first national measurement since Fujimori took office on July 28, after winning the June 7 runoff by one of the narrowest margins in Peruvian electoral history. The Fuerza Popular leader took 50.135% of valid votes, or 9,223,396 ballots, against 49.865% for Roberto Sánchez of Juntos por el Perú, who received 9,173,755. The gap was 49,641 votes.

Despite that result, approval exceeds disapproval in every macro-region. It stands at 66% in the north, 64% in Lima and Callao, 62% in the central region and 54% in the Amazon east. In the south, where she lost the election, approval reaches 44% against 39% disapproval. By age group, the strongest backing comes from those aged 18 to 24, at 71%.

Sixty-two percent of respondents said they feel optimistic about the country's future, while 32% said they were pessimistic. On her first address to the nation, 62% said they had seen, heard or read about it; among those, 84% rated it positively and 13% negatively.

Expectations of the new administration center on the economy. Seventy-one percent expect the government to boost private investment, 66% to create jobs and 65% to improve the economy. Sixty-two percent believe it will bring order to the country, 60% that it will reduce crime and 51% that it will reduce corruption.

Security drew the widest consensus. Eighty-seven percent said they agreed with the armed forces joining National Police duties and with soldiers patrolling the streets, a measure announced by Fujimori. Some 86% support the military leading citizen security in jurisdictions under a state of emergency, and 85% back its taking charge of security in prisons.

On the new bicameral Congress, installed on July 24 after 34 years of a single-chamber system, 47% anticipate a confrontational relationship with the executive and 44% expect dialogue. Fuerza Popular is the largest bloc, with 22 of 60 senators and 41 of 130 deputies, short of an absolute majority. Sixty-seven percent said Congress should grant the legislative powers the executive has announced it will request on El Niño prevention, citizen security, economic affairs and labor.

The survey covered 1,205 people nationwide between August 5 and 7, with a margin of error of 2.8% and a 95% confidence level.

World.title: Bolivia records its first same-sex civil marriage after a court ruling
World.content:
Bolivia records its first same-sex civil marriage after a court ruling

9th Sunday, August 2026 - 20:44 UTC Full article

The couple, Fabiana Banzer and Scarlett Rocha, formally applied for a civil marriage on October 12, 2022

Bolivia has recorded its first civil marriage between two people of the same sex, held on Friday, August 7, in Santa Cruz, the country's most populous city, following a legal process that lasted three years and ten months.

The couple, Fabiana Banzer and Scarlett Rocha, formally applied for a civil marriage on October 12, 2022. The non-governmental organization IGUAL Bolivia, which provided legal support, said the union was completed after a lengthy administrative process and two constitutional injunctions filed by its team, until the couple obtained recognition and legal protection from the Bolivian state.

“Scar and I have been together for more than 4 years. It makes me very happy to announce to our family and friends that after a legal fight of 3 years and 10 months we have finally been able to access civil marriage as two women,” Banzer wrote on social media.

The decision does not alter Bolivia's legal framework. Article 63 of the constitution states that marriage is constituted between a woman and a man through legal bonds, and the Banzer-Rocha union was authorized through the courts in an individual case rather than by legislative reform. Bolivia therefore remains among the South American countries that do not recognize same-sex marriage in law, alongside Peru, Paraguay and Venezuela.

The immediate precedent dates to December 2020, when David Aruquipa and Guido Montaño secured registration of the country's first free union between two people of the same sex, following a ruling by the Second Constitutional Chamber of the La Paz departmental court that was later upheld by the Plurinational Constitutional Court. The Civil Registry Service has since recorded dozens of such unions.

Aruquipa said on Sunday that he and Montaño were marking the Banzer-Rocha marriage as a new and significant milestone in the advance of rights for same-sex couples in Bolivia, and as a development that widens the boundaries of equality. He argued the case should be read as part of a sequence: “Rather than speaking of a beginning, we should speak of a historical continuity: from the first recognized union to the first civil marriage.”

The transfeminist collective La Pesada Subversiva said the process involved a harsh legal battle against Bolivian institutions, marked by what it described as discrimination and mistreatment by authorities and public officials. The group noted that the application drew on advisory opinion 24/17, issued in 2017 by the Inter-American Court of Human Rights on gender identity and equality for same-sex couples.

The collective also argued that the free union, recognized since 2020, does not carry the same social recognition and standing as marriage. Bolivian authorities have not issued public statements on the case.

World.title: Uruguay's Partido Nacional sets a 2030 return to government as its goal
World.content:
Uruguay's Partido Nacional sets a 2030 return to government as its goal

9th Sunday, August 2026 - 20:37 UTC Full article

Former president Lacalle Pou also took part in the event and closed the proceedings. It was one of his first party appearances since he left office. Photo: Gastón Britos / EFE

The president of the board of Uruguay's Partido Nacional, Álvaro Delgado, on Sunday called on members of the country's main opposition force to “build the history of the future” and set a return to government in 2030 as the first objective, so that Uruguay can “find direction again.”

Delgado spoke at the central ceremony marking the party's 190th anniversary, held outside the party headquarters in Montevideo's Plaza Matriz. Founded on August 10, 1836, the Partido Nacional is Uruguay's oldest political party and one of the longest-running in Latin America.

“The first milestone of that history of the future that we all have to build together is to govern the country again from 2030, so that Uruguay finds direction again and so that people have hope again,” he told lawmakers, mayors, local councilors and party members who traveled from across the country.

Delgado said he perceives discouragement among part of the population and argued that his party has an obligation to build an option that restores people's hope. When hope recedes, he added, resignation sets in, and he pledged that the Partido Nacional would replace “resignation with expectation.”

Referring to the governing Frente Amplio administration, Delgado said the opposition should not confine itself to waiting for the government to fail. “We cannot wait for the government to make mistakes, which it does often. We are not going to wait. We are not going to keep complaining about the lack of direction and, obviously, the lack of results,” he said. To achieve that, he added, the party must have the humility to work every day and to listen to citizens.

He also called for safeguarding the record of the administration led by Luis Lacalle Pou between 2020 and 2025. “There are many who want to undo, out of ideological prejudice placed even above the national interest, many of the things we achieved in government. And we have to protect that,” he said.

Former president Lacalle Pou also took part in the event and closed the proceedings. It was one of his first party appearances since he left office on March 1, 2025, after a period of low public profile.

Delgado was the Partido Nacional's presidential candidate in the 2024 elections and lost the runoff to Yamandú Orsi of the Frente Amplio, who took office in March 2025, ending five years of government by the coalition led by the Nationalists.

Uruguay's electoral calendar explains the horizon set out by Delgado: the next general elections are scheduled for October 2029, with the handover of power due on March 1, 2030. Anniversary events continue on Monday with a Mass, a formal session of the party board and the presentation of a commemorative stamp.

World.title: Machado congratulates De la Espriella and says Venezuela will soon follow suit
World.content:
Machado congratulates De la Espriella and says Venezuela will soon follow suit

9th Sunday, August 2026 - 20:05 UTC Full article

“As sister peoples, united by a common history and culture, we know that our future is also inseparably linked,” she wrote

Venezuelan opposition leader and 2025 Nobel Peace Prize laureate María Corina Machado congratulated Colombia's new president, Abelardo de la Espriella, and said Venezuela would “very soon” undertake a process of institutional and democratic strengthening similar to the one she said is beginning in the neighboring country. The Colombian president replied on Sunday thanking her for the support.

Machado posted her message on Friday, the day of the inauguration, on her X account. “As sister peoples, united by a common history and culture, we know that our future is also inseparably linked,” she wrote. She added that both countries would need to work together to guarantee the full exercise of national sovereignty in their respective territories, the safety of their people and the prosperity of both nations.

De la Espriella responded two days later through the same channel. “Colombia and Venezuela are sister peoples, united by a history that no border can separate. I long for the day when our countries can move forward together, with strong institutions, full freedom, security and prosperity for our people,” he said. He added that Colombia would always extend a hand to Venezuelans and to those who defend democracy and freedom.

The Colombian president took office on August 7 for the 2026-2030 term at a ceremony held in Cali, the country's first presidential inauguration staged outside Bogotá. He won the June 21 runoff against Iván Cepeda of the Pacto Histórico by 250,830 votes. Machado backed his candidacy during the campaign.

The exchange comes as talks proceed in Caracas between the government of acting president Delcy Rodríguez and a section of the Venezuelan opposition. The delegations, led by National Assembly president Jorge Rodríguez and former lawmaker Dinorah Figuera, agreed on a first round of talks running through August 12. The process has the backing of the United States government.

Neither Machado nor fellow opposition figure Edmundo González Urrutia is taking part in those negotiations. Rodríguez has held the acting presidency since January 5, two days after Nicolás Maduro was captured in Caracas during a US military operation.

Colombia and Venezuela share a 2,219-kilometer land border running from the Caribbean to the Amazon, much of it through sparsely populated territory.

On Saturday, Venezuelan singer Ricardo Montaner addressed a message to the new Colombian president during a concert in Barranquilla, the city designated as the government's alternate seat. Montaner said Venezuela had endured severe abuses for 25 years and asked Colombia to help the country recover democracy and freedom. “I asked God to give the new president of Colombia wisdom, humility and awareness,” he said.

World.title: De la Espriella sworn in before Congress in Cali, delivers first speech to the military
World.content:
De la Espriella sworn in before Congress in Cali, delivers first speech to the military

8th Saturday, August 2026 - 07:52 UTC Full article

Abelardo de la Espriella delivers his first speech as president at the Pichincha Battalion in Cali

Abelardo de la Espriella took office as president of Colombia in Cali on Friday, the first time a Colombian leader has been sworn in outside Bogotá, and delivered his first speech at an Army battalion rather than before Congress, breaking with the country's institutional tradition.

The oath was taken at the Santiago de Cali University Arena, an auditorium seating more than 2,500. Senate President Honorio Henríquez placed the presidential sash on him before the full Congress. Shortly afterwards, De la Espriella moved to the Pichincha Battalion, where he spoke for more than an hour before the commanders of the armed forces and the police.

“The time has come to restore order, authority and freedom,” he said. He declared himself president of all Colombians, thanked Jesus Christ for sustaining the country through a history marked by violence, and said his victory was a victory for Colombian democracy against what he called totalitarian Bolivarian models.

The change of venue was decided at the last minute. The president-elect had intended to be sworn in at a military garrison, which Gustavo Petro blocked by barring military and police facilities from making preparations, arguing that a civilian should take office before the people and not before arms. Congress authorized only the university venue. Congresswoman Mafe Carrascal, of the Pacto Histórico, said moving the speech to a battalion amounted to bypassing the legislature.

His announcements included a tax reform aimed at discouraging evasion, the elimination of the wealth tax, the publication of a list of narco-terrorist organizations, the eradication of coca crops and financial inclusion for informal workers. He also promised measures on health, education and energy, and ordered action against all criminal structures.

De la Espriella, a 47-year-old criminal defense lawyer with no previous experience in public office, won the June 21 runoff by 250,830 votes, less than one percentage point over Iván Cepeda, the narrowest margin in a Colombian runoff in 32 years. He will govern until 2030 alongside Vice President José Manuel Restrepo.

The ceremony brought together ten heads of state, two vice presidents and fifteen foreign ministers, among them King Felipe VI of Spain and the presidents of Argentina, Javier Milei; Ecuador, Daniel Noboa; Paraguay, Santiago Peña; and Panama, José Raúl Mulino. In the morning, the new president held bilateral meetings with Milei, Noboa, Chile's José Antonio Kast, the US delegation and the king.

The United States sent a mid-ranking delegation led by acting Attorney General Todd Blanche, along with the director of the Office of National Drug Control Policy, Sara Carter, and the vice president's national security adviser, Cliff Sims. Donald Trump, JD Vance and Marco Rubio did not travel.

Nayib Bukele, Keiko Fujimori, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, Claudia Sheinbaum and Yamandú Orsi also stayed away. Petro, who does not recognize the election result, left the Casa de Nariño in the morning and said the popular mandate must be respected. Pacto Histórico lawmakers led marches in Bogotá, Barranquilla and Cali. Former presidents Juan Manuel Santos and Ernesto Samper were excluded from the guest list; Álvaro Uribe attended.

At the end of the day, Cepeda announced the creation of a shadow cabinet to oppose the new government.

The ceremony included remarks by a rabbi, an evangelical pastor, a Catholic priest and a monsignor. More than 11,000 security personnel guarded the city and Kfir jets flew over Cali during the speech. The choice of venue reflects a campaign pledge to govern from the regions: De la Espriella has said he will make Barranquilla an alternate capital and turn Cali and Medellín into satellite seats of the presidency.

World.title: Falklands: 'South Atlantic Sentinel' exercise involves all three services
World.content:
Falklands: 'South Atlantic Sentinel' exercise involves all three services

8th Saturday, August 2026 - 07:48 UTC Full article

BFSAI ground forces simulate the defense of Mount Pleasant Complex against attempts to seize it.

In late July, forces from the three services stationed at Mount Pleasant Complex in the Falkland Islands — headquarters of British Forces South Atlantic Islands (BFSAI) — took part in a series of military exercises designed to demonstrate their speed of response and operational integration, under the banner of the deployment's name, South Atlantic Sentinel.

As defined by military sources, Operation Sentinel demonstrated the defense commitment to the Falkland Islands. It was carried out along the edges of the Islands' waters Conservation Zone, a specific area of maritime and air protection for BFSAI. Taking part were the Falklands patrol vessel HMS Medway, working in coordination with an RAF A400M Atlas.

The series of exercises included firing the machine guns mounted on the offshore patrol vessel, simulating a range of scenarios, together with a coordinated “man overboard” rescue with the RAF.

“A deployment that maintains a visible presence, capable of rapid response, and that deters potential adversaries.”

Similarly, in early July, BFSAI ground forces took part in a no-notice exercise simulating incidents and attempts to breach the perimeter and gain access to the Mount Pleasant Complex, with casualties.

According to the explanation given, the exercise rigorously tested the procedures for such scenarios along with the communications network, with several teams responding quickly and effectively in what was described as a strong demonstration of professionalism, team spirit and alertness.

The motto for the day of exercises was: “training today, preparing for tomorrow, always ready and capable.” (Photos by Cpl Braithwaite)

World.title: Celtic roots of both the Falklands and Malvinas names?
World.content:
Celtic roots of both the Falklands and Malvinas names?

8th Saturday, August 2026 - 07:38 UTC Full article

The coarse sheet smuggled into the pitch by some fan, and displayed by Argentines players following victory in the match with England

The Irish Times has published a very interesting piece from Tomaí Ó Conghaile following on the fallout from the World Cup, who argues that both the English and Spanish versions of the Falkland-Malvinas Islands names have their roots in Celtic languages.

The fact is that forty-four years after the Falkland Islands made headlines around the world, 24 letters written in black paint on a white sheet catapulted the long-standing territorial dispute between Argentina and Britain into the spotlight once again.

But leaving the competing sovereignty claims aside for now, let us focus instead on a less controversial – though no less intriguing – question: the origins of the islands’ names.

What do the Falklands and Las Malvinas actually mean?



Well, you might be surprised to learn that both the English and Spanish versions ultimately have their roots in the Celtic languages.

First of all, let’s take the F-word. The English language place-name can be traced back to Anthony Cary, aka Viscount Falkland, a wealthy aristocrat who financed an expedition to the islands in 1690 the same year another military campaign left Sasana’s shores for a colony much closer to home.

Cary, it appears, made some of his fortune pillaging treasure from a wrecked Spanish galleon in the Caribbean, briefly became head of the British navy, spent several days imprisoned in the Tower of London on corruption charges, and died of smallpox before reaching 40.

Initially, a strait running between the two main islands was named after him, and by 1765 the Falkland Islands had become the English name for the entire archipelago.

But where does the word Falkland itself comes from?



It refers to the small town of Falkland in Fife, Scotland. (The Cary family had received the title from a Stuart king, even though they themselves were based in England and originally from Devon.)

While there remains some speculation that the name may preserve an older Pictish word, the most widely accepted explanation is that it derives from Gaelic.

The first element may come either from falach (meaning “hidden”) or falc (“to wash” or “heavy rain”), with the second part being the common, lann, which means “plot of land” or “church enclosure”.

A suitably damp toponym, you might think, for a town in the east of Alba and its rugged namesake in the South Atlantic, though in both spots the rain isn’t as relentless as you would imagine.

The Celtic connections don’t end there, however.

The Spanish name, Las Malvinas, derives from the French Îles Malouines, the title stamped on the islands by musketeer mathematician Louis Antoine de Bougainville in 1764. This imperial explorer would later become the first Frenchman to circumnavigate the globe and brazenly claim Tahiti for Louis XV.

Malouines itself means “people from Saint-Malo”, the Breton port from which de Bougainville’s crew set sail. Today the town is famous for its magnificent walled old town, popular crêperies and bustling cider houses.

But who was St Malo?



It turns out he was a Welsh monk who is said to have taken part in the legendary voyage of our own St Brendan before travelling to Brittany to spread the gospel. His name likely derives from the Old Breton Machlou, meaning a “beautiful hostage” or “bright pledge”.

Once again, the title is quite fitting: a seafaring saint who sailed the high seas lending his name, indirectly, to a distant ocean-bound archipelago.

While the Celtic language origins of the Falkands-Malvinas may have no impact on the ebb and flow of contemporary geopolitics, they do offer a clear reminder of how meanings and labels evolve across time and tides, how conquest marks both land and sea, and how unlikely linguistic connections can span the globe.

One story told about St Malo is that he once left an island community in Brittany because of a bitter dispute over land. The people later begged him to return, which he did, and he duly restored peace and order.

The Mapuche claim



Said that, another claim to the windswept Islands comes from the Mapuche – an indigenous nation whose ancestral territory encompassed much of what is now Argentina, long before the current state existed – and whose activists have suggested in the past that the Falklands should be transferred to them as compensation for the lands they lost in Patagonia during Spanish and Argentine colonial expansion.

Although it’s agreed there were no human settlements on the isolated Falklands before Europeans arrived, it’s not difficult to understand their point.

World.title: Falklands: rise in the CPI, caused by the conflict in the Middle East
World.content:
Falklands: rise in the CPI, caused by the conflict in the Middle East

8th Saturday, August 2026 - 07:26 UTC Full article

The Islands' Head of Policy, Roddy Cordeiro, warned of volatile oil prices and said the United Kingdom is already anticipating that they will give inflation a further push.

The Consumer Price Index (CPI), according to official Falkland Islands figures, recorded a quarterly increase of 3.4% as a result of the impact of higher fuel prices.

The phenomenon, as the entire world is experiencing in energy and hydrocarbons, stems from the confrontation between the United States and Israel with Iran, which has escalated into a regional conflict by disrupting maritime traffic through key straits. According to estimates from international organizations, 20% of the world's oil, 30% of natural gas and 50% of urea — a fertilizer critical to agricultural production — pass through those waters.

In the Falklands, on July 29, during his presentation to the Standing Finance Committee, the Islands' Head of Policy, Roddy Cordeiro, said international prices remain volatile for the time being, and that in the United Kingdom a further push to inflation is anticipated.

Following the presentation of the official financial report and the fuel situation, the Standing Committee became the setting for a debate over the £16 million surplus shown in the Falklands national budget toward the end of June, the second quarter of the financial year — although it is understood that payments and applications deferred to the following quarter will almost certainly reduce the size of that surplus.

The occasion was used to ask members whether they were satisfied with the amounts allocated to the budget for rural roads in Camp.

The Financial Secretary clarified that these files had been released under the information and transparency arrangements promoted by his department and by elected members.

The item was approved, though there was room for some members to joke about whether the full £1 million allocated might end up entirely spent on the construction of a single cattle grid. Similarly worded budgets were also agreed for the construction of jetties or landing stages on Speedwell and Barren islands, located off the extreme south-west of East Falkland.

The Falklands CPI is based on a basket of 175 products, which are taken to represent the consumption patterns of goods and services of the population of the capital, Stanley. It does not, however, take into account changes in consumption that may emerge as a result of price movements.

World.title: Postcards from Mexico: On the beach in Playa del Carmen
World.content:
PLAYA DEL CARMEN, Quintana Roo, May 25, 2022 — Over coffee with a friend I’ll call Luisa, I’m given the rundown on some system we’re all complicit in. That there are dark forces in the world, shadowy figures that want us to be unwell, eat foods that make us sick, use devices that facilitate the tracking of our movements and submit to vaccinations that were hastily manufactured.

She offers no specifics but adds ominously that when the time comes, their identities will be revealed and their comeuppance will be swift.

“I’m manifesting it,” she says.

Somewhere off 10th Avenue in Playa del Carmen

Then, just as quickly, she shifts, raving about some cleansing ceremony she went to the previous weekend — cacao, Reiki, Rainbow Rhythms, I can’t keep track.

It’s a little past 6 p.m. on a Wednesday somewhere off 10th Avenue in Playa del Carmen, and had I known our catch-up session would go like this, I’d have proposed a happy hour instead. You can never quite tell what mood someone will be in at this time of day, though I’m sure Luisa could recommend a retreat in Tulum that, for a nominal fee, could empower me to do so with no more than someone’s birth information. A cheaper option can be found on nearby blocks.

A golden hour tug-of-war

On Playa’s busiest walking streets, you sense the tug-of-war of golden hour most acutely. On some stretches, house music throbs lazily from restaurants as the sun sinks beyond the shore and people make their way home from the beach. But elsewhere, an undercurrent of reggaetón simmers, gradually coming to a boil as bars brace for nighttime business.

Beach cruisers glide along bike lanes, and taxi drivers idle along Avenida Benito Juárez, impassive and happy to loiter, yet willing to take you where you want to go as long as it’s really close or really far, never anything in between.

A slog of traffic

Their colectivo-driving counterparts enjoy no such luxury. Along 30th Avenue, their vans stop incessantly, either at designated locations or at the requests of passengers. Each time they lurch forward, a plume of black smog seeps out, lingering momentarily before the sea breeze folds the smell of engine exhaust into the city’s default aroma of brine and sargassum.

On single-lane streets, their progress grinds to a crawl, each van inching its way forward, hoping for an opening amid dense pedestrian traffic. Rarely, they’ll honk, startling meandering tourists whose faces are either red from embarrassment or too much sun. If all goes well, a path will open, allowing the van to slip through. Yet strangely, at this hour, the road traffic still flows more smoothly than foot traffic on the congested Quinta Avenida.

From Avenida Fundadores to Avenida Constituyentes, every block feels like a slog. The tourists are leisurely, stopping here and there to gander at gewgaws from storefronts whose gaudy signs advertise cheap tequila, handicrafts, flavored rum and “cloting.” Along the way, they’ll be intercepted intermittently by salespeople calling out, “Hola, bienvenidos” to Mexican-looking passersby and “Shopping, guys?” to gringos. A few others suggest services I won’t mention.

‘An evening stroll becomes a sport’

Farther north, stocky, straight-haired women will woo them with offers of “massage information,” an invitation that usually goes unanswered. Yet, as I was reminded when I opted to take this scenic route to my coffee date, even the slightest pause from a pedestrian entertaining this option can jam everything up.

An evening stroll becomes a sport, slithering through a sea of semi-static bodies. Older men in white linen shirts and pants, with acoustic guitars slung over their shoulders, looking for someone to serenade. Mariachis in cream-colored jackets, red bow ties and black chaps lined with gold buttons that run the length of the leg. A handful of Hasidic Jews waving yellow flags with Hebrew lettering, blasting some house rendition of Marc Anthony’s “Vivir Mi Vida.” Slender Mexican women with hair wrapped in tightly braided buns dressed like catrinas. And for some reason, a woman using an unoccupied stroller to wheel her husband’s now-empty case of beer around.

What’s a local?

The thing is, in the midst of this morass, I’ve lost the ability to discern who’s who. The term “local” becomes increasingly ill-defined because the only real common denominator is transience: wellness babes and crypto bros brushing shoulders with tourists and Mexican transplants here for high season. Elderly couples escaping the snow back home for a few months, then gone again. But while they’re here, they all become something else. A self-contained version that affirms their unique worldview without ever needing to apologize to woke folk or curmudgeonly conservatives back home. They become Luisa.

There’s a mystique around the Riviera Maya that attracts a certain kind of person. To simply label them “snowbirds” or “digital nomads” wouldn’t do them justice. “Entrepreneurs” abound. Life coaches, spiritual healers, Reiki therapists, ayahuasca shamans. Their qualifications aren’t always clear or existent, but what do I know?

‘Free to be who you want’

Sometimes, you hear them lean on words synonymous with metamorphosis in casual conversation, especially when promoting their services. I have to think it’s the cyclical nature of this place that lures them. If you know that people are only going to be here for so long, yourself included, the person you were before doesn’t matter — you’re free to be who you want, who you wish you were.

With enough practice, you may even become that person, or at least convince everyone else that you have. Maybe that’s what Luisa means when she says she’s manifesting.

Ethan Jacobs is a freelance writer and writing coach based in Playa del Carmen. He has written extensively in narrative and short fiction formats, and his work has received recognition both domestically and internationally in microfiction, short fiction and narrative essay formats.

World.title: El Jalapeño: Tulum named world’s happiest destination by company no one has ever heard of
World.content:
All stories in El Jalapeño are satire and not real news. Check out the original article here.

TULUM, Mexico — An exhaustive, algorithmically driven study conducted by an overseas travel insurance broker has officially designated Tulum as “the happiest place on Earth,” determining that visitors to the coastal town experience absolute human fulfillment — at least according to the keywords used in their online reviews.

Researchers at Dublin-based firm JustGoNow arrived at the score of 100 out of 100 after scanning more than 1 million online ratings for high-frequency terms like “euphoria,” “bliss” and “transformative,” while successfully filtering out secondary search terms such as “pothole,” “taxi union” and “sargassum.”

“The mathematical evidence is indisputable,” said Arthur Higgins, chief data analyst for JustGoNow, who conducted the global happiness assessment from an office park outside Dublin. “When a reviewer writes, ‘Swimming in an underground cenote makes me feel completely aligned with the universe,’ our software registers that as pure, unadulterated joy. We then tally these ‘happiness’ indicators compared to other destinations to come up with accurate rankings requiring no actual travel on our part.”

The study praised Tulum’s unique ecosystem, noting that tourists achieved peak tranquility through a balanced routine of eco-friendly boutique stays, jungle wellness retreats and online posts expressing how satisfied they are with the experience so far.

According to local tourism officials, the perfect score highlights a growing international demand for second-hand travel experiences recorded on high-end smartphones and immediately uploaded to social media.

“We are deeply honored to be declared the global capital of happiness by a company that sells emergency flight cancellation policies,” said Roberto Morales, a regional hospitality coordinator. “It proves that true inner peace is achievable for anyone willing to pay a US $200 day-bed minimum and disregard the sound of heavy construction equipment coming from behind the palm trees.”

The index placed Tulum ahead of other top-ranked joy centers, including Las Vegas and New York — two locations long celebrated by travel experts as global sanctuaries of unhurried, serene reflection.

World.title: Discovering Mexico: Puebla
World.content:
Listen to this article

Puebla is for you if you like: Colonial history, sweeping mountains, racing while holding tortillas

Mexico’s fourth-largest city, Puebla, has more going on beneath its colonial facades than most visitors realize. Its historic center, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1987, holds 2,619 monuments — more than any other city in the Americas — plus the tallest cathedral bell towers in the country. The city’s well-preserved architecture has also made it a go-to filming location, standing in for 18th- and 19th-century Mexico and Spain in productions including “Frida” and “Man on Fire.”

All of this is before you get out into the wider state, where sweeping mountain ranges, active volcanoes and enormous cacti dot the landscape. The state is one of the last stops in southern Mexico before the jungle claims the country. We’ve collected some of our best pieces from the last few years, to help you experience one of Mexico’s most genuine — and stunning — regions.

Puebla’s capital — also, conveniently, called Puebla — is filled with the sort of magic that only Mexico’s oldest cities can really offer. Many of the nation’s most definining moments and people have filled these streets (and the tunnels underneath them).

Puebla’s identity is tied up in origin stories, although some more verifiable than others. Its early name, Puebla de los Ángeles, traces to a 1531 account of a bishop’s vision guiding Spanish settlers to the site. Its signature dish, mole poblano, is said to have been improvised by nuns at the Convent of Santa Rosa in 1680 when an archbishop arrived unannounced and the kitchen had little to offer but chilis, chocolate, nuts and stale bread. And on Nov. 18, 1910, the Serdán family home became the site of the first armed clash of the Mexican Revolution, two days before Francisco Madero formally launched the uprising; the bullet-scarred house is now a museum.

While its days of defining Mexico’s future are probably behind it, Puebla remains a fascinating destination for anyone who wants to understand how the modern country truly came to be.

While Oaxaca, Sonora and Yucatán often vie for the title of Mexico’s gastronomic heart, it’s really Puebla that deserves the credit for much of the nation’s great cuisine.

Puebla’s culinary reputation rests on three dishes with stories as rich as their flavors. Mole poblano, which rumour claims is a single flash of nun-driven inspiration, remains the most famous of Mexico’s 300-plus regional moles. Chiles en nogada, with its patriotic red, white and green color scheme, traces back to a 1821 feast honoring independence figure Agustín de Iturbide. Tacos árabes, born from Middle Eastern shawarma techniques brought by 1930s immigrants, is the progenitor of the iconic pastor.

The state is quite a bit more than just colonial architecture and great food, though. Just outside Tehuacán, Puebla’s second-largest city, sits a landscape that looks like it belongs on another planet.

The Tehuacán-Cuicatlán Biosphere sprawls across 145,255 hectares of protected desert, home to more than 2,500 species of cacti — tall and candle-thin, round as beach balls, or shaped like something out of a sci-fi set. A day inside it turns into a full sensory tour of the region: 2,000-year-old salt flats still worked by hand at Zapotitlán Salinas, a lunch built around cactus flowers and hibiscus water (with insects on offer for the adventurous) and a pottery workshop in Los Reyes Metzontla where clay deposits — leftovers from an ancient sea — get shaped into earthy, hand-thrown crockery.

In a small Puebla town two hours north of the city, an entire industry is built on Christmas spirit. Chignahuapan produces an estimated 70 million hand-blown ornaments a year, and inside the country’s largest esfera factory, the process starts with nothing more than a glowing-hot glass tube and a steady breath. From there, silver coatings, hand-mixed paint and careful dabs of glitter transform each piece into something ready for the tree — some ornaments even take a year to master.

Step inside the traditional workshop where trompos, Nativity scenes and piñata-shaped baubles come to life, one painstaking layer at a time.

In the days before Day of the Dead, the Puebla town of Huaquechula holds a tradition unlike anywhere else: the trueque, an ancient barter market where locals swap goods — peanuts, sugar cane, homemade bread — for everything needed to build their altars. Families trade for marigolds and cockscomb flowers, while vendors carry stacks of pan de muerto in its many forms, from bone-topped loaves to body-shaped muertitos dusted in red sugar.

Beyond the market, the town runs on hospitality: cooks prepare meals for hundreds of festival participants around the clock, and visitors are waved into strangers’ homes to see their altars up close. Huaquechula offers a rare, local variation on Mexico’s most iconic holiday — equal parts market day, family reunion and open-door celebration of the dead.

Our glimpse into Puebla ends on a unique note. The annual Carrera de la Tortilla, a 5-km race through Tehuacán that retraces the daily walk local women make to market, tortillas and all. Most runners came from Santa María Coapan, the self-proclaimed “Tortilla Capital” of Mexico, who run decked out in traditional Mixtec dress.

Part sporting event, part tribute to the women who keep the tradition alive, it’s one of Puebla’s more charming annual customs.

Puebla, Where Magic Lives in Every Journey / Sub English

Watch this video on YouTube

How to get there

When it comes to arriving in Puebla, it really only makes sense to arrive from Mexico City.

By air

Puebla International Airport: 45 minutes from the city center, the airport offers connections to almost every major Mexican destination, plus Newark, Houston and Los Angeles.

Mexico City Benito Juarez (AICM): The big one. About 2 hours (traffic permitting) from central Puebal. Available from everywhere in Mexico, and almost every major global airport besides.

Felipe Ángeles International Airport (AIFA): The eternally troubled AIFA is finally beginning to come into it’s own. 2.5 hours away, it offers similar domestic connectivity to AICM and flights in from Colombia, Venezuela, the Dominican Republic and Cuba.

By road

Mexico City: 135km (83 miles) somewhere between 90 minutes and 3 hours, depending on when you travel. National holidays often lead to enormous tailbacks, but tackling the drive early on a weekday often means you can get there in less than two hours.

World.title: Ohuira Bay communities weigh federal plan for Sinaloa ammonia plant
World.content:
TOPOLOBAMPO, Mexico — When federal officials finally unveiled a plan last week to address the 12-year conflict over a nearly completed ammonia plant beside Ohuira Bay, Indigenous Yoreme activist, rural sociologist and law student Melina Maldonado did not feel relieved.

She felt crushed.

After six days of roundtable discussions, she had begun to feel hopeful; it seemed they were really taking in new information and seeing a different side to the debate. The proposal led her to believe otherwise.

“They didn’t listen to our reasons for saying no,” Maldonado said. “They listened for a way to make it a yes.”

The federal proposal promises environmental safeguards, community monitoring and public investment around the German-backed GPO-Proman plant in northern Sinaloa state. But it leaves the project’s operation largely intact — and that has exposed the fundamental divide at the heart of the conflict: The government is offering ways to make the plant safer, while the communities closest to the bay are still adamant that it should not operate at all.

Those communities must now take the proposal into their own assemblies and, using their traditional Indigenous consensus-based governance model, decide whether to accept it. Until then, the blockade outside the gate to the plant — now in its 72nd day — remains in place.

A proposal, not an agreement

The plan emerged after six days of talks involving federal and state officials, representatives of GPO-Proman and members of the ¡Aquí No! (Not Here!) collective, which is led by Yoreme-Mayo communities surrounding Ohuira Bay and has become the principal force opposing the plant.

Federal officials presented the proposal as a path toward resolving a conflict that has become one of Mexico’s longest-running and most contentious environmental battles. But movement leaders emphasized that no agreement has been reached and that they do not have the authority to accept the plan on behalf of their communities.

The proposal must first be explained and discussed in assemblies in Ohuira, Paredones, Lázaro Cárdenas and Topolobampo. These communities surround the Santa María-Topolobampo-Ohuira lagoon system, a Ramsar wetland of international importance, and would bear the plant’s most direct impacts.

Community response to the proposal

“We have to hold our own internal assemblies,” said Claudia Susana Quintero, a Yoreme educator, resident of the village of Ohuira and one of the leaders of ¡Aquí No! “We have to explain it to the community, analyze it and decide how we are going to reach consensus.”

The representatives’ role is to take the proposal home and return with a decision reached collectively — not to accept it on their communities’ behalf.

The US $1.6 billion plant, designed to produce 2,200 metric tons (2,425 tons) of ammonia a day, is reportedly about 88% complete. Opposition began soon after the project was approved in 2014 and has centered on threats to fishing, the lagoon ecosystem, industrial safety and what Yoreme communities describe as a deeply flawed Indigenous consultation.

The current protest began in late May, when residents tried to block the movement of massive absorption towers from the port. Protesters later shifted their encampment to the plant entrance, where they have remained through extreme heat and intense storms.

A project the government considers strategic

President Claudia Sheinbaum has defended the plant as important to Mexico’s goal of achieving greater food sovereignty. Ammonia is a principal raw material in nitrogen fertilizers, and Sheinbaum has said Mexico currently imports nearly all the fertilizer it uses, apart from production by state-owned company Fertinal.

She has also emphasized that the plant is nearly finished, and that it underwent an environmental review and received majority support in the government-led Indigenous consultation — a process the four communities closest to Ohuira Bay continue to dispute.

The Economy Ministry says the GPO plant could reduce Mexico’s fertilizer imports by as much as 70% and keep approximately US $500 million now spent on imports within the Mexican economy.

For the federal government, the plant is part of a broader strategy to reduce dependence on imported agricultural inputs. Opponents say that national goal does not justify concentrating the risks in their communities.

What the government put on the table

The proposal leaves the ammonia plant in place, but would significantly alter how it operates. Among its most significant provisions, the plan calls for GPO-Proman to stop drawing water directly from Ohuira Bay and instead use water discharged through a nearby Federal Electricity Commission canal.

Opponents have long warned that the plant’s authorized system would pull large volumes of seawater from the lagoon and return warmer, saltier water, potentially disrupting fish and shrimp nurseries. Under the new plan, wastewater would instead be carried offshore rather than released back into the lagoon system.

The plan also proposes a new environmental baseline study, continuous water-quality monitoring and an oversight body made up of community members, scientists, government officials and company representatives. Additional measures would address sewage and agricultural runoff already entering the bay, as well as emergency preparedness and civil protection.

Other commitments focus on longstanding community needs, including housing, education, fishing infrastructure and assistance in certifying local shrimp and crab products so they can command higher prices.

Economic development plans in Topolobampo

Federal commissioner Mauricio Rodríguez Alonso, who has led the talks, stressed at a Tuesday news conference that the plan grew out of dialogue among the communities, GPO-Proman and government agencies. He said the company had agreed in principle to its commitments.

Ulises Pinzón, Topolobampo’s municipal representative, said the package could bring meaningful benefits. He was particularly encouraged by provisions giving communities a voice over future petrochemical development.

That is especially significant in Topolobampo, which the federal government has designated as an economic development hub where chemical and petrochemical industries are among the priority sectors. The plan would also keep proposed methanol and urea plants and a port terminal on hold unless the communities agree to them.

But Pinzón noted that many of the promises involve responsibilities the government should already be fulfilling, rather than concessions from GPO-Proman itself.

“On paper, honestly, I see an attractive proposal,” he said. “The question is how we can ensure that these commitments are actually fulfilled.”

That distinction — between a promising announcement and a binding, enforceable agreement — is now one of the central questions confronting the communities.

The risk that remains

For opponents of the plant, the most troubling unresolved issue is the danger of a catastrophic ammonia release. The government proposal does include new safeguards: an emergency-response center, joint industrial-risk monitoring, water curtains around pipelines and storage tanks, and a regional civil-protection plan — something Rodríguez acknowledged does not currently exist.

But movement leaders say emergency planning and mitigation cannot eliminate the underlying danger documented in the company’s own risk assessment.

According to that assessment, a five-minute leak could create a high-impact zone extending roughly 15 kilometers (9 miles) from the plant, encompassing Topolobampo and nearby Yoreme communities. A broader impact zone could extend as far as 45 kilometers (28 miles), reaching toward Los Mochis and other surrounding communities.

“That risk is still there, and it is still not clear to us,” Pinzón said. “The first people affected would be those of us who live in Topolobampo.”

Loss of life is not remediable

Company project documents show the plant is designed to store up to 75,000 metric tons (82,670 tons) of anhydrous ammonia near populated communities. Quintero said the proposal may reduce certain environmental impacts, but it cannot eliminate the consequences of a major industrial accident.

“You can remediate many things,” she said. “What you cannot remediate is the loss of life.”

For Maldonado, this is where the government’s proposal misses the point. Her own community, the Yoreme fishing village of Lázaro Cárdenas, looks across the bay at the plant every day.

The communities’ opposition has never been limited to the plant’s effects on water quality or fisheries, she said. It is rooted in the belief that a facility carrying such risks should not operate near people’s homes. She pointed to the company’s brightly colored risk map.

“This is the risk zone the company itself identified,” she said. “And now they are minimizing it or pushing it into the background.”

A decision made under threat

The communities will not consider the proposal in a political vacuum. Several of the movement’s most visible leaders have received threats related to their opposition to the plant and now live under government protection measures.

Four of ¡Aquí No!’s most visible leaders, including Maldonado, Quintero and Ohuira traditional governor Felipe Montaño, have been enrolled in Mexico’s federal protection mechanism for human rights defenders and journalists. Protection measures can include bulletproof vests and government-issued panic buttons intended to summon help in an emergency.

But Quintero said such equipment offers little comfort as the communities prepare to deliver an answer that government officials and project supporters may not want to hear.

“I know my community is going to say no,” she said. “But now the government is putting us in the line of fire against the rest of society that says yes.”

She worries that the plan could recast defenders as obstacles to jobs and economic development, increasing the pressure on people who have already spent years facing intimidation for speaking publicly.

“A bulletproof vest and a panic button are not going to help me much if someone decides to act tomorrow,” Quintero said.

The experience, she added, has gradually consumed the rest of their identities.

“We are no longer mothers, daughters or sisters,” she said. “We are nothing more than defenders.”

From shock to strategy

By Thursday evening, the mood inside the movement had begun to shift.

Enrique Ayala, a longtime activist staying at the blockade, said movement leaders spent six hours Thursday with scientists and lawyers analyzing the proposal and plotting their next steps.

“The government proposal is one-sided,” Ayala said. “They are pushing ahead with their project.”

But after years of being ignored, Ayala sees the government’s willingness to sit down with them as progress.

“We have to get up, keep going and make proposals of our own,” he said. “After 12 years when they paid us no attention, now we have them sitting at the table.”

And despite the government’s apparent intention to move the plant toward operation, Ayala said the movement has not abandoned its original goal.

“We still believe we can get the company to leave,” he said. “Sometimes you have to dream.”

Tracy L. Barnett is a Guadalajara-based freelance writer and the founder of The Esperanza Project.

World.title: From the archive: A guide to Mexican nicknames and how they’re given
World.content:
The goal of our “From the Archive” series is to revisit popular stories that capture the unique history and culture of life in Mexico. This Sarah DeVries article — originally published in February 2025 — is a perfect example, offering humorous insight into the fine art of giving nicknames in Mexico.

If you’ve spent much time among Mexicans, you’ve probably realized something. They love to give each other — and consistently use — nicknames.

I’m not just talking about diminutives of names, though these are also popular. Guillermo, for example, is Memo for short, the same way Bob is a diminutive of Robert.

How nicknames work in Mexico

There’s Alex for both Alejandro and Alejandra, Chio for Rocío, Lalo for Eduardo, Lola for Dolores and Chava for Salvador. There’s also short versions of double names, like Mafer for María Fernanda, Majo for María José and my favorite, Lucifer for Lucía Fernanda, a name most people do not give their kids. And of course, the classic “-ito” and “-ita” can go at the end of many names. So sometimes people call me Sarita, and my partner Juanito. Careful with using these, though, as they’re often infantilizing, and as you very likely know, some people do not like being infantilized.

So you get the idea: most names here have a shortened version. But Mexicans don’t stop there!

My nicknames

I’ll admit that this makes me very happy. As a kid, I never had a nickname, and I was jealous that I didn’t. Thinking back, it’s probably better; it wouldn’t have necessarily been a nice one, as I was both a crybaby and a showoff. Come to think of it, I might still be both of those things. Thankfully, I don’t currently have any nicknames related to either of those characteristics. Yet.

I do have some other fun ones though. “Sirena polar” — polar mermaid — might be the most creative, given to me by a friend of my ex-husband who was amazed that I insisted on swimming in ice-cold water after a hike. For reasons unknown to me, this same friend also often called me “cara de nutria”: otter face. Maybe because otters swim in cold water, too? Another friend, not quite as creative, simply calls me “mi gringa favorita.” I’d be more flattered if I weren’t one of the only gringos she knows.

The futility of protesting against your nickname

Many nicknames are purposefully funny, and sometimes shocking. And from what I can tell, people don’t seem to be insulted by them. Sometimes I wonder if they actually are bothered but know that trying to fight back against the Mexican urge to make fun of everything is futile.

So when you get a name like “El Frijol” because you’re very dark-skinned, you just go along with it, I guess?

In the particular case of another acquaintance, the guy was tall and good-looking. He was married, but seemed to have no shortage of women interested in him, or of self-esteem.

I always wanted to ask him if the nickname bothered him, but we were never close, so the opportunity was lost. But I did get to ask my ex-husband, who his friends had nicknamed “el bello camello” — the beautiful camel — supposedly because they thought he looked Arab.

The new generation of nicknames

Could this be one of those cultural things that’s dying out with more socially conscious and sensitive younger generations? I don’t think it is, as my daughter, age 11, has several nicknames herself. At school, her friends sometimes call her Plana, which means flat. It’s a synonym of her name, Lisa, which means “smooth” in Spanish and is often featured on hair conditioner bottles. And in her Scout troop, every kid has a nickname, each one the name of a bird. She’ll also respond to “Mona,” which is kind of nice. “Mona” is more of a Spanish-from-Spain word for “pretty,” but in this case, of course it’s about the Mona Lisa.

So perhaps the tradition will continue?

Don’t take yourself too seriously

After several years of watching the issue of how people address them being taken very, very seriously north of Mexico, I’ll admit that I find the ability to joke around with silly nicknames refreshing. Like all humor, though, it’s very culturally specific; there are plenty of unspoken rules regarding when it’s funny and good-humored and when it’s not.

It’s not that I want the freedom to be gratuitously mean, which is something very different. But I do think that it’s always worth it to not take ourselves so seriously all the time, something most of us can agree makes us generally unlikable.

So if you get a nickname here, try to go with it. Because people don’t get nicknames when they’re not being included in a group. Even if it’s not one you’d have chosen for yourself, it’s a signal that you are part of a community; people know you.

They might be making fun, but it’s affectionate fun. Try to take it that way.

Sarah DeVries is a writer and translator based in Xalapa, Veracruz. She can be reached through her website, sarahedevries.substack.com.

World.title: Mexico’s week in review: US suspends avocado certs, fracking studies continue and Peru rift ends
World.content:
Listen to this article

President Claudia Sheinbaum’s daily press conferences set much of the week’s agenda, moving from children’s social media use to a government transparency decree, a high-profile murder, fracking policy and a diplomatic breakthrough with Peru. Economic data told a mixed story too, with a strengthening peso set against a sharp drop in Pemex profit and a battered Sinaloa economy.

Security developments also kept pace, including the arrest of a former Guerrero governor on Ayotzinapa-related charges, a jump in U.S. rewards tied to CJNG’s new leadership, and a fresh U.S. suspension of avocado certifications in Michoacán. On the public health and safety front, a UNAM cheating scandal, a UNESCO deadline to protect the vaquita and a cyclosporiasis scare linked to Riviera Maya travel all drew attention.

Didn’t have time to catch this week’s top stories? Here’s what you missed.

Economy: Peso strengthens and avocado trade swings

Mexico’s currency extended a 10-day rally to reach its strongest level since February, helped by the Bank of Mexico holding its benchmark rate at 6.5% and a weaker US dollar following a soft American jobs report. The gains came even as Pemex reported a 70% annual drop in second-quarter net profit, which the state oil company attributed to higher financial costs, tax obligations and an unfavorable exchange rate. Economic disparities varied widely by region, with Sinaloa’s economy posting the worst quarterly contraction of any Mexican state, a result economists linked to the ongoing cartel conflict in the region.

Tourism data added to the mixed picture: Tourism GDP fell 0.8% quarter-over-quarter in the first three months of the year, according to INEGI, driven by a 5.9% quarterly drop in spending by foreign visitors, even as domestic tourism consumption rose 0.5%.

Mexico’s avocado trade also had a volatile week. New data showed exports to the U.S. jumped 35% in the first quarter compared to the previous year, according to Sader. Days later, however, the United States suspended avocado export certifications in Michoacán, citing an unspecified “threat against U.S. interests” — the third such suspension in just over four years. Michoacán’s governor deployed additional state security operatives and the Defense Ministry sent more than 1,500 soldiers to the region in response.

Energy: Government edges toward fracking while banning it in Mexico’s top basin

A government expert committee tasked with assessing “sustainable fracking” recommended prohibiting hydraulic fracturing in the Tampico-Misantla basin, Mexico’s largest-potential shale region, citing environmental, social and biodiversity concerns. Sheinbaum said her government would respect that recommendation, which she reaffirmed at Friday’s mañanera.

However, the committee recommended continued evaluation of two other northern basins. Reuters reported that pilot projects in Coahuila and Tamaulipas could begin as soon as next month if approved, as Mexico looks to reduce its reliance on natural gas imports from the United States.

Security: Pressure builds on cartels and past officials

U.S. authorities raised the reward for CJNG’s new leader, Juan Carlos Valencia González, to $25 million following the February death of cartel founder “El Mencho,” as part of more than $100 million in reward offers and new visa restrictions. Domestically, federal agents dismantled four illicit fuel processing centers in San Luis Potosí, Hidalgo and Morelos, seizing roughly 1 million liters of fuel. In Sinaloa, Sheinbaum acknowledged the murder of content creator César Gastélum, the ninth social media personality killed in the state since 2024. And in a case tied to one of Mexico’s most notorious unsolved crimes, federal authorities arrested former Guerrero Governor Ángel Aguirre on charges of concealing video evidence related to the 2014 disappearance of 43 Ayotzinapa students; Sheinbaum said the arrest was not politically motivated.

Public health, environment and education

Sheinbaum laid the cornerstone for a new IMSS hospital in Oaxaca, part of a three-facility “Health City” complex the government frames as a step toward its planned Universal Health Service. And after the U.K. reported dozens of cyclosporiasis cases among travelers, Mexico stepped up health inspections at Riviera Maya hotels, while officials said the country has not been identified as the outbreak’s source.

Officials at the National Autonomous University of Mexico (UNAM) confirmed that nearly 60,000 applicants must retake its entrance exam after widespread cheating undermined its first-ever online exam.

Separately, UNESCO gave Mexico until February to show concrete action to protect the critically endangered vaquita porpoise, of which only seven to 10 are believed to remain.

Diplomacy and governance

Sheinbaum signed a decree aimed at strengthening federal government transparency, which officials said would compel departments to disclose more information following the 2024 elimination of the INAI watchdog agency.

On the diplomatic front, Sheinbaum announced that Mexico and Peru would restore relations severed since November, after former Peruvian Prime Minister Bettsy Chávez was granted safe passage from asylum in Mexico’s Lima embassy.

Looking ahead

The coming weeks will test several threads left open this week: whether Mexican and U.S. officials can resolve the security concerns behind the avocado certification suspension, whether President Sheinbaum’s panel of experts finds acceptable conditions in northern Mexico to move fracking pilot projects forward, and how UNAM’s rescheduled in-person exams — set for mid-to-late August — play out after the cheating controversy. Mexico also faces UNESCO’s February deadline on vaquita protections and continued scrutiny of Sinaloa’s cartel-driven economic slowdown.

World.title: Lula to Send Trump Amazon Data in Tariff Spat
World.content:
Brazil · Trade

Key Facts New tariffs — The US imposed a 25% duty on most Brazilian imports, with some exceptions like beef and coffee.

— The US imposed a 25% duty on most Brazilian imports, with some exceptions like beef and coffee. Deforestation cited — Washington said illegal deforestation was one reason for the measures, a claim Lula disputes.

— Washington said illegal deforestation was one reason for the measures, a claim Lula disputes. Data to send — Lula will forward Inpe figures showing a 36.87% drop in Amazon losses from August 2025 to July 2026.

— Lula will forward Inpe figures showing a 36.87% drop in Amazon losses from August 2025 to July 2026. Lowest since 2016 — The deforestation rate is the lowest in the series since 2016, according to Inpe.

— The deforestation rate is the lowest in the series since 2016, according to Inpe. Diplomatic tensions — The US also revoked the visa of Brazil’s ambassador, adding to the strain.

— The US also revoked the visa of Brazil’s ambassador, adding to the strain. No retaliation yet — Lula has not announced immediate countermeasures, focusing instead on rebutting the US rationale.

— Lula has not announced immediate countermeasures, focusing instead on rebutting the US rationale. Trade at stake — Brazilian exporters face higher costs in the US market, a key destination for manufactured and agricultural goods.

Brazil’s president will challenge the US justification for new tariffs by sending the latest deforestation figures, after a 25% duty on most Brazilian goods.

Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva said on Saturday that he will send Donald Trump the latest Amazon deforestation figures, aiming to undercut a key justification for the new US tariffs on Brazilian goods. This move, Lula to Send Trump Amazon Data in Tariff Spat, is a direct challenge to Washington’s claims.

Speaking in Taboão da Serra, São Paulo, Lula said the data – released by Brazil’s space agency Inpe on Friday – show deforestation fell 36.87% between August 2025 and July 2026, the lowest in the series since 2016. “I want to send these numbers to the US government,” Lula said, according to local media.

The US has cited illegal deforestation among the reasons for the tariff package, which imposes a 25% duty on most Brazilian imports, with exceptions for products like beef and coffee. For investors and exporters, the dispute raises the cost of doing business with the US, Brazil’s second-largest trading partner, and adds uncertainty to supply chains that rely on cross-border trade.

Lula’s move is a diplomatic gambit: rather than escalate with retaliation, he is betting that hard data can change the narrative. But the tariff dispute is not just about forests – Washington has also raised concerns about digital trade, intellectual property, and ethanol.

The coming weeks will show whether data can cool a trade war that is already affecting real money.

President Lula. He again attacked the US tariffs on Brazil and vowed to send Trump fresh Amazon deforestation data. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

What Are the New US Tariffs on Brazil?

In July 2026, the United States imposed a 25% tariff on most goods imported from Brazil, a sweeping measure that affects a wide range of sectors. Some products, including beef and coffee, were exempted, but the broad scope has sent a shock through Brazilian export industries.

The official justification from Washington points to a mix of trade grievances: digital trade barriers, intellectual property protections, ethanol tariffs, and forest-related policies, including the handling of illegal deforestation.

For a Brazilian exporter, this means a 25% surcharge on goods sent to the US market, which can erode profit margins or force price increases that reduce competitiveness. The tariff rate is significant – it is not a symbolic gesture, but a substantial barrier that could reshape trade flows.

While some products are spared, the majority of Brazilian exports to the US now face the higher duty, creating a clear incentive for companies to seek alternative markets or renegotiate contracts.

What the US Tariffs on Brazil Put at Stake

The US has explicitly cited illegal deforestation in the Amazon as one reason for the tariffs, linking environmental policy to trade. This is a sensitive issue for Brazil, where the Amazon is a global symbol of climate action and a source of national pride.

Lula has made reducing deforestation a cornerstone of his administration, and the latest Inpe data supports his claim of progress: a 36.87% drop from August 2025 to July 2026, the lowest level in the series since 2016.

By sending these figures to Trump, Lula is directly challenging the factual basis of the US justification. He referred to the US president as ’my friend’ in his remarks, according to VEJA, signalling a desire to keep dialogue open even as tensions rise.

For investors, the deforestation argument is more than rhetoric – it could determine whether the tariffs stay or go. If Brazil can prove its environmental record, it may weaken the case for the duties, but the US may have other economic motives that data alone cannot address.

For Brazilian exporters, a 25% US tariff on most goods is a direct hit to margins—steel, aircraft, processed foods, and manufactured goods face a surcharge that can price them out of a key market. The Amazon-deforestation justification is contentious because Brasília can point to a 36.87% drop in clearances, the lowest since 2016, which undercuts Washington’s stated rationale and suggests protectionist motives.

Investors face uncertainty over trade flows and diplomatic friction, as seen in the ambassador’s visa row. Brasília could negotiate bilaterally, escalate at the WTO, or impose reciprocal tariffs—though Lula’s immediate move is data, not retaliation, keeping de-escalation alive.

Lula to Send Trump Amazon Data in Tariff Spat

Beyond deforestation, the tariff package is part of a larger pattern of US trade pressure. Washington has also acted on other fronts: this week, the US revoked the visa of Brazil’s ambassador in Washington, a move G1 reports was a response to Brazil’s delay in approving Trump’s ambassador-designate to Brasília, Daniel Perez.

This diplomatic friction adds another layer to the economic conflict, making it harder to separate trade from politics.

For Latin American markets, the Brazil-US dispute is a reminder of how tariff decisions in Washington can ripple across the region. Brazilian exporters face higher costs, which could slow growth in key sectors like manufacturing and agriculture.

At the same time, Lula’s strategy of using data to counter the narrative offers a potential path to de-escalation, but it is untested. If the tariffs persist, Brazilian companies will need to adapt, and investors should watch for signs of retaliation, which Lula has not yet announced.

The stakes are high: the US is a major market for Brazilian goods, and any sustained tariff could reshape trade relations for years.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the current US tariff on Brazilian goods? The US imposed a 25% tariff on most Brazilian imports in July 2026, with exceptions for some products such as beef and coffee. The rate applies broadly, affecting a wide range of sectors. How is deforestation linked to the tariffs? Washington cited illegal deforestation in the Amazon as one reason for the tariffs. Lula is challenging this by sending Inpe data showing a 36.87% drop in deforestation from August 2025 to July 2026, the lowest since 2016. Why did the US revoke Brazil’s ambassador’s visa? The US revoked the visa of Brazil’s ambassador in Washington as a response to Brazil’s delay in approving Trump’s ambassador-designate to Brasília, Daniel Perez, according to G1. This has added to diplomatic tensions between the two countries. Is Lula planning to retaliate against the US tariffs? As of August 2026, Lula has not announced immediate retaliation. Instead, he is focusing on rebutting the US justification by sending deforestation data, though the dispute remains unresolved.

Sources: Presidência da República (Planalto); Reuters; G1.

World.title: Panama Canal Deepens Draft to 48 Feet, Boosting Cargo Limits
World.content:
Latin America · Trade

Key Facts Draft increase — maximum authorised draft rises to 48.0 feet (14.63 meters) from August 26, 2026.

— maximum authorised draft rises to 48.0 feet (14.63 meters) from August 26, 2026. Further rise — draft climbs to 48.5 feet (14.78 meters) from September 3, 2026.

— draft climbs to 48.5 feet (14.78 meters) from September 3, 2026. Lake recovery — Gatun Lake levels have recovered after severe drought, enabling deeper transits.

— Gatun Lake levels have recovered after severe drought, enabling deeper transits. No transit cut — ACP confirms daily transit numbers remain unchanged.

— ACP confirms daily transit numbers remain unchanged. Cargo boost — deeper draft allows Neopanamax ships to carry more containers or gas.

— deeper draft allows Neopanamax ships to carry more containers or gas. Regional impact — lower freight costs and improved reliability for Latin American exporters.

The Panama Canal Authority is raising the maximum draft for Neopanamax locks from August 26, easing drought-era restrictions and allowing ships to carry more cargo.

If you’re shipping goods through Latin America, the Panama Canal draft increase is about to let bigger ships through again. On August 26, the Panama Canal Authority (ACP) will raise the maximum authorised draft for Neopanamax locks to 48.0 feet (14.63 meters), followed by a further rise to 48.5 feet (14.78 meters) on September 3.

For exporters and shippers, this means more cargo per vessel, lower freight costs per container, and a welcome easing of the drought-driven restrictions that have squeezed regional trade for months. Draft is the depth of water a ship needs to float — the deeper the draft, the heavier the load.

After a punishing El Niño-driven drought that forced the ACP to cut vessel numbers and draft limits last year, Gatun Lake’s recovery now allows the canal to return to near-normal operations. The ACP said the adjustment reflects current water levels and projected conditions, and it has confirmed the number of daily transits will not be reduced.

A ship transits the Panama Canal’s locks, where the maximum draft has been raised to 48 feet. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)
