World.title: Netanyahu bluntly rejects Trump’s Gaza plan to disarm Hamas
World.content:
WorldMiddle EastIsraeli-Palestinian conflict Netanyahu bluntly rejects Trump’s Gaza plan to disarm Hamas Dan Williams and Fares Akram August 10, 2026 — 5:56am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Jerusalem: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu rejected a proposal by US-backed mediators for disarming Hamas, hardening his position after voicing misgivings at the suggestion that Israel reciprocate with phased withdrawal from Gaza. “Israel does not accept the 15-point document,” Netanyahu told his weekly cabinet meeting on Sunday (Israel time), according to an official translation. In his original remarks, he used a Hebrew verb that could be understood as “Israel rejects” or “rules out”. “The IDF will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is genuinely disarmed, and it will continue to thwart threats against our forces and citizens,” Netanyahu added, referring to the Israel Defence Forces. He was responding to a “roadmap” published last month by the Board of Peace, an international consortium set up to implement US President Donald Trump’s postwar vision for the ravaged Palestinian territory. The president has lauded the roadmap as an “historic agreement” and “a major milestone”.



There was no immediate White House comment on Netanyahu’s statement. Hamas has given only a hedged consent to the roadmap, saying it would hand over heavy weapons to a proposed new Gaza administration and conditioning this on Israeli withdrawals and the creation of a Palestinian state. The roadmap speaks of the new administration empowering individual Palestinians to keep their small arms. US President Donald Trump at the Trump National Golf Club in New Jersey on Sunday. Getty Images Trump’s original plan envisaged Israeli troops and tanks leaving the Gaza Strip entirely, and discussions of eventual statehood – while casting these as end results of a complete demilitarisation and post-Hamas stabilisation of the territory. The Board of Peace sounded circumspect about Netanyahu’s remarks, describing the road map as its deal with Hamas, rather than with Israel – and the timeline as protracted.



“Nobody is required to do anything, last of all lsrael, before we actually have verified steps on the ground” by the Palestinian cadres, the board’s top envoy, Nickolay Mladenov, told Israel’s Channel 12 television. While predicting that decommissioning Hamas tunnels – another requirement of Trump’s plan – may take years, Mladenov said that with each eventual success in clearing a sector of territory “Israel is required to move back, progressively, step by step, in stages, ultimately to the fence of Gaza”. A Palestinian woman walks along tents at a makeshift camp for displaced people in Deir al-Balah, central Gaza Strip, last week. AP Photo/Abdel Kareem Hana The initial, ceasefire phase of the Trump plan was clinched in October. There’s been little diplomatic progress since, and the Israeli army has advanced beyond armistice lines against a shrinking Hamas fiefdom where some 2 million Palestinians are crammed. Israel launched the war in response to an October 2023 invasion by Hamas that blindsided Netanyahu’s religious-rightist government. Three years on, Netanyahu is hoping for re-election in October. With Hamas still undefeated, he has pointed to Israel’s continued grip on Gaza as a lesser victory.



Far-right ministers in Netanyahu’s coalition have been upset by the roadmap. One of them, Orit Strock, called it a “bloodshed map” in a radio interview before Sunday’s cabinet meeting. Following Netanyahu’s remarks, her party’s leader, Bezalel Smotrich, praised the prime minister for issuing the “clarification”. Related Article Updated

Israeli-Palestinian conflict ‘Monumental step’: Hamas to disarm under deal for Gaza to get new government Hamas, which is blacklisted as a terrorist group in the West, said it was committed to the roadmap and accused Netanyahu of “obstructing the process for domestic, political and electoral reasons”. “We expect the mediators and the US guarantor to exert pressure on Netanyahu and his government to compel him to abide by the roadmap,” Hamas negotiator Bassem Naim said in a statement. A surge of Israeli air strikes in July that targeted Hamas commanders – which also killed dozens of civilians – has ceased since August 3, a tacit sign that Netanyahu heeded Mladenov’s calls not to endanger the diplomacy.



A source familiar with Israel’s position said it had agreed that the military would only act against what it perceives as immediate threats in Gaza and no longer carry out targeted assassinations as it had been doing on a near-daily basis, Reuters reported. Related Article Middle East at war ‘Middle of the game’: Iran renews list of demands around Strait of Hormuz In another signal of potential progress, the Board of Peace on Saturday said it brought together experts to plan temporary housing for displaced Palestinians, an interim measure before the permanent reconstruction that Mladenov has said would require Hamas to disarm first. Separately, Netanyahu’s office said work was underway on a new tent city, funded by the United Arab Emirates, in an area that the IDF had cleared of Hamas and weaponry. World.title: Rewritten mental health report scrubs critical findings, doubles progress
World.content:
An independent report that found just 54 of the government’s 270 promised mental health reforms had been completed was reworked ahead of its publication to credit it with doubling progress on royal commission recommendations. The Mental Health and Wellbeing Commission’s original report also had its judging criteria changed, its ratings improved, and its most critical findings removed in the months after it was first presented to the government. The delayed release and reworking of the report has drawn criticism over the stalled overhaul of the sector following the royal commission and raised concerns that the government is undermining the independence of bodies meant to hold it to account. Even the original report’s author, former Commissioner Annabel Brebner, cast doubt over the credibility of the re-worked findings.



“The initial method emphasised transparency of reporting of progress in implementing the recommendations, and the categories used to assess progress reflected this,” she said in a short statement. “In my view, the difference in methodology raises questions about the overall reliability and validity of the assessments made.” Brebner added she had not contacted the MHWC or sought and explanation on why the report’s content had altered so dramatically. The commission’s long-awaited status update into Victoria’s mental health reforms was presented to the government in December 2025. However, it was not published until June 24, 2026, and, during the six-month delay, at least 75 of the independent commissioners’ original 270 status ratings were improved.



A leaked draft of the commissioners’ original report, which was sent to the Department of Health and some key stakeholders, reveals huge changes were made to the MHWC’s assessments to favour the government’s position. Many of the strongest concerns raised in the original draft – including the impact of budget cuts, a lack of evidence to support government claims and the refusal of stakeholders to work with the Department of Health – are also missing from the publicly released version in June. In one example, four of the five sub-recommendations relating to Aboriginal social and emotional wellbeing reforms have been upgraded from “partial progress” in December, to “in place” in July, while the sentence “the 2025-26 Budget did not include funding for further development of these initiatives” was cut from its findings. By the time the report was released the commissioners who wrote the original version had been removed from their positions by an act of parliament, and an interim commissioner, appointed directly by Minister for Mental Health Ingrid Stitt, had overseen its redrafting and public release.



Three senior mental health figures familiar with the report’s delay refused to discuss the circumstances of its rewriting on the record, fearing reprisals from the government and further financial cuts to vital services. Related Article Exclusive

Mental health Mental health watchdog muzzled by ‘drastic’ budget cuts “We have essentially lost independent oversight of the royal commission,” one source said. Another accused the government of undermining the commission’s ability to monitor the failing sector, including slashing its 2025-26 budget to 40 per cent below its forecast expenses, cutting its staff from 54 to 27, and hobbling its independence. “The royal commission’s findings were not just about new services, but about improved system governance, outcomes, and culture,” they said.



“To have such a governance body be defunded and demoted before an election, and information withheld by bureaucrats until the minister’s appointee is in control, shows that not much has actually changed on that front, if not getting worse.” It follows revelations in July that a 33-page CFA report, which gave a blunt assessment of the shortcomings in the state’s firefighting capability, was whitewashed after talks with the state government and cut back to 18 pages. An Instagram post from the Mental Health and Wellbeing Commission on April 28, 2026 - the day an act of parliament eliminated the role of the commissioners, and the day the Department of Health provided new information to allow for the redrafting of their independent evaluation of the government’s mental health system overhauls. The MHWC was established in 2022 to independently monitor and report annually on the Victorian government’s progress of implementing the mental health royal commission’s recommendations. It was headed by four commissioners, including two with lived experience. Work on its latest report was led by Brebner during 2025 before being reviewed by the watchdog’s full team of commissioners and the CEO.



The commission briefed the Department of Health about its findings in November 2025, and asked for a government response so it could be included in the document before its potential publication in December or January. Related Article Exclusive

Mental health ‘Serious step backwards’: Furious response from mental health sector to cost-cutting bill Two sources familiar with those discussions said Brebner and her team grew frustrated at the government’s refusal to provide a response,and agitated to release the report without one, but were blocked by the then commission chair Maggie Toko. On December 4, 2025, the government introduced to parliament a controversial bill to overhaul the commission’s leadership and limit it’s investigative remit - in contravention of the royal commission’s recommendation - paving the way to replace the four independent commissioners with a single commissioner. A fortnight later, on December 16, the MHWC report was sent to staff and key stakeholders to brief them ahead of a possible January release, which was then repeatedly delayed.



Brebner, fellow commissioners and MHWC staff continued to push for the report’s release up to April 27, when the legislative changes came into effect and their positions were eliminated. Toko was appointed interim Mental Health and Wellbeing Commissioner by Stitt. Footnotes in the published report show that just one day later the Department of Health provided the MHWC with a raft of “authorised information”, allowing for the document’s redrafting. Some of those familiar the original MHWC’s original independent assessments said they were shocked at the extent of changes when the implementation status update was finally released on June 24. A comparison of the documents shows while the original report assigned five possible status ratings for progress on each of the royal commission’s 270 sub-recommendations, the published report cut that to just three.



That included the removal of a category titled “limited evidence of progress available publicly”, which had been assigned to 32 cases where no evidence of work being undertaken, other than press releases and other announcements, could be found. Another rating category, “to be assessed later”, was also deleted. It had been given to 26 sub-recommendations in the original report, where the commissioners deemed new programs were too fresh to be assessed in a meaningful way. The changes left three wider ratings remaining - Not Yet Commenced; Partial Progress; and In Place - and saw at least 75 grades from the original report improved in the one published June. Transparency International Australia chief executive Clancy Moore said the commission had been established to hold government and service providers to account. “The claims that the government re-wrote and delayed a critical report assessing the government’s performance on mental health is a blow for transparency and accountability,” he said.



“Under the legislation the commission is meant to act as an independent body. This means being free from government interference.” “Good government requires independent advice, scrutiny, and accountability. Yet the Labor government has long engaged in the politicisation of the public service, and independent bodies like the commission, which only weakens democracy.” When asked why its assessments changed, the MHWC told The Age that its December 2025 version was “an early, incomplete draft” that had “gaps or inaccuracies” because it had not been provided with departmental information, and was not approved for release at that stage. It said the report was updated when the department’s response was provided, and this information “informed, but did not determine” its findings.



“At the halfway point of the 10-year mental health reform agenda, the commission sought to highlight both – the progress to date in delivering on recommendations since the royal commission, as well as to highlight the important work still ahead, with detail, accuracy and balance,” Interim Commissioner Maggie Toko said. “It is important that the commission’s reporting provide the community and all stakeholders with an accurate and comprehensive view on the status of the implementation of the recommendations for mental health reform, that conveys the progress to date, and a sense of optimism and continued commitment towards the ongoing work in improving outcomes into the future.” The Department of Health said it had been provided with a draft of the MHWC’s report at the end of 2025, and provided “factual and technical feedback” between December 2025 and May 2026 to ensure it had up-to-date information. “The MHWC is an independent statutory authority – it is responsible for its own reports, findings and assessments, including decisions about content and publication dates,” a department spokesperson said. World.title: Australia news LIVE: Frydenberg reveals he will not appear before royal commission; Coalition accuses Labor of funding ‘ghettoisation’ of migrant communities
World.content:
One Nation leader Pauline Hanson has blamed rising rents and low wages on Labor’s migration policies in a sweeping attack on Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke, as she accuses the government of planning to bring in an additional million migrants over the next four years.

“Tony Burke isn’t cutting migration ... Labor is lying again. And here’s the worst part. You can’t even trust them to stop at a million. This weak government has never once hit a migration target it set. Not once, in four years,” Hanson wrote in a post to X this morning.

The sledge comes a week after Burke delayed a speech outlining the government’s migration overhaul amid a dispute in cabinet. Hanson said the minister was planning to announce “another million people” migrating to the country.

“They already brought in 1.5 million in four years. That’s why your rent exploded, your pay went backwards, and your kids can’t buy a home. It’s why hospitals are turning away sick people.”

After abruptly delaying the announcement of a migration overhaul last week, Burke is expected to provide more detail in coming days, on a package of new measures to cut the net overseas migration intake to its budget forecast of 225,000 per year.

Nine months after the Bondi massacre enlivened debate over social cohesion, Labor is toying with proposals to rework the skills program to better serve the economy, put stricter rules on working holidaymakers and family reunion visas, and cut work rights from visa overstayers. Polls suggest there is support among voters for tighter controls on migration.

World.title: ‘Shocking’: Body of woman stuffed in suitcase found after ‘weekend drive’, police say
World.content:
A body, believed to be that of a woman, has been found in a “state of decomposition” inside a suitcase near Goulburn in NSW’s Southern Tablelands, police say. Two men on a weekend drive had stopped on the side of Wolgon Road at Oallen, about 60 kilometres south of Goulburn, when they made the “shocking discovery” on Sunday afternoon, according to Hume District Commander Linda Bradbury. The body was found in a suitcase under a pine tree on the fringes of dense bushland, metres from the road, triggering the call to emergency services just before 1pm on Sunday. The body was found on Wolgon Road, south of Goulburn. Google StreetView The body is yet to be formally identified, and it is unclear how long the body had been there.



Officers have established a crime scene under Strike Force Bryton and have seized the suitcase for further examination. The State Crime Command’s Homicide Squad has been sent to Goulburn to assist the investigation. Forensic teams placed evidence markers and photographed the crime scene on Sunday night. Detectives conducted preliminary investigations at the scene, including an initial review of the body, aided by forensics officers. The body was removed from the scene late on Sunday. Bradbury said Wolgon Road was not a heavy route for traffic but was “travelled frequently”. She said the body was in a “state of decomposition”. “Forensic examination is under way to assist us in identifying how long that suitcase has been there,” Bradbury told ABC 702 radio on Monday morning.



“There’s very little we know at this point in time. The investigation is in the early stages, and we really are relying on forensic evidence to tell us a bit more.” Detectives will return to the crime scene on Monday, where they will canvass the road and surrounding bushland for any further evidence or information to assist with the investigation. Police are working to match the remains with any outstanding missing persons on record. Goulburn is 194 kilometres south-west of Sydney via the Hume Highway.

World.content:

Despite a “clunky start”, Kyle Sandilands’ new digital radio show, Kyle Sandilands Live made its debut on Monday morning, with guests including NSW Premier Chris Minns and celebrity psychic John Edwards. “It is live. We’re going to lose all audio, all lights. Screens are going to shut down.”



But it wasn’t just tech causing problems. Within the first five minutes of the show, Sandilands introduced Jaimee “Mayo” Blazquez as his executive director, prompting Bouchet to refer to her using an expletive. Sandilands replied jokingly: “Bruno, I made it quite clear to the ensemble cast. This isn’t some potty-mouth all-boys’ club filth nest”. Celebrity psychic John Edwards joined via Zoom during the first 30 minutes of the show, though his feed was impeded by technical issues and different presenters’ microphones talking over him. Sandilands was able to, however, squeeze in a question about whether Edwards had witnessed “anyone giving themselves a fiddle” while travelling through the spirit world. NSW Premier Chris Minns was the show’s first live in-studio guest, with Sandilands recalling recently running into Minns in the Blue Mountains and mistaking him for a “meth head”.



“You know what I like about you?” Sandilands said, after the pair shared a laugh. “People on all sides of politics – Labor, Liberals, One Nation types, the Nationals … you don’t seem very Labor.” Minns replied: “Well, we try and be common sense”. Sandilands’ only political question to the premier was whether he would get rid of e-bikes, or Lime bikes, after he revealed he had gifted one to his 11-year-old son, which had made him start “behaving” by getting him out of the house. Six months ago, the Minns Government announced a crackdown on e-bikes allowing police to seize and crush illegally modified e-bikes.



“When there’s a new technology, like anything, there are people that take it too far,” Minns replied, talking about how rules evolved with use of the technology. Minns then cut a golden ribbon to commemorate the occasion before leaving. Earlier in the show, Sandilands said there would also be a potential call-in from One Nation leader Pauline Hanson, and joked about having Prime Minister Anthony Albanese on as well. Despite costing $99.99 a year – with an upfront payment being the only payment method available – Sandilands said the show is not running s “because of the female militant activist group, the Mad F------ Witches”. “They tried to threaten all the clients. We’ll work around them. We’ll go straight to the consumer’,” Sandilands said.



And the first song aired? Josh Fawaz’s controversial AI-cover of Madonna’s Like A Prayer.
